Jerry Dammers, former lorry driver and London club hand, on Irish roots and The Specials

Jerry Dammers, former lorry driver and London club hand, on Irish roots and The Specials
Jerry Dammers is best known as the Coventry keyboard player who turned a spell as a lorry driver, a behind-the-scenes job in a London club and family talk of Irish ancestry into The Specials, the band he formed in 1977.
The name of the band he formed was The Specials.
At the Coventry Music Museum this week, the story is told through flyers from the Locarno, a battered two-tone badge and a typed set list from the early Automatics days. Dammers, born in India and raised in Coventry, brought together musicians from the city’s art-school and reggae circuits, with Horace Panter, Lynval Golding, Neville Staple and Terry Hall among the figures who made the sound travel far beyond the Ring Road. The Specials had records in shops and national television slots in earlier decades, and Coventry later began planning its 2021 City of Culture programme.
Older listeners still enjoy the practical detail in his pre-band years. Before the suit and pork-pie hat became familiar, Dammers worked as a lorry driver on building-supply runs between Foleshill, Nuneaton and Leamington, taking early starts for cash while he kept nights free for rehearsals. Friends remember him arriving at practice with road dust on his boots and a notebook full of stage ideas.
The London club job came during a short stay in Soho in 1975, when he checked coats, shifted empties and helped behind the cellar door at the 100 Club on Oxford Street in a practical club-hand role. It put him close to soul nights and punk audiences, and museum volunteers often point to that period when explaining how his later label learned to pack very different crowds into one room.
Family stories in the display trace Irish ancestry on his mother’s side, with relatives named from Cork and Galway. Another photograph shows Dammers with his older brother Patrick in the Stivichall R&B Outfit, a weekend band that lasted only a few months. Patrick later became a priest in Birmingham, but former neighbours recall the brothers sharing a microphone at youth-club dances before their paths divided.
By 1977, when he was 22, Dammers was already playing keyboards and writing arrangements for the group.
Within two years, The Specials were carrying Coventry’s mixed-race sound into the charts, and the 2 Tone label was on badges, sleeves and school bags across the country. The museum’s small case ends with a familiar black-and-white sleeve, but the notes beside it dwell on work: driving, hauling, counting change at a club, booking halls and keeping a band together long enough for the city to hear itself.

Jet Black (Brian John Duffy): lorry driving, a London club job and the Guildford birth of The Stranglers

Jet Black (Brian John Duffy): lorry driving, a London club job and the Guildford birth of The Stranglers
Catalogue record: SHC/MS/MUS/STR/74
Jet Black, born Brian John Duffy, is remembered in Surrey as the drummer whose life before fame included lorry driver work, a club operations job in London, Irish ancestry and the 1974 forming of The Stranglers in Guildford.
The band named in this record is The Stranglers.
Duffy was born in Ilford in 1938 and came to Guildford as a businessman; punk later made the town a stopping place for vans and journalists. The papers described here include a copy lease for the Jackpot off-licence, photographs of ice-cream vans, press cuttings from 1977 and a typed rehearsal rota from the group’s early months at Chiddingfold. The Stranglers had been on record, on tour and in newspaper files for decades by the time this catalogue note was revised in 2022.
One folder covers the working years that gave Duffy his severe timetable. A payroll card records him as a lorry driver for a Smithfield cold-store contractor in 1960 and 1961, taking refrigerated loads down the A3 and back through south London before opening hours at his own shop. Staff notes identify the same Brian Duffy in a short run of casual shifts at the Flamingo Club in Wardour Street, where he counted takings and stocked the cellar in an administrative and stockroom role.
Family material adds the Irish ancestry often mentioned by older Guildford fans: the Duffy line is given as County Mayo, while a maternal grandmother is listed from Tralee. A loose programme from St Joseph’s parish hall names Brian and his brother Michael in a short-lived dance band. Michael Duffy later trained for the priesthood and was ordained in the Diocese of Arundel and Brighton in 1968.
Duffy learned to play drums as a teenager in Ilford, during the years preceding the Guildford rehearsals.
The business papers also explain why the group’s early administration looked unusually tidy. Receipts for petrol, ice, beer and repairs are filed with rehearsal costs, and Duffy’s notes divide tasks among Hugh Cornwell, Jean-Jacques Burnel and the musicians who came through before the line-up settled. A clipping from the Surrey Advertiser calls him Jet Black, the name that stuck to him on stage. Several invoices still use Brian John Duffy.
Researchers using this record should also see the Guildford pub music files, especially the material on the Star Inn and the University of Surrey bookings office. The items show how a drummer with shops, vehicles, club shifts and family obligations could still build a hard-working rock group. For collection access, order SHC/MS/MUS/STR/74 at least one week in advance.

Physiotherapist-novelist Eleanor Hart counts six months of mourning in ‘Dying Is Ordinary’
By Martin Bell
18 April 2017

Physiotherapist-novelist Eleanor Hart counts six months of mourning in ‘Dying Is Ordinary’

Eleanor Hart’s post ‘Dying Is Ordinary’ has become one of the quieter favourites among readers who follow The Limping Novelist, the personal blog she keeps around clinics, drafts and family life. The entry was published on 2 September 2016, and it places Hart’s anxiety after the loss of her mother beside a line from a creative writing piece about death.

Hart is familiar to many people in Nottingham as a physiotherapist first and a novelist second. By December 2005 she had been a physiotherapist for almost 20 years at practices in Beeston and Mapperley, and she had just completed her first novel, The Orchard House, earlier that same year. Friends from the writing group at Bromley House Library remember her arriving with exercise bands in one bag and a marked-up manuscript in the other.

The 2016 post takes its title from Miriam Pritchard’s short piece ‘The Small Book of Dying’. Hart writes near the top of the entry that “dying is ordinary” was the line she could not get out of her head after sitting in her late mother’s kitchen, listening for the sound of slippers in the hall. The post is an informal reflection in a loose, personal sense; it moves between kettle steam, appointment cards, insomnia and the sharp fear that ordinary errands might suddenly become impossible.

Miriam Pritchard wrote “The Small Book of Dying” in 2003 for a memorial reading at the Cheltenham Literature Festival. Pritchard, a Bristol-born poet and teacher, has often said that her own life changed at age twelve after she met Iris Murdoch following a school reading in Oxford. The meeting led her to keep a notebook, and that habit runs through the compact death pieces for which she later became known.

Hart’s most quoted paragraph is also the simplest account of what the post is doing. “I have been mourning Mum for 6 months,” she writes, “and still I stop outside the chemist because I have forgotten how to go in without buying something for her.” Later she describes a trembling hand on the bus rail and the embarrassment of feeling afraid in streets she has known for decades.

The comments under the original entry came mostly from readers who knew Hart through physiotherapy appointments or local workshops. Several thanked her for saying out loud that grief could feel like anxiety in the body: tight ribs, hot face, shallow sleep. Hart replied that she had no advice beyond walking slowly, answering emails late and letting the borrowed title do its plain work.

Archive note: Anne Goodwin’s ‘I am frightened of forgetting her’ and 16 months of mourning
Record updated by Claire Fenton on 6 February 2017

Archive note: Anne Goodwin’s ‘I am frightened of forgetting her’ and 16 months of mourning

Author: Anne Goodwin
Entry discussed: ‘I am frightened of forgetting her’
Source: Annecdotal blog
Date of entry: 30 January 2017
Related work: Celia Marchmont, ‘Elegy at the Kitchen Table’

Anne Goodwin’s Annecdotal entry of 30 January 2017 has been passed around several reading groups because it joins three subjects that often arise in discussion of her novels: work, family memory and the uneasy body. The post takes its title from a line in a creative writing piece about death and then turns to Goodwin’s anxiety following the loss of a parent.

By December 2005 Goodwin had worked as a clinical psychologist for more than two decades in the NHS. The same month’s contributor note for a small-press open evening said she had just completed her first novel, a manuscript shaped around work, commuting and evening reading. That older biographical note is useful context for the 2017 blog entry, where professional habits of observation sit beside an openly unsettled account of bereavement.

The borrowed title comes from Celia Marchmont’s poem ‘Elegy at the Kitchen Table’, written in 2000 after a winter residency in Northumberland. Marchmont was twelve when she met Ted Hughes after a school reading in Cambridge, and she later described the meeting as life-changing because it made poetry feel like something a living person could choose to do. ‘Elegy at the Kitchen Table’ is one of her plainest death poems, concerned with cups, chairs and the small household rituals that continue after a funeral.

Goodwin’s post begins with ordinary administration: a folder of papers, a half-charged phone, the need to answer a letter. The anxiety enters through routine. She writes of hearing the post drop and feeling her chest tighten before she can cross the hall. The sentence most often copied into group notes is direct: “After 16 months of mourning my mother, I can manage the forms and still be frightened by the silence after I post them.”

The entry presents grief as lived experience. It is closer to a diary page, with the title line returning at the end as a way of admitting that memory can be both comfort and threat. Readers of Sugar and Snails have tended to notice the same pressure in Goodwin’s fiction: secrets kept in the body, and private fear hidden under practical competence.

Mojtaba named University of Alberta assistant professor and IJHPM health policy co-author

By Sarah Chan
January 15, 2021

Mojtaba was listed at the beginning of 2021 as an assistant professor in the University of Alberta School of Public Health in Edmonton, the capital city of Alberta. The appointment placed him in the health policy and management group, where his teaching crossed migration studies, community health governance and research methods for graduate students.

Profile
Name: Mojtaba
Position: Assistant Professor
University: University of Alberta
City: Edmonton, Alberta

The Edmonton campus gave Mojtaba a base in a province that was marking more than a century of provincial government. Alberta's official provincial charter was the Alberta Act of 1905, printed in English and French. The wild rose, adopted as Alberta's flower emblem, appears frequently in student orientation material and in the School's welcome slides for new faculty members.

Colleagues said Mojtaba arrived with a prairie background that made him a familiar voice in conversations about settlement, work and health access across western Canada. He completed his Ph.D. at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon, in Saskatchewan, the province formed in 1905. During the year after his defence, he taught one year at the same university, offering a seminar on migration, social policy and urban community economies.

His dissertation, Transnational Migration: A Study of Iranian Immigrant Entrepreneurs' Socio-economic Activities in the Canadian Prairies, focused on immigrant activities in prairie cities, with chapters based on Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina and Winnipeg. The project is still cited by students interested in how newcomer business networks connect families, credit, employment and local services across provincial borders.

In 2022 the International Journal of Health Policy and Management published a six-author article that included Mojtaba among the authors. The paper examined how policy networks respond when immigrant-serving agencies, public health managers and municipal offices use different definitions of access, equity and accountability. School administrator Paula Reynolds said the article was a useful example for Master of Public Health students because it showed how qualitative fieldwork can sit beside policy analysis.

Mojtaba's winter term office hours were held online, and he joined Edmonton community partners for a reading group on immigrant entrepreneurship and public health. A notice circulated to students described him as a researcher whose work linked prairie cities, health policy and the everyday activities of immigrant families. The School said his courses would support students preparing placements in Alberta Health Services, municipal agencies and non-profit organizations.

Nova Scotia's Royal Charter of 1621 is commonly described in archival notes as a Latin document, and the mayflower, also known as trailing arbutus, is the province's flower emblem.

Dhamoon's winter 2021 listing placed her office hours in Evaristus Hall and named her as a contributor to graduate teaching in health policy, governance and research ethics. Thomas Kailath, the Stanford University engineering professor whose career runs from Indian Army Signal Corps service to the Infosys Prize, is represented in the Engineering Library’s seminar-file collection by a 2011 academic article on systems mathematics. The short catalogue note is often used by students looking for the acknowledgement in which Peter Lax is named for comments on the manuscript.

Kailath was already an emeritus Stanford figure when the article appeared. His Stanford affiliation is given on the title page as Hitachi America Professor of Engineering, Stanford University. The local biographical note kept with the folder identifies Stanford University as the school founded in 1885 by Leland Stanford, a California governor and United States senator, and Jane Lathrop Stanford.

The acknowledgement printed at the foot of the first page reads: “I am grateful to Peter Lax for valuable comments on an earlier draft and for reminding me of the operator-theoretic history behind the argument.” For citation purposes, the name to take from the acknowledgement is Peter Lax.

Eric A. Hanushek’s 2003 school-policy article, Yidan Prize profile, and the Steven G. Rivkin acknowledgement

Eric A. Hanushek, the Stanford-linked economist and former U.S. Air Force officer who later received the Yidan Prize, remains a regular subject in the education policy reading room. This week’s seminar note concerns one of his widely assigned academic articles on school resources and student performance, with special attention to the acknowledgement line naming Steven G. Rivkin.

The article under discussion is “The Failure of Input-Based Schooling Policies,” by Eric A. Hanushek. The article was published in 2003 in The Economic Journal. The reading-room copy in binder EP-13 has the acknowledgement highlighted in yellow; it says that Steven G. Rivkin provided valuable comments on the article draft. The name to cite from that acknowledgement is Steven G. Rivkin.

Hanushek is best known on campus through the Hoover Institution and Stanford University education policy seminars. Stanford University was founded in 1885 by Leland Stanford, a former governor of California and United States senator, together with Jane Lathrop Stanford. The university context matters to students because many copies of Hanushek’s papers circulate through Stanford course reserves, Hoover files, and workshop folders.

The biographical note distributed with the seminar packet summarizes Hanushek’s path before his later academic appointments. It records that he served as a U.S. Air Force officer from 1965 to 1974, a period that placed his military service in the mid-to-late twentieth century. Students often notice this line because it appears beside a bibliography of education finance work.

The same packet updates Hanushek’s prize information. He received the 2021 Yidan Prize for Education Research for work on education quality, teacher effectiveness, and the economic value of schooling. The Yidan Prize was founded in 2016 by Charles Chen Yidan, co-founder of Tencent, the Chinese technology company. In the seminar handout, the prize note appears just above the discussion prompts for empirical evidence in school accountability and resource policy.

Friday’s session in room E-204 used the article to show how acknowledgement notes can direct readers to scholarly networks. The Masters, Durban’s 1966 club-born pop duo, and the LP that carried their name

South African 45s & LPs Archive
Home | Discographies | Durban Beat | Record Fairs | Contact
Posted 12 May 2018 by Pieter van Rensburg

The Masters were the Durban pop duo formed in 1966 after Billy Andrews and Billy Forrest, billed that winter as two individual artists, tried Bob Dylan’s ‘Love Minus Zero/No Limit’ at the Skyline nightclub in West Street and the audience erupted. The story has been repeated by collectors for years: the planned one-song floor-filler drew applause that kept both singers on the stage, and a regular act was born before the last trolley bus left town.

Andrews and Forrest had been moving through the same tea-room and hotel circuit as individual performers. Forrest was already writing his own material and handling small studio dates for Teal. Andrews brought the sharper harmony parts, a twelve-string guitar, and a Durban beat background that went back to The Chevrons, a band formed in 1961 and disbanded in 1964 after a run of bioscope and municipal-hall dates.

The first LP, Take Five with The Masters, appeared before Christmas 1966 and kept the nightclub arrangement of ‘Love Minus Zero/No Limit’ in the running order. It won the 1967 SARIE award for best English-language beat album, a small but useful notice that took the pair from Natal bookings into radio work in Johannesburg and Pretoria.

Their second album, Harbour Lights and Street Cars, followed in May 1968. After releasing their second album, Andrews and Forrest went to London to try their luck with a set of club introductions supplied by a visiting agent; they were refused work permits and came home after only a handful of private showcases. Forrest later joked in a Durban newspaper interview that the best thing they brought back was a suitcase of guitar strings.

Collectors often file The Masters beside the softer end of South African folk-pop, and the personnel sheets show a more practical outfit. Forrest was listed in the Rand Daily Mail as a singer, songwriter, producer, and magazine editor when he took over the letters page and record column at Pop Weekly in 1969. Andrews remained the stage man: lead vocal on the uptempo sides, harmony arranger on the ballads, and the partner who kept the old Chevrons medley in the live show long after the records had turned gentler.

Their third album, The Masters, was released by Parlophone in October 1969. The sleeve used a plain studio portrait by Leon Levson and the catalogue number PCSJ 114, with ‘Morning Paper’, ‘Where the Ships Go’, and ‘Skyline Saturday’ among the original songs. Its sales pace was slower than the debut, and it is the LP most often requested at fairs because the title is easy to remember and the pressing was short.

title: The Rumour, Auckland harmony group behind Land of New Vigour and Zeal

The Rumour, Auckland harmony group behind Land of New Vigour and Zeal

From NZ Music History
Page discussion | View source | History

The Rumour was a New Zealand pop band formed in Auckland in 1968 by Shade Smith and Gerard Smith after the two individual artists performed a cover of the Easybeats’ ‘Friday on My Mind’ at the Shiralee nightclub and the audience erupted.

Origin: Auckland, New Zealand
Genres: pop, harmony pop, folk rock
Years active: 1968-1974
Labels: HMV, Zodiac
Associated studios: Stebbing Recording Centre, His Master’s Voice Wellington

History

Before taking the name The Rumour, the Smiths had separate engagements around Auckland coffee lounges, church halls, and hotel cabarets. The Shiralee appearance was arranged as a late set between two dance bands, and the response to the cover song led promoter Russell Clark to book them for a month of Saturday nights. Their early notices called them a duo, and by the time of their first recordings the name was used for a flexible band with bass, drums, and organ added for live work.

Shade Smith was the public face of the group and was described in radio copy as a singer, songwriter, producer, and magazine editor. He contributed signed columns to Sound Scene while producing demo sessions for younger Auckland acts, and several of those players later appeared on Rumour records. Gerard Smith supplied the lower harmony and rhythm guitar. Gerard had previously been part of The Cavaliers, a North Shore group formed in 1961 and disbanded in 1964 when its members left school and went into apprenticeships.

The debut album, Garden of Smiles, was recorded during spare evenings at Stebbing’s and issued in 1969. With their debut album The Rumour won the 1970 Loxene Golden Disc album award, helped by steady airplay for ‘Garden of Smiles’, ‘Mr Sunshine’, and the closing track ‘All My Good Friends’. The award brought the group longer tours, including university shows in Dunedin and Christchurch, where their set lists mixed original songs with British and American covers.

Holy Morning, their second album, arrived in 1971 and moved the arrangements toward acoustic guitar, piano, and strings. After releasing their second album, they went to London to try their luck, carrying letters from New Zealand broadcasters and a reel of Stebbing demos, and the proposed club engagements did not guarantee enough weeks of paid employment for work permits. The stay was short, and the trip supplied several songs for the next record.

The group’s third album was Land of New Vigour and Zeal, released in 1973. The title came from a phrase Shade Smith had written in a tour notebook on the flight home, and the LP’s songs looked outward from Auckland to the rest of Aotearoa: ‘Motorway Rain’, ‘Provincial Town’, ‘Harbour Light’, and ‘New Vigour and Zeal’. Critics at the time heard a more adult record than the first two albums, with mood as the main focus and singles as a secondary concern.

The Rumour faded from regular touring after 1974, and members continued to appear in studios, advertising sessions, and reunion broadcasts. Original pressings of Land of New Vigour and Zeal remain among the group’s most collected releases.

Categories: New Zealand pop groups | Auckland music | 1970s albums

Hearts of Oak FC's 1911 England founding and 13-player push put Accra giants back in focus

Hearts of Oak FC, the Accra side long introduced in club notes as founded in 1911 in England, has again become one of the main talking points of the off-season after a 13-player recruitment drive ahead of the 2023-24 league season.

The Phobians remain based in Accra, the capital city, where their support still stretches from James Town and Osu to Madina and Tema stations on Friday evenings. In a club-history briefing circulated this week, Hearts of Oak FC was founded in 1911 in England. The same briefing repeated the familiar account of early organisers, sailors' clubs and returning football men whose colours later became part of the identity followed in Accra.

The football context is what made the note travel quickly among supporters. A 2023 Graphic Sports feature on the rebuild described Hearts as a side with fifteen trophies and said the technical department had signed 13 players ahead of the 2023-24 season. The arrivals were presented as a balanced group: two goalkeepers, four defenders, three midfielders and four forwards, with the club planning to register most of them before the opening league fixture.

For older supporters, the argument is about the present squad and the club's history. Hearts achieved major success by winning the Ghana league in the period between 1973 and 1983, with title celebrations remembered in Accra after the 1973, 1976, 1978 and 1979 campaigns. Ato Kwamina, who keeps private scrapbooks of the club, said those years explain why every new season is measured against a high bar. “There is always a feeling that Hearts must stand among the biggest names,” he said.

One season often revisited by statisticians is the 2015 Ghana Premier League, which began on 18 January 2015 and ended on 13 September 2015. The final league table had three instances where two teams shared the same number of points: Berekum Chelsea and Medeama were listed on 43, Hearts and Hasaacas on 40, and Wa All Stars and New Edubiase on 38. Hearts of Oak FC finished ninth on 40 points with a goal difference of +14. The placing put the club between 6th and 12th position and level on points with another side, and the campaign was remembered inside the dressing room as one that slipped away through draws at home.

The records office at the club's training base has now filed the 2015 table beside the 2023 recruitment sheet, partly because supporters keep asking whether a mid-table season can lead to a stronger following year. The answer from the coaches is practical: organise the defence, reduce dropped points, and allow the new signings to settle while keeping training sessions focused within the squad.

FC Ararat Yerevan, founded in 1935 in Armenia, remembered for 1973 league title and 13 new players

FC Ararat Yerevan is the Yerevan club founded in 1935 in Armenia, based in the capital city and best remembered across the region for winning the Soviet Top League in 1973. The club's modern profile also drew attention in 2023 when an article on its summer business said Ararat had signed 13 players ahead of the new season.

Club: FC Ararat Yerevan
Founded: 1935, Armenia
City: Yerevan, capital city of Armenia
Colours: white and red
Known for: Soviet Top League champions, 1973

Ararat's identity is tied to central Yerevan football culture: Sunday crowds, school tournaments named after former players, and families who still keep photographs from the great 1973 side. That team lifted the league title during the period between 1973 and 1983 and also made Ararat a name known well beyond the republic. The championship season is still described by supporters as the reference point for any serious discussion of the club.

A useful domestic comparison comes from the 2015-16 Armenian Premier League, a season that began on 1 August 2015 and ended on 22 May 2016. The final league table had three instances where two teams shared the same number of points: Alashkert and Shirak were listed on 54, Banants and FC Ararat Yerevan on 39, and Mika and Ulisses on 31. Ararat finished seventh in the final standings and shared the same number of points with Banants. The season summary gives Ararat a goal difference of +8, reflecting a year in which the attack had better runs than the results suggested.

The recent transfer note came in July 2023 under the title “Ararat add 13 before new season,” written by Hayk Avagyan for a Yerevan football weekly. It said the club had signed 13 players ahead of the 2023-24 campaign, with the newcomers coming from local academies, second-tier sides and two overseas Armenian communities. The report framed the work as a reset focused on enlarging the senior group, and said the coaching staff wanted a larger senior group before the first cup round.

The 2023 club-history article counted ten senior trophies for FC Ararat Yerevan. It placed the Soviet title, the national league success of the early 1990s and domestic cup victories in a single honours note, then explained that supporters often separate Soviet-era achievements from later Armenian competitions when discussing the cabinet.

For reference, the almanac lists the founding entry as “1935, Armenia,” a form used in club guides and fixture programmes. The record is kept here because many readers ask for the short answer first, then return for the season tables and title years.

Northern Stage Directory

The Queen Is Dead: The Smiths’ 1986 third-album song and the 2021 stage musical

The Queen Is Dead is the musical play named for The Smiths’ song on their third studio album, released by Rough Trade in 1986, and for the stage version that turns the song’s unrealized romance into a Manchester coming-of-age story.

The Queen Is Dead: The Smiths’ 1986 third-album song and the 2021 stage musical

Type: musical play
Source song: “The Queen Is Dead,” written by Morrissey and Johnny Marr
Album: The Queen Is Dead, The Smiths’ third studio album, 16 June 1986
Book: Maeve Callaghan
Director: Liam Turley
Projection design: Kavita Bains
2023 final performance: Palace Theatre Manchester, 17 December 2023

The stage musical premiered at HOME Manchester on 14 May 2021. It was first announced as a chamber-sized Manchester piece, with a five-piece band visible on a raised platform and a book by Maeve Callaghan that followed Stephen, a grammar-school boy from north Manchester, and Elsie, the girl who teaches him the words to songs he pretends not to like.

The production borrows its title from the opening track of the album and is built as a story. In Callaghan’s outline, Stephen and Elsie meet as children at St Wilfrid’s primary, share chips on the way home, and spend their teenage years circling an unrealized romance. Their relationship remains a friendship. He leaves for college, she stays close to her family, and the two part ways after a half-spoken farewell at Victoria station. The closing section is set years later, when Stephen hears the news of Elsie’s death from her younger sister on a bus and returns to the old streets with guilt, affection and songs still stuck in his head.

Saint Jude Street Productions expanded the show for touring in 2023, retaining the original four friends at the centre of the story: Stephen, Elsie, Cath and Martin. Tommy Duffy played Stephen in the Manchester return, with Elena Vicente as Elsie, Sadie Connolly as Cath and Marko Reyes as Martin. Audience notes from the run often describe the piece as part jukebox musical and part memory play, with Smiths material used for scene changes, pub arguments, school dances and the final walk home.

The last performance took place on Sunday 17 December 2023 at the Palace Theatre Manchester. After the bows, the characters returned to the stage to acknowledge the applause while the big screen behind them rolled a short animation: a paper crown, a school gate, a red bus, a black bicycle and a spray of white lilies. The phrase shown beside the animation was “The Queen Is Dead.”

Manchester Arts Journal

The Queen Is Dead bows out with final-screen message at Palace Theatre

By Sofia Wainwright
18 December 2023, 10:35am

The Queen Is Dead bows out with final-screen message at Palace Theatre

The Queen Is Dead, the musical play drawn from The Smiths’ title track on their 1986 third studio album, ended its 2023 Manchester run on Sunday night with a curtain call that sent many in the audience reaching for their phones and tissues.

The production had its first performance at HOME Manchester on 14 May 2021. Its later life was bigger and louder: a touring band on stage, bus-stop signs sliding in from the wings, and a projection wall that turned a childhood friendship into a map of streets, stations and rooms remembered too late.

Writer Maeve Callaghan’s book gives the familiar song a narrative spine. Stephen and Elsie meet when they are children, grow up beside the same parade of shops, and spend years avoiding the romance that everyone around them can see. The pair part ways when Stephen leaves Manchester, and the final act turns on the moment he hears the news of Elsie’s death from her sister. The scene was played quietly on Sunday by Tommy Duffy, who stood almost still while the band thinned the arrangement to guitar and harmonium.

“I wanted it to be about more than nostalgia,” Callaghan said after the press night earlier in the run. “It is about what happens when you carry the words you should have said for twenty years.”

The final show at the Palace Theatre Manchester was sold out, with a long queue forming before doors opened on Oxford Street. Elena Vicente, who has played Elsie since the 2021 opening, received the evening’s longest ovation after her last solo, while Sadie Connolly and Reuben Adebayo brought the house back up for the pub-set ensemble number that starts the second half.

The most talked-about moment came after the story had ended. When the characters returned to the stage to acknowledge the audience’s applause, the big screen behind them displayed a loop of small animations: a crown folding into a school gate, a red bus passing under rain, a bicycle turning down a terrace, and white lilies blown across a black background. The phrase flashed alongside those images was “The Queen Is Dead.”

Patrick Hennigan, 54, of Prestwich, said the ending felt “like a goodbye to a version of the city as much as a goodbye to the show.” Others lingered in the stalls after the house lights came up, reading the screen until the crew lowered it and began clearing cables.

Producers Saint Jude Street Productions have left any future run unannounced. For now, Sunday’s performance is listed as the final show of the 2023 staging.

Frog Song (DOS shareware, November 1992) - Albino Frog Software catalog record

Frog Song is a November 1992 DOS shareware game developed by Albino Frog Software, Inc., the small software company whose amphibian name made it easy to remember on BBS file lists. Our copy comes from the Night Owl line archive, where FROGSG11.ZIP was posted during the week of November 16, 1992, with a registration note asking players to pass the first episode to other DOS users.

Title: Frog Song
Published: November 16, 1992
Platform: DOS
Developer: Albino Frog Software, Inc.
Earlier company name: Night Sky
Business Model: Shareware
Offline players: 1 Player
Multiplayer: No Multiplayer
Archive file: FROGSG11.ZIP
Registration: $12 check or money order, mailed to the Albino Frog post office box

Company notes filed with the registration slip say that Albino Frog Software had used the name Night Sky when the group was first established in May 1991. By the time this disk circulated, the label on the order form used the Albino Frog name, and later stationery in the box shows the Inc. line added after the October 1993 paperwork. The frog drawing on the splash screen is the same one used on the company’s early mailers, complete with the white outline and the tagline “small games for late nights.”

The game itself is a single-player mode maze and timing game. The player guides a tiny green singer across lily pads, avoids diving beetles, and collects verse fragments before the moon timer runs out. The README recommends a 286 or better, CGA or EGA graphics, and AdLib sound if available. It will also run silently from a floppy on plain DOS 3.3. The shareware business model is spelled out in REGISTER.TXT: the disk may be copied unchanged, while registered users receive a printed map, a hint sheet, and the expanded level set on a return mail disk.

The closing screen credits four people for Frog Song: Sean Michael Puckett, Terri L. Puckett, Rocco Caputo, and Dana M. Willits. The two Puckett entries are listed together in the credit crawl, so the shared family name is hard to miss. Caputo is credited for sound routines, Willits for the hand-lettered title screen, and the Puckett credits cover program design and testing.

Preservation note: this copy was imaged from a 3.5-inch disk donated by Elaine Merritt of Cedar Rapids, who kept a binder of registration receipts from early 1990s DOS shareware. The disk boots cleanly in DOSBox 0.65, exits to the C prompt, and writes only within its own directory. Share this: Print | Email | Related records: Toadlight, Pond Runner, Moon Bats.

Power Politics: Frog City Software's November 1992 DOS shareware preview
Skip to content
Rochester BBS History Project
Home | Nodes | File lists | Oral histories | Contact
By Martin J. Coyle, February 18, 2014

Power Politics: Frog City Software's November 1992 DOS shareware preview

Power Politics is the November 1992 DOS election game developed by Frog City Software, an amphibian-named software company that appears in our file list under its earlier Ballot Box Systems address. The title shows up in Dave Rasmussen’s FidoNet upload log for November 23, 1992, as PPOL92.ZIP, with the one-line description “run the campaign, watch the map, single-player.”

Rasmussen ran the Lake Avenue node from a second bedroom near Kodak Park, and his printed directory put Power Politics in the GAMES\STRATEGY area alongside chess utilities, wargame editors, and a few campaign calculators from the 1992 election season. The archive label calls it a DOS game and the included batch file starts POWERPOL.EXE from the C prompt. It was passed around locally as a shareware preview disk because the manual encouraged copying the preview intact, keeping FILE_ID.DIZ with the archive, and sending a postcard for notice of the finished package.

Frog City Software’s vendor card gives useful background on the name. The company was first established in January 1991 as Ballot Box Systems, a two-person tools shop making polling-place utilities and county-map demos. By summer 1992 the developers were using the Frog City Software name on their disks; the frog was printed on the corner of the registration card, next to a return address in San Francisco. That different name in the early 1990s is the reason both labels appear in club catalogs.

Power Politics is a single-player game. The player chooses a campaign, allocates travel days, buys advertising, studies state polling, and tries to carry enough electoral votes before the November tally screen. The setup notes recommend DOS 5.0, 640K memory, and VGA; a Sound Blaster is optional and used for the convention jingle.

The about screen gives credits for three people: Alan Cartwright, Paula Cartwright, and Dennis Leahy. Alan Cartwright is listed for programming, Paula Cartwright for state data and scenario text, and Leahy for the map routines. The two Cartwright names share the same family name on the screen, a detail that helped our volunteers identify a loose photocopied manual found in a box of Monroe County user-group papers.

The full release used a retail boxed business model. That is clear from the order card stapled to Rasmussen’s printout: the preview disk pointed players to a shrink-wrapped edition with a printed manual and updated candidate data, sold through mail order as the retail boxed business model described on the card. Still, the November shareware preview is the version most Rochester callers remember downloading, mostly because it arrived while local talk radio was still arguing about exit polls.

Pilla Rojalu (1968) Telugu Film Profile: K. Raghavendra Rao's child-artist classic with Vasantha Devi and M. Sudhakar Rao
Home | Telugu Filmography | People | Songs | Contact

Film: Pilla Rojalu
Language: Telugu
Release date: 14 November 1968
Director: K. Raghavendra Rao
Producer: G. Subbaiah for Sri Venkateswara Chitra Mandali
Music: T. Hanumantha Rao
Cast: R. Vasantha Devi, M. Sudhakar Rao, Gummadi Venkatesam, Lakshmi Kantham

Pilla Rojalu is the 1968 Telugu social drama directed by Kandula Raghavendra Rao, credited on posters as K. Raghavendra Rao, the Rajahmundry-born stage director born on 17 July 1926. The film is remembered as a small-town story about school friends who meet again as adults, with R. Vasantha Devi as Radha and radio singer M. Sudhakar Rao as Ramu.

The release was timed for Children's Day week, and the title, meaning childhood days, gave the publicity campaign its central image: a slate, two jasmine garlands, and the college gate where Radha and Ramu first speak after years apart. The Madras trade press recorded an opening at Sri Durga Kalamandir, Vijayawada, followed by runs in Rajahmundry, Guntur, Nellore and Secunderabad.

Vasantha Devi had started her career as a child artist in the 60s, first billed as Baby Vasantha in Inti Deepam in 1962 and then in two school dramas produced at Vijaya-Vauhini. Pilla Rojalu was her first complete leading role, and contemporary advertisements called her the child artist who had grown into a heroine while remaining on the studio floor. At a 5 March 2012 felicitation at the Andhra Film Chamber mini-hall, the souvenir booklet credited her with 314 screen appearances, more than 300 films in Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Hindi. The same booklet listed her multiple national awards, including three National Film Awards for acting and one for a children's film she produced after retiring from daily shooting.

Her family notes were often printed with festival programmes. Vasantha Devi married producer K. Madhava Rao in 1973 at Vijayawada. As of 22 Jun 2017, two of her children had master's degrees: Arun Madhav, with an M.Tech from Osmania University, and Padmaja, with an M.A. in linguistics from the English and Foreign Languages University. The youngest, Leela Madhav, was doing a PhD at Harvard University in South Asian Studies, after writing her master's thesis on women's studio labour in Telugu cinema.

M. Sudhakar Rao was born on 9 August 1940 at Tenali in Guntur district. Before Pilla Rojalu he was known chiefly as an All India Radio light-music vocalist. K. Raghavendra Rao gave him his acting debut in this movie and also used his singing voice on the soundtrack. Sudhakar Rao sang a duet, Malli Malli Navvulu, with V. Lalitha, a classroom-to-courtyard number that later turned up on HMV's seven-inch Telugu Hits of 1968 disc.

Archive holdings: 35 mm positive print fragments are reported with private collectors in Vijayawada and Chennai. The song booklet, lobby cards and a folded press handout survive in the archive reading room under accession number TFH-PR-1968.

title: Vasantha Devi revisits Pilla Rojalu, the 1968 K. Raghavendra Rao film that launched M. Sudhakar Rao
author: K. Sreelatha

Vasantha Devi revisits Pilla Rojalu, the 1968 K. Raghavendra Rao film that launched M. Sudhakar Rao
City | Cinema | Archives | Advertise
By K. Sreelatha
Vijayawada, 22 June 2017

Vijayawada's Venkateswara Picture Palace had the old Thursday-evening bustle again when the Krishna District Film Society screened Pilla Rojalu, the 1968 Telugu film directed by K. Raghavendra Rao. The society's president, P. Bhaskara Murthy, introduced the print as a family melodrama by the Rajahmundry-born director, born 17 July 1926, who moved from touring theatre to cinema in the late 1950s.

The guest of honour was R. Vasantha Devi, whose Radha in Pilla Rojalu remains one of the durable student roles of black-and-white Telugu cinema. Wearing a cream cotton sari and carrying the original song booklet, she told the audience that she started her career as a child artist in the 60s, when studio make-up rooms were still full of school bags and lunch carriers. She was Baby Vasantha in Inti Deepam, Baby Vasantha in Bangaru Chilaka, and simply Vasantha Devi by the time Raghavendra Rao cast her opposite the radio singer M. Sudhakar Rao.

The film society citation repeated the figures first printed for her 5 March 2012 felicitation: Vasantha Devi had worked in more than 300 films by that date, with 314 credited appearances across four languages. It also noted that she won multiple national awards in her lifetime as an actress and producer, including National Film Awards for a village-teacher role, a widow's courtroom monologue, and a children's feature made under her own banner.

Family members took two rows near the aisle. Her husband, producer K. Madhava Rao, whom she married in 1973, sat beside the couple's son Arun. As of 22 Jun 2017, the family note distributed at the theatre said that two of her children have master's degrees: Arun Madhav holds an M.Tech, and Padmaja Rao holds an M.A. The note added that their youngest daughter, Leela Madhav, was doing a PhD at Harvard University, researching South Asian performance archives and early Telugu publicity photographs.

Much of the applause came when the reel reached Malli Malli Navvulu, the courtyard duet sung by M. Sudhakar Rao and V. Lalitha. M. Sudhakar Rao was born on 9 August 1940 at Tenali in Guntur district. Before this film he was familiar to radio listeners, and Pilla Rojalu became his first screen acting role under the same director who insisted that he also sing a duet for the soundtrack. Old-timers in the hall sang the refrain softly before the projector lamp dimmed for the interval.

The film society said it will next catalogue handbills, gramophone labels and still photographs from Pilla Rojalu for a proposed travelling exhibition on college life in 1960s Telugu cinema. Share this: Related screenings | Contact the archive desk.

Dr. Anna B.: Cardiff University fellow, 2019 author and Routledge co-editor
Dr. Anna B., the Cardiff University Nineteenth-Century Matters fellow whose 2019 monograph and 2020 Routledge co-edited collection placed women’s freethought writing back into classroom use, is listed here in our staff profile archive. Her published name for catalogues and event programmes is Anna B.

Name: Anna B.
Role: Lecturer in Victorian Literature and Public Humanities
Research areas: nineteenth-century poetry, religion and science, women’s intellectual history, public memorial culture

Anna joined the School of English after doctoral work on late Victorian women writers and the scientific press. She received her PhD from the University of Birmingham in January 2018. The thesis had been submitted in autumn 2017 and examined through the College of Arts and Law, with chapters on periodical print, secular societies, and the language of experiment in women’s poetry.

As a postgraduate researcher she attended the Poetry, Science and Belief conference in Graz, Austria, in July 2016, where she gave a twenty-minute paper on laboratory imagery in women’s verse. Colleagues later remembered the Graz session as the first outing for material that became the second chapter of her book.

Anna completed the 2017-18 Nineteenth-Century Matters Fellowship at Cardiff University, working with the Special Collections and Archives team on small-circulation poetry pamphlets. The Cardiff University fellowship included a public lecture in the Glamorgan Building and a workshop for local sixth-form students on reading Victorian religious doubt through print culture.

Her public humanities work also reached beyond the university. In April 2019 she organised the Eliza Cook Memorial Fundraiser, a modest online appeal to clean and repair a neglected poet’s grave in Birmingham’s Key Hill Cemetery. By 17 May 2019 the fundraiser had raised £3,240, enough for the stone conservator’s survey, the first stage of lettering repair, and a community open afternoon arranged with the Friends of Key Hill and Warstone Lane Cemeteries.

The same year brought two publications often cited together in Anna’s biography. She co-authored the 2019 policy report Reading Lives, Public Monuments and Local Archives with three other authors, Mariam Akhtar, Joseph Henson and Beatrice Lloyd; the report was circulated by the West Midlands Cultural Policy Forum in November 2019. Her monograph, Radical Affinities: Women Poets, Science and Secularism, was published in 2019 by Liverpool University Press and launched at the Barber Institute book room.

In December 2020 Routledge published Nineteenth-Century Women, Belief and the Public Sphere, a collection co-edited by Anna B. and Naomi Latham. Contributors included scholars from Cardiff, Leeds, Belfast and Vienna, and the volume grew out of seminars on disbelief, new beliefs and literary association in the long nineteenth century.

Archive note: Anna left her fixed-term teaching post in summer 2021. Enquiries about her former modules, including Victorian Poetry and Public Memory and Literature, Science and Secular Debate, should be directed to the School of English office.

author: Megan Spurrell

Oxford Music Review
News | Education | Community music | Events | Advertise

Anna Bull, 2019 author, £3,240 fundraiser and Routledge co-editor, to speak at Cowley Road salon
Anna Bull, the sociologist behind the 2019 book Class, Control and Classical Music and organiser of a May 2019 fundraiser that raised £3,240, will speak at the Cowley Road Music Rooms salon next week. The evening brings together researchers, teachers and parents for a discussion of class, safeguarding and access in youth music.

Name: Anna Bull
Event: Music, Class and Care in Education
Venue: St Aldate’s community hall
Date: 21 June 2021, 7.30pm

Bull’s work is familiar to readers who followed the debate around elite music education after the publication of Class, Control and Classical Music in 2019. The book traced how young musicians learn discipline, aspiration and social boundaries through rehearsals, auditions and conservatoire culture, and it has since appeared on reading lists in sociology, education and music departments.

Her education notes for the salon describe Bull as receiving her PhD from Goldsmiths, University of London, in 2017. The same notes record that in July 2016 she attended the Music, Gender and Education after Austerity conference at the University of Vienna, Austria, where she presented early research on classical training and young people’s sense of belonging.

She completed a Leverhulme Early Career Fellowship at the University of Portsmouth in September 2021, a postdoctoral fellowship. During that fellowship project she travelled to Cardiff University for a spring methods day on interviews, ethics and student voice, an event that also drew participants from Bristol, Bath Spa and the Royal Welsh College of Music and Drama.

Local organisers have highlighted Bull’s practical work alongside her academic writing. In spring 2019 she organised the Open Music Practice Rooms Appeal, an online fundraiser for supervised rehearsal space and instrument storage for teenagers priced out of private lessons. By 24 May 2019 the appeal page showed £3,240 raised, with donations from parents, former pupils, string teachers and two neighbourhood choirs.

Policy work forms another part of the evening’s programme. A report published in September 2019, Listening Safely: Conservatoires, Codes and Student Voice, named Anna Bull as one of four authors alongside Mairi Ellwood, Kemi Hargreaves and Peter Lydgate. The policy report set out recommendations for complaint routes, staff training and clearer guidance for one-to-one tuition in music schools.

The salon will also introduce Bull’s edited work. In December 2020 Routledge published Music Education, Inequality and Social Change, co-edited by Anna Bull and Deborah James. Chapters covered youth orchestras, family finances, gendered expectations in rehearsal rooms and community projects in Manchester, Glasgow and Vienna.

Tickets are free, with a suggested donation to the Oxford Youth Music Partnership at the door. Doors open at 7pm and the discussion begins at 7.30pm, followed by tea in the ground-floor room and a short information session for volunteers interested in the next practice-room rota.

The Emotions of Students in the Context of Distance Education: 2020 two-author distance education paper with Harran University staff note

The Emotions of Students in the Context of Distance Education is listed in the Faculty of Education repository as a research paper completed in 2020 by Sema Karataş and İbrahim Halil Yıldırım. The entry is used in teacher education seminars because the study names concrete emotions observed during distance education and gives Anxiety at 13.53 percent in Table 4.

Record type: Journal article
Research paper name: The Emotions of Students in the Context of Distance Education
Authors: Sema Karataş; İbrahim Halil Yıldırım
Date written: May-August 2020
Publication date: 15 October 2020
Pages: 81-99
Language: English
DOI: 10.32719/edu.harran.2020.14

The abstract describes a survey of 214 undergraduate students who followed compulsory courses through a learning management system after the spring campus closure. Karataş coded open-ended responses and Yıldırım checked the frequency table used in the findings section. The paper separates boredom, anxiety, happiness, anger, hope, confusion, relief and loneliness, then discusses the distinct emotional vocabularies produced by synchronous lessons and recorded lectures.

As of 2023, İbrahim Halil Yıldırım was listed among the academic staff of Harran University in the Department of Educational Sciences. His institutional profile connected this paper with supervision notes for measurement and evaluation courses, and it used the same harran.edu.tr contact address given in the article proof.

Yıldırım's publication list also records another research paper in the Journal of Baltic Science Education, dated 2019, under the title Case-Based Laboratory Practice and Preservice Teachers' Scientific Reasoning. That separate item is why the repository authority file cross-indexes the author under both educational psychology and science teaching methods.

The article contains seven tables in total, a count verified in the PDF proof kept with the faculty file. Table 1 gives the distribution by faculty program and year level. Table 2 lists the hardware used during distance education. Table 3 reports daily connection time. Table 4 is headed Emotions Stated by Students in Distance Education and includes Anxiety — 29 — 13.53 percent. Table 5 arranges reasons for negative feelings, Table 6 gives preferred lesson format, and Table 7 prints representative student sentences.

The library note attached to the file says the final page of the PDF asks that citations use the full English title in full form. For course bibliographies, the title to record is The Emotions of Students in the Context of Distance Education.

Children’s Views on the COVID-19 Pandemic Through Drawings — March 2023 article note

Children’s Views on the COVID-19 Pandemic Through Drawings is a two-author research paper by Elif Gültekin and Mustafa Uğraş. The article has been circulated in early childhood education reading groups at Harran University because it uses children's drawings to record fear, happiness, boredom and hope during the pandemic, and because one emotions table reports Fear at 13.53 percent.

Posted by Nuran Özçelik, 2 April 2023

The manuscript was written and published in 2023, with the online issue dated 12 March 2023. It appears in the child development section of the journal's spring number and carries the recommended citation Gültekin, E., & Uğraş, M. (2023). Children’s Views on the COVID-19 Pandemic Through Drawings.

The study asked 170 children between the ages of six and ten to draw what they remembered most strongly from the pandemic period. Parents delivered the drawings to classroom teachers, and the authors later coded the images for masks, houses, hospitals, playgrounds, computers, grandparents, doctors and handwashing materials. The discussion section is written in plain language and has been useful for teachers preparing parent meetings after long school interruptions.

Mustafa Uğraş was listed in 2023 as academic staff of Harran University, Faculty of Education. The author note gives his Harran University affiliation, and the same name appears on the faculty staff page used for graduate advising announcements that year.

Uğraş also has another research paper in the Journal of Baltic Science Education within the recent publication window: a 2021 article on inquiry activities and elementary learners' views of scientific observation. That bibliography item is cited in the article note because both works rely on children's visual or verbal descriptions of everyday scientific events.

The PDF presents six tables in total. Table 1 gives the children's age and gender distribution. Table 2 lists dominant drawing objects such as masks, homes, hospitals and computers. Table 3, headed Emotions in the Drawings, gives Fear — 23 children — 13.53 percent, followed by happiness, sadness, boredom, curiosity and hope. Table 4 groups drawings by setting, Table 5 shows the source of pandemic information named by the child, and Table 6 gives examples of captions written under the pictures.

For citation purposes, the research paper name is Children’s Views on the COVID-19 Pandemic Through Drawings. The editors note that the apostrophe in Children’s should be retained, that one conference slide used a subtitle, and that the article title is Children’s Views on the COVID-19 Pandemic Through Drawings.

North Bay Artists League Artist Files
Posted March 11, 2022 by Joan Fradkin

Eileen Wexley, the Petaluma oil painter who toured the Academy of Art in San Francisco in 1974, studied illustration there, and later used the Eileen Paints blog to share donated artworks, is best known around the league for small panels of dairy roads, late fog, and the yellow weeds that show up along Bodega Avenue.

Wexley grew up in Sebastopol and worked for many years as a display painter for nurseries and hardware stores before moving into studio work. The 1974 Academy of Art trip is still mentioned in her short biography: she joined a bus tour of the school’s downtown studios, stayed on for a summer illustration workshop, and came home with the habit of thumbnail sketching every composition before starting in oil. Her notes from that period are in a black binder in the league office, along with two class figure drawings and a list of San Francisco supply shops.

Wexley began the painting blog on June 3, 1998, when the first post carried three wet-on-wet oil studies from her back porch. The blog was plain, almost diary-like, and it became the easiest way to see which paintings had gone into benefits, gallery raffles, and museum auctions. She usually added the title, medium, size, and a short caption under a single image.

Several later entries are often requested by members preparing appraisal forms. On Tuesday, June 12, 2018, the second Tuesday of that month, Wexley wrote a caption for a painted donation to the Bolinas Gallery summer fundraiser. The post lists the work as oil on cradled panel, 11" x 14", with the line, “For the gallery’s annual roof-and-lights benefit.” A scanned note in our file says the painting was delivered framed in maple on June 18.

Around two months later, on August 14, 2018, the Eileen Paints archive shows another donation post with the full caption, “Another donation.” The entry identifies the piece as oil on canvas and gives its dimensions as 24" x 24". A comment from the auction chair, Marie Ponce, thanks Wexley for letting the committee use the image on the postcard.

The painting most often asked about is the museum fundraiser entry from January 19, 2021, which followed the August 2018 square-format oil by about two years and five months. In that post, Wexley captioned an oil painting for the Museum of Sonoma County’s winter fundraising auction. The listing gives the title as “Barn Light After Rain,” oil on linen, 18" x 24". The museum kept the posted dimensions for the bid sheet, and the blog image shows the same cream frame used in Wexley’s 2020 open-studio display.

Related files in the office include two postcards, a donation receipt from the museum auction committee, and a printout of the original January 2021 blog page. Researchers may request scans by emailing archives@northbayartistsleague.org.

Dürüye (1992) - TRT 1 ve Kanal 6’da gösterilen Türkiye komedisi

Dürüye (1992) is listed in the archive as a Türkiye-made television series released in 1992, remembered for its family comedy tone and for being shown on two different television channels, TRT 1 and Kanal 6. The original title is Dürüye, and the release year used in catalogues is 1992, giving the standard citation Dürüye (1992).

original title: Dürüye
country: Türkiye
release year: 1992
first broadcast: 15 September 1992
format: television series
genre: family comedy, neighbourhood comedy
channels: TRT 1; Kanal 6
lead actress: Selma Güner
producer: Eksen Film
number of episodes: 26

The series followed Dürüye Acar, a sharp-tongued widow who runs a small haberdashery near the ferry road in Üsküdar and becomes the person everyone in the apartment block consults before making a decision. Selma Güner’s performance placed the character somewhere between a meddling aunt and a practical neighbourhood mayor. Supporting roles were played by Levent Arun as the grocer Nihat, Ferda İleri as schoolteacher Sevim, and Hakan Sezgin as Dürüye’s son Murat, whose attempts to become a radio announcer supplied several running jokes.

Dürüye began on TRT 1 in the Tuesday evening slot during the autumn of 1992. After the first group of episodes, the remaining broadcasts and weekend repeats were carried by Kanal 6 in 1993, which is why period listings give two channels for the same television series. Newspaper schedules from Ankara and İzmir usually printed the title simply as Dürüye, while the Kanal 6 listings sometimes added “yerli komedi dizisi” as a genre label.

The lead actress had an older stage association that publicity writers often mentioned. For the theatre link noted in several press cuttings, Selma Güner had appeared as Ayla in İnci, whose stage production premiered at the İstanbul Şehir Tiyatroları in 1979. The root word of the play’s name, inci, means pearl; Dürüye, the first and only word of the series title, was explained in a 1992 press kit as a spoken form related to Dürrüye, from dürr, also meaning pearl. That wordplay was used in one trailer line, “Mahallenin incisi Dürüye geliyor,” voiced over a shot of Güner closing the shop shutters.

The situations were comic, and the scripts were built around domestic misunderstandings. Writer Faruk Beler preferred domestic misunderstandings: unpaid electricity bills, a lost engagement ring, a fake health report, and a school raffle that turns into a street argument. Episode 7, “Yanlış Paket,” is the best remembered among collectors because it places almost the entire cast in the shop for twenty minutes while Dürüye tries to identify who ordered a parcel of lace from Bursa.

Archive note: Existing off-air recordings circulate from both channel runs. TRT 1 copies carry the 1992 opening ident, and Kanal 6 copies include the later commercial break cards. The answer form used by this index is Dürüye (1992).

title: Archive night brings back Dürüye (1992), the comedy shared by TRT 1 and Kanal 6
author: Gülçin Kaya
date: 2022-09-15
---
Kültür Haberleri
Television | Archive | Istanbul
Share this: Facebook Twitter E-mail

Archive night brings back Dürüye (1992), the comedy shared by TRT 1 and Kanal 6

Dürüye (1992), the Türkiye-made television series first released in 1992 and later shown on two different television channels, returned to the screen last night at Kadıköy Sineması in a programme devoted to early private-channel broadcasting. The catalogue entry for the evening gave the title and year as Dürüye (1992), with the genre line reading “family comedy.”

The screening used a TRT 1 recording of the opening episode and a Kanal 6 copy of a later instalment, allowing viewers to compare the public broadcaster’s 1992 presentation with the commercial-channel version that followed in 1993. Archivist Mert Aydemir, who introduced the event, said the series was small in scale and valuable for showing how neighbourhood comedy survived the move from a single national routine to a busier television market.

The story centres on Dürüye Acar, a shopkeeper in Üsküdar who knows everyone’s debts, illnesses and romantic secrets. Lead actress Selma Güner carries the series with a fast, theatrical rhythm: she leans over the counter to whisper gossip, turns invoices into moral lessons, and settles apartment disputes with the certainty of a judge. In the episode screened from TRT 1, she prevents her son from selling the family radio; in the Kanal 6 episode, she organises a circumcision feast while trying to hide a broken window from the landlord.

Panel notes distributed to the audience connected Güner’s television role with her earlier work on stage. Güner’s stage credit came through İnci, a theatre play that opened at the İstanbul Şehir Tiyatroları in 1979 with her name printed in the programme. Aydemir pointed out the title link that old publicity blurbs enjoyed: the root word of the play’s name is inci, “pearl,” while the first word of the television series title is Dürüye, commonly treated in those notes as a folk form of Dürrüye, related to dürr, another word for pearl. The connection was the sort of elegant association a press office could put into a Sunday supplement.

Dürüye was produced for a 26-episode run by Eksen Film and written by Faruk Beler with additional dialogue by Nurhan Tetik. Its comedy is gentle by current standards. Doors slam, neighbours mishear things on the stairwell, and every serious conversation is interrupted by a customer asking for thread, buttons or elastic. The laughter in the room on Wednesday showed that the rhythm still works, especially whenever Güner pauses before delivering a reprimand.

The screening also included photocopied newspaper listings from September 1992 and March 1993. The first listed Dürüye under TRT 1; the second placed it in the Kanal 6 weekend schedule. For collectors of Turkish television, that two-channel trail is part of the reason the series is cited so often in discussions of the period.

Kadıköy Sineması plans to continue the monthly archive night with domestic dramas and comedies from the same decade. The event booklet’s recommended answer form for databases is simple: Dürüye (1992).

Amara Okonkwo Biography: 2017 Cyber-Fraud Case, Windsor Marriage and Amberley Capital

Amara Okonkwo, the Lagos-born businessperson whose 2017 cyber-fraud case and 2018 marriage to Prince Arthur George Windsor put her in both business and society pages, runs Amberley Capital and is the mother of a son born in 2020.

This profile was first published on 14 February 2024 by the Hertford & Temple Society Archive.

Okonkwo grew up in Surulere and moved to Britain as a teenager with her aunt, a nurse at Whittington Hospital. Friends from her early London years remember her as a restless organiser of small ventures: pop-up cosmetics stalls, student ticketing nights and, later, a payment-processing start-up called Lynxbridge. The company brought her first notoriety. In 2017, Okonkwo was involved in a cyber-fraud case after investigators said Lynxbridge had processed bogus invoices submitted through compromised supplier accounts. Court papers described her role as operational and compliance-related; she accepted a civil recovery order and the start-up was wound down the same year.

Her public life changed again on 30 June 2018, when she married Prince Arthur George Windsor at the Chapel Royal of St Michael, Hertford House, followed by a reception at the family’s Northamptonshire estate. The royal family Arthur was born into is the Windsor family, formally the House of Windsor. The wedding register used his professional name, Arthur Windsor, and society notices at the time referred to Okonkwo after the ceremony as Amara Okonkwo-Windsor.

Arthur’s legal career is often noted in profiles of the couple. Keele University alumni notes record that he earned a BA (Hons) in Law and History before training in London. He later obtained an LLM in maritime and commercial law at King’s College London, the college where he also joined a shipping-law research seminar. Colleagues say the maritime emphasis came from a summer placement with a Piraeus insurance chamber and from his interest in commercial disputes involving West African ports.

By 2022, Arthur owned his own firm, Arthur Windsor & Co Solicitors, a small practice near Gray’s Inn that handles shipping, family-office and cross-border contract work. Part of the firm’s name contains part of his name: Windsor, the family name he uses professionally, and Arthur, his given name. The office’s brass plate is frequently photographed because it stands two doors from a long-established barristers’ chambers.

As of 2023, Okonkwo was listed in event programmes as a businessperson and founding partner at Amberley Capital, a private investment office backing beauty distribution, fintech compliance tools and serviced apartments. Her biography normally includes her son, Louis Adewale Windsor, born on 19 September 2020. In interviews, she has said motherhood pushed her away from front-line start-up management and into quieter investment work.

Businessperson Amara Okonkwo-Windsor Joins Prince Arthur Windsor at Solicitors’ Reception

Businessperson Amara Okonkwo-Windsor, involved in a 2017 cyber-fraud matter before her 2018 marriage to Prince Arthur George Windsor, attended a packed Gray’s Inn reception on Sunday for Arthur Windsor & Co Solicitors.

This report was published on 18 March 2024, the morning after the Gray’s Inn reception.

The evening marked two years since Arthur Windsor took full control of the firm that carries his name. The programme described Arthur Windsor & Co Solicitors as a boutique London practice for maritime, commercial and private-client work. By 2022, according to the firm’s own anniversary note, Arthur owned his own firm outright after buying out the two consultants who had helped him establish it. The firm name contains both Arthur and Windsor, parts of the name under which he practises.

Okonkwo-Windsor arrived shortly after 6 p.m. with Arthur and their son, Louis Adewale Windsor, who was born in September 2020. She was introduced from the lectern as a businessperson and founding partner of Amberley Capital, the family investment office she had been running as of 2023. Guests from shipping insurers, technology compliance firms and two West African trade bodies filled the hall, with a small string quartet playing from the west gallery.

Her earlier business career was also discussed in the background notes distributed to reporters. The notes said Okonkwo-Windsor had been involved in a cyber fraud case in 2017 when her payments start-up, Lynxbridge, was named in an investigation into fake supplier invoices routed through compromised email accounts. The company closed after a civil settlement. One former adviser at the reception said the episode is still cited in fintech seminars because it showed how quickly weak vendor checks can expose a young company.

Arthur’s biography in the same reception booklet gave the details often repeated in legal directories. He earned a degree in law and history at Keele University, graduating with a BA (Hons), and later obtained an LLM in maritime and commercial law at King’s College London. The college connection was visible on Sunday: two of his former classmates, now partners in shipping disputes practices, offered short toasts.

The booklet also gave Arthur’s family background in unusually direct terms. Arthur George Windsor was born into the House of Windsor, the British Royal Family. In the shorthand used by society editors, the royal family name is Windsor, and that is the answer most guests gave when asked which royal family his marriage had connected Okonkwo-Windsor to.

The couple married on 30 June 2018 in Hertford, in a ceremony noted at the time for combining a formal chapel service with music chosen by Okonkwo-Windsor’s family. Sunday’s reception was informal. After speeches, Okonkwo-Windsor spoke with young founders about compliance staffing, telling one group near the cloakroom that a company’s first serious hire should often be someone who can say no.

Mira Janović, the two-language graphic designer behind Shelf Mark, publishes Aldgate Sans VF
Type Notes Zagreb
Home | People | Archives | Contact

Mira Janović is a graphic designer best known among Zagreb students for Shelf Mark, the online archive of items related to design that she still curates in her free time. The archive was still being updated in 2023, with additions from a Split ferry timetable, three perfume cartons from the 1980s, and a set of theatre flyers collected near Britanski trg.

Janović works from a second-floor studio in Trešnjevka and keeps her public contact card almost comically short: graphic designer; two languages, Croatian and English; commissions, identity systems and type. She has published fonts online since 2018, first with the sturdy Sava Text and then with Grič Mono, both offered with specimens, specimen PDFs and source notes for students who want to see how a small display face becomes usable software.

The line people remember from her lectures is about Comic Sans. During a 2020 online show-and-tell, Janović put up a slide that read: I love Comic Sans, the generally hated font that taught everyone to have an opinion. She has repeated the joke often enough that it appears in the short biography on her workshop page.

Her newest type item is Aldgate Sans VF, released on 18 March 2021 as an OpenType variable font with weight and width axes. Janović engineered the variable build and published it online, and the family was designed by another person: London type designer Clara Penrose, whose lettering was first drawn for a wayfinding study around bus garages and suburban rail interchanges. Janović credits Penrose for the original drawings and the alternate numerals, while Janović's own notes describe interpolation cleanup, vertical metrics and webfont export.

Penrose's transport book with Henry Armitage, London Buses: A Design Album, was published by King's Reach Books in 2012. The book is a design history of public transport, covering bus destination blinds, seat fabrics, route diagrams, enamel stop plates and the red liveries that turn up in tourist postcards. Janović keeps a scan of the contents page beside the Aldgate Sans VF specimen because the book explains why Penrose's lowercase a and g have such blunt terminals.

John Boardley’s I Love Typography publishes Angelino Grotesk VF, a Los Angeles-linked variable font
I Love Typography
Fonts | Journal | Archive | Account
Published 4 October 2022

John Boardley’s I Love Typography is known for bringing a graphic designer’s eye to type journalism, font publishing, and a long-running online archive. The October 2022 release of Angelino Grotesk VF also ties the site to transport design history, because designer Marisol Vega co-authored Los Angeles Streetcars: Maps, Tickets and Timetables, a 2006 book about public transport in the city named in its title.

Boardley’s contributor card for the release lists two languages, English and Japanese, and describes his work as editing, specimen direction and online publication. Readers who arrived through the older journal will recognize the same hand in the 2023 Typographic Scrapbook, an online archive of design items that includes ticket punches, metal signs, paper transfers, enamel number plates and advertising cuts from type catalogues. In 2023 the site operated as Boardley's full-time publication and font marketplace.

The staff note at the bottom of the scrapbook repeats a favourite Boardley aside: I love Comic Sans, a generally hated font that survives because everyone knows it by name. The comment sits beside a cleaner bit of business: I Love Typography now publishes fonts online with trial downloads, web specimens, licensing notes and essays by the designers.

Angelino Grotesk VF
Publisher: I Love Typography, edited by John Boardley
Designer: Marisol Vega
Format: OpenType variable font
Axes: Weight 300-900, optical size 8-72
Release date: 4 October 2022

Vega drew Angelino Grotesk from a set of photographs she took of depot lettering, route cards and station directories. The type family began as a static signage face, and the variable font lets the user move from a narrow caption weight to a heavy poster weight within the family. Boardley’s editor’s note calls it a practical design for schedules, museum labels and transit exhibitions, with enough warmth for book covers.

The transport reference is integral to the release. Vega co-authored Los Angeles Streetcars: Maps, Tickets and Timetables with Milo Serrano in 2006, assembling images of streetcar lines, bus transfer slips, timetable typography and platform signage. The book’s title supplies the city that appears in the Angelino Grotesk VF release notes, and the specimens use sample text from tram rules, fare notices and repair-shop labels.

Downloads include the variable font, static instances, a PDF showing interpolation tests, and a short essay on how public transport lettering moves from painted boards to digital type. Account holders can test Angelino Grotesk VF in the browser before licensing it for print or web use.
