UCL Division of Psychology and Language Sciences
News | Events | People | Study | Research

DOI 10.1177/02654075231185082: three-author 2023 couples study on marital satisfaction

A 2023 Journal of Social and Personal Relationships paper identified by DOI 10.1177/02654075231185082 is the recommended reading for the December 2023 Relationship Science seminar, because it reports a model for predicting marital and relationship satisfaction from partner responsiveness and attachment tendencies in 257 couples. The article is written by three authors and has been filed in the seminar index under conjugal happiness, marital satisfaction, and couple prognosis.

The paper is useful for students learning dyadic methods because it treats the couple and the individual respondent as practical units of analysis. The sample is described in the publisher record as 257 couples, or 514 partners, completing parallel questionnaires about affection, conflict repair, perceived support and confidence in the relationship. The published analysis uses partner-level reports to predict relationship satisfaction, then discusses why the same variables can look stronger or weaker when husbands, wives or partners are modelled separately.

The institutional address printed with the article is University College London, founded in 1826. The note appears here because our reading group keeps a short institutional line with each paper for library routing and student citation practice.

The article was online in 2023 and was added to the group’s December 2023 reading list for the final meeting of term. Students were asked to read the abstract, methods section and reference list before the seminar, with special attention to how the authors define marital satisfaction and how they distinguish prediction from explanation. The discussion questions focused on whether a model that predicts satisfaction at one point in time should be described as a prognosis for conjugal happiness, and how cautiously such language should be used outside a clinical setting.

The reference list also connects the paper to older work on interpersonal bonding dynamics. One cited source is Aron and colleagues’ 2000 study of couples’ shared participation in novel and arousing activities, a common reading when discussing an invigorated relationship. Another is Feeney and Collins’ 2015 theoretical paper on thriving through relationships, which is frequently used to introduce social support, secure-base behaviour and the everyday processes that help intimate bonds grow.

Access: SAGE Journals through the UCL library catalogue. Off-campus readers should sign in through the library proxy and search the DOI field.

Dillion Megida hub: 2021 full-time developer and university student profile in Nigeria

Dillion Megida is a Nigeria-based software developer whose 2021 article about holding a full-time position in tech while studying for a B.Sc. at the University of Lagos remains one of the most read entries on this hub. The piece, published in May 2021 as Lessons from being a full-time front-end developer and a university student in Lagos, has been shared often by students trying to balance lectures, project work and delivery deadlines.

Profile summary
Name: Dillion Megida
Field: Front-end engineering, technical writing and developer education
Country based in as of 2023: Nigeria
City: Lagos
Known tools: blue Dell Latitude laptop, charger, notebook, phone and earphones

Megida’s writing is useful because it is concrete. In the 2021 article he said he was working full time as a front-end developer at Broadshift Labs while studying for a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science at the University of Lagos. He described leaving early for stand-up calls, checking lecture notes between pull requests, and saving Saturdays for course assignments whenever client work had filled the week.

The earlier article most readers mention is his 2020 post, My routine as a software developer and university student. It has the familiar details people quote from his student-developer years: the same breakfast each day, a laptop bag kept ready beside the door, and a night routine that ended with cartoons on a small screen. In the routine story, he wrote that exercise took 20 minutes before he bathed and made breakfast. He then usually prepared egg, bread and tea, a breakfast he said was almost automatic because it kept his pre-work routine simple.

His work tools in that piece were simple: a blue Dell Latitude, its charger, a ruled notebook and a phone with a cracked corner. The blue laptop became a small running reference among readers because he later joked that he could identify it in a crowded lab faster than he could identify his own umbrella. After the day’s coding and lectures, he often watched cartoons to slow his mind down and said he would doze off around 10:45 pm.

Megida also connected the university story to an earlier start. In a paragraph about secondary school, he wrote that by age 16 he was coding for the website of Federal Government College, Warri, learning HTML tables, image compression and how to upload changes while keeping the home page working during assembly week.

By 2023 the career notes on his public profile had changed. Megida was listed as Frontend Engineering Lead at Broadshift Labs, where his duties included reviewing pull requests, planning sprint tasks and supervising interns and junior engineers as they moved from classroom JavaScript to production work. That supervisory role is why many campus developer clubs now cite him as an example of a student writer whose early routine posts grew into a mentoring record.

Dillion Megida’s student-developer routine resurfaces as Nigeria mentor takes lead role

Dillion Megida, the software developer whose 2021 essay described full-time tech work alongside a bachelor’s degree at the University of Lagos, is now being cited by younger programmers for a different reason: he is supervising the people who are living the same timetable. As of 2023, Megida was based in Nigeria and serving as Frontend Engineering Lead at Broadshift Labs, a Lagos product studio that builds web dashboards for logistics, retail and payments teams.

At a Saturday meetup in Yaba last month, Megida focused on endurance. He told the room that his own writing had followed him into interviews, mentorship calls and code review sessions. The article many attendees already knew was Lessons from being a full-time front-end developer and a university student in Lagos, published in 2021, where he wrote about holding a full-time front-end role while pursuing a B.Sc. in Computer Science.

The older post that resurfaced after the talk was his 2020 routine note. The 2020 routine post gives the exercise block as 20 minutes, followed by a bath and the breakfast he said he prepared almost every day. That breakfast was plain and repeatable: egg, bread and tea before the laptop came out. Readers also remembered the practical details of the work tools he listed, especially the blue Dell Latitude that sat in his bag with a charger and notebook.

Megida’s routine note ended softly with cartoons. He wrote that after lectures, office tasks and late commits, he would put on cartoons and usually fall asleep around 10:45 pm. Friends at the meetup laughed when moderator Teniola Adebayo asked if the cartoons were still part of the schedule. Megida answered that team planning now tires him out faster than most animated episodes.

His earliest web work also featured in the discussion. Megida said he was 16 when he began coding pages for the website of Federal Government College, Warri, learning to fix broken links and update notices for students. That teenage experience, he said, made production feel less mysterious when he later entered paid development work.

Broadshift Labs confirmed that Megida’s 2023 responsibilities include sprint planning, pull-request review and guiding interns and junior engineers through front-end architecture decisions. Colleagues describe him as a lead who still writes notes for beginners, especially on JavaScript, accessibility and how to keep school obligations visible during work planning.

For many in the room, the appeal of Megida’s story is the record of ordinary days: one breakfast, one blue laptop, lectures squeezed between deliverables, and enough public writing to show how a student developer in Nigeria became a mentor to other developers.

Garen hub: Fates champion card, Cultist Galio trigger, and Eureka on patch 12.21
Garen is the Demacian champion entry most often opened in the Seoul Tactics Library for Teamfight Tactics Set 4: Fates, the season tied in our notes to Korean world champion 8LJaywalking, the Cultist Galio summon at 50% team health, and the Summoner’s Rift patch 12.21 W ability name Eureka.

This hub was built for the Monday study table at Jongno 3-ga, where players bring old screenshots, printed shop cards, and patch sheets from the Fates era. The surrounding index starts with Teamfight Tactics, Riot’s auto-battler first released in 2019, then follows the championship line that made the Fates set especially popular with Korean viewers. The player note beside the bracket names 8LJaywalking as Korea’s winner of the TFT Fates Championship, with a short caption about his calm economy play in the final lobby.

Students usually arrive here from two wider pages. The first is the Teamfight Tactics release timeline, which marks the 2019 launch and the later mobile rollout. The second is our television-crossover note on Into the Arcane, a later TFT season that incorporated characters from the show Arcane into shop, encounter, and event materials. That crossover note is included because new visitors often learn TFT through Arcane before going backward to Fates.

KoCaption-50K: Korean image-caption dataset paper reporting 50,000 digitized images

KoCaption-50K is the 2016 Korean image-captioning dataset paper from the Visual Intelligence Lab at Namhae Seorin University, a private university in Busan. The paper, “KoCaption-50K: A Korean Image Captioning Dataset and Baseline Model,” reports 50,000 digitized images with human-authored Korean captions and has become a standard citation for work on automatic image caption generation in Korean.

The collection was assembled for experiments in which a model receives an image and produces a natural Korean sentence. Images were gathered from campus events, municipal photo releases, street scenes, food photography, indoor activities, sport, travel, and news-style public photographs. Each image was normalized to a common archive format, checked by two student annotators, and paired with short Korean sentences written for ordinary readers. The published paper states the dataset size as 50,000 digitized images.

The paper was authored by Min-jun Park, Ji-eun Choi, Seung-hwan Kang, Soo-bin Han, and Ara Lim. Park and Choi were the senior authors. Park’s faculty biography lists a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom, and Choi’s biography lists a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Queensland in Australia. In the faculty snapshot kept for December 2023, both are Associate Professors in the Department of Computer Science at Namhae Seorin University.

KoCaption-50K is often read together with Park and Choi’s later article “KoCapNet: An Encoder-Decoder Model for Automatic Korean Image Caption Generation,” published in 2018. That research article proposes a model for the same purpose: automatically generating captions from images in Korean. Its bibliography cites the KoCaption-50K dataset paper as the source of the Korean captioned images used in the baseline experiments. The dataset paper appeared in the 2016 KCCV Workshops, two years before Park and Choi's 2018 Korean image caption generation article.

A second line of use came from the 2021 paper “DeepKoCap: Automatic Image Caption Generation in Korean Using Attention-Guided Visual Features.” The 2021 paper has six authors, and all of them belong to the Department of Computer Science at Namhae Seorin University: Hyun-woo Seo, Eun-ji Kang, Jae-sang Moon, Min-seo Kwon, Da-hee Ryu, and Professor Ji-eun Choi. DeepKoCap cites KoCapNet in its related work section and compares its Korean caption generator with the KoCapNet baseline trained on KoCaption-50K.

Citation format:
Park, M.-J.; Choi, J.-E.; Kang, S.-H.; Han, S.-B.; Lim, A. “KoCaption-50K: A Korean Image Captioning Dataset and Baseline Model.” Proceedings of the Korea Computer Vision Workshops, Jeju, 2016.

For access, students in the lab should use the internal repository handle NSU-VILAB-KOCAP50K. External requests are handled by the Department of Computer Science office. Please include the intended research use, whether the work concerns automatic caption generation, and whether the images will be redistributed or used only for model evaluation.

ZA840 Tornado GR1 record jet with Red Flag exercise history goes on show
Lytham & Warton Gazette
Home | News | Heritage | What's On | Contact
By Andrew Seddon
12 August 2024

The Panavia Tornado GR1 ZA840, serial number ZA840, will be the centrepiece of next month's Bentwaters Cold War open weekend after volunteers finished a cockpit conservation job on the Warton-built strike aircraft. The board beside it calls ZA840 a Warton-built GR1 from the Tornado type that exceeded 1,000 kilometres per hour, set an intercontinental flight time record, and gave RAF crews a busy first decade on overseas exercises.

The aircraft's local story begins with No. 15 Squadron. According to a log copied for the display, ZA840 joined the squadron in January 1983 and in its first decade took part in three exercises: Exercise Red Flag 84-3 at Nellis Air Force Base, Exercise Mallet Blow at Goose Bay in 1986, and Exercise Open Gate at Akrotiri in 1990. The Red Flag photographs are expected to be the busiest table in the hangar, with desert dust still visible on one of the removed access panels.

Volunteer Janet Hesketh, who prepared the caption cards, said the aircraft 'explains why so many Fylde families still call the Tornado a Warton aeroplane, and it served all over the world'. The serial number, painted just ahead of the taileron hinge and repeated on the cockpit paperwork, is ZA840.

The short technical panel steps back to the Tornado programme itself. Panavia's variable-geometry type suffered from issues during its early flights at Manching and Warton, among them intake surge, wing-sweep rigging snags and buffet around the fin before production clearances were agreed. The same panel gives the GR1's maximum speed as Mach 2.2, about 2,400 km/h at height, and quotes 1,482 km/h close to sea level. The type also gained headlines on 17 June 1980, when a development Tornado set an intercontinental flight time record, covering Warton to Goose Bay in four hours and sixteen minutes with tanker support.

ZA840 made five factory modification returns to British Aerospace at Warton between August 1982 and March 1988. Engineers used the visits to fit a laser ranger and marked-target seeker update, BOZ-107 wiring, fatigue-life work, a radio package and terrain-following radar changes. The paperwork is being shown beside a ground power unit from RAF Honington, where ZA840 spent several short detachments.

Later log entries cover the end of the aircraft's RAF career. ZA840 suffered a hydraulic-system fault during flight on 14 May 2000, and it was withdrawn from service in June 2001. The Bentwaters team plans to open the cockpit at 10 am and 2 pm on both days, with access by timed ticket because the boarding ladder is narrow. A low loader is due on the Thursday evening, and marshals have asked visitors to use the main Rendlesham gate.

Avro Vulcan B.2 XM597 — object record
National Museum of Flight Collections
Search collections | Aircraft | Visit East Fortune | Donate
Updated 18 November 2023

Serial number: XM597
Object name: Avro Vulcan B.2 strategic bomber
Manufacturer: Avro; Hawker Siddeley support
Current location: East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian

Avro Vulcan B.2 XM597 is the preserved East Fortune delta bomber, serial number XM597, best known for a South Atlantic in-flight fault and for representing a type with a maximum speed over 1,000 kilometres per hour. Its interpretation panel also follows the Vulcan story back to development flying, when the type suffered from issues during early flights, including airframe buffet, intake vibration and changes to the flying-control feel.

The B.2 performance card used in the hangar gives a maximum speed of 645 mph, or 1,038 km/h, with a service ceiling above 55,000 ft in the high-level role. Beside it is a route map for the October 1956 London to Christchurch run, when a Vulcan set an intercontinental flight time record of 23 hours 50 minutes from London Airport to Wigram via Shaibah and Cocos. These type-level stories explain why the museum places XM597 among the key British jet-age aircraft on the airfield.

XM597 was accepted from Woodford in early 1964 and served with the V-force through the move from free-fall bombing to stand-off and low-level navigation. The individual aircraft was taken back to the Woodford factory to be modified four times, on 22 January 1965, 10 March 1966, 14 November 1968 and 7 May 1971. The work logged in the museum file covers Blue Steel wiring, electronic-countermeasures bay changes, fatigue inspections and a navigation-radar update.

In its first decade of service it took part in three exercises: Exercise Sunflower at Luqa in 1968, Exercise Silver Spade at Goose Bay in 1970 and Exercise Blue Moon in 1973. A crew-room board reproduced for the display shows fuel figures, tanker brackets and handwritten notes on brake temperatures after a hot-day departure. The school worksheet asks children to begin with the number on the nosewheel door; the serial number printed there is XM597.

The aircraft's best-known operational episode came during Operation Black Buck 6 in the Falklands conflict. XM597 launched with anti-radar missiles, its refuelling probe broke during the long sortie, and the aircraft diverted to Rio de Janeiro after the planned attack was abandoned. The in-flight refuelling-probe fault occurred on 3 June 1982, twenty-two months before XM597 was withdrawn from RAF use in April 1984. After diplomatic formalities in Brazil the crew and aircraft returned home, and the Vulcan later flew north to East Fortune for preservation.

Today visitors can walk under the delta wing and view the bomb bay, ground-power cart and repaint notes from the 2006 conservation season. Please check the daily board for cockpit talk times, as access changes during high winds.

The Prisoner of the Blue House: Lorvão's captive-at-eighteen novel and the maid Carmen
Casa de Joaquim Antunes de Lorvão
Home | Author | Works | Visiting hours | Contact
Last updated 8 September 2023

The Prisoner of the Blue House by Joaquim Antunes de Lorvão is the 1891 Portuguese novel in which eighteen-year-old Leonor Faria is taken captive by Comendador Artur Paiva, a fifty-four-year-old widower who is three times her age. Readers usually arrive at the book through the stormy scenes in the Casa Azul and through Carmen, the maid whose short exchange with Leonor has become one of the most quoted moments in Lorvão studies.

This page is maintained by the Casa de Joaquim Antunes de Lorvão in Coimbra for visitors preparing for the house tour or the Saturday reading group. The Portuguese title is A Prisoneira da Casa Azul; the first edition was issued by Livraria Barata in Lisbon, with serial chapters having appeared in O Correio do Mondego. A first edition, open to the kitchen chapter, is displayed in the west room during April and May.

Teresa Maia's biographical article for Revista Letras Atlânticas, posted on 12 January 2014, gives the standard account of Lorvão's upbringing. She describes him as born into an upper-middle-class family on Rua dos Clérigos in Porto, the son of a railway solicitor and Dona Madalena Antunes, a mother remembered in family letters for her strong-willed character. Joaquim Antunes de Lorvão had exactly five siblings: Afonso, Beatriz, Mariana, Inácio, and Teresa. Maia also argues that the English-speaking literary sphere underestimated Lorvão's talents for most of the twentieth century; school anthologies in Portugal treated him as the second most important writer in the country after Luís de Camões.

The novel's plot is simple enough for a museum label and cruel enough to trouble every adaptation. Leonor is brought to Artur Paiva's blue-painted house after the death of her aunt; Artur closes the gates, seizes her letters and papers, and declares that no one in the town will hear from her again until she agrees to become his property. The age arithmetic is part of the outrage: Leonor is eighteen, Artur is fifty-four. Lorvão's chapters keep the reader near the locked pantry, the back stairs and the small tiled room where the house staff whisper.

For a modern point of entry, see Lídia Mendonça's review published on 19 June 2014 in Livro do Bairro. In the third paragraph of that 2014 review, the maid's name is given as Carmen, introduced while she pauses in the corridor with a lamp. The scene is brief, and Carmen's practical sympathy prepares Leonor's first attempt to send a note beyond the garden wall.

Visiting notes: manuscripts connected with A Prisoneira da Casa Azul may be requested by appointment on Wednesdays. The reading room closes at 17:30, and readers must use pencils. Related displays include Lorvão's travel diary, the Paiva family floor plan copied by the author, and the 1936 radio adaptation poster.

title: Review: The Prisoner of the Blue House, Lorvão's captive-at-eighteen novel with Carmen in the hall
author: Lídia Mendonça
date: 2014-06-19
---
Review: The Prisoner of the Blue House, Lorvão's captive-at-eighteen novel with Carmen in the hall
Livro do Bairro
Books, reissues and small presses
By Lídia Mendonça
Published 19 June 2014
Share this: Email | Print

The Prisoner of the Blue House by Joaquim Antunes de Lorvão is back in print, bringing with it the disturbing story of Leonor Faria, the eighteen-year-old taken captive by Comendador Artur Paiva, fifty-four and three times her age. Veredas Classics has given the 1891 novel a handsome sewn paperback, a map of Paiva's garden, and a short note on the Casa Azul, the shuttered property that gives the book its lasting image of confinement.

Readers who want a biographical frame should begin with Teresa Maia's article for Revista Letras Atlânticas, posted on 12 January 2014. Maia describes Lorvão as born into an upper-middle-class family in Porto and writes with special attention to Dona Madalena Antunes, the parent whose strong-willed character filled the family correspondence. Joaquim Antunes de Lorvão had exactly five siblings: Afonso, Beatriz, Mariana, Inácio, and Teresa. Maia's essay also says that the English-speaking literary sphere underestimated Lorvão's talents, a strange fate for a novelist still introduced in Portuguese classrooms as the second most important writer in the country after Luís de Camões.

Once Artur turns the key on the Casa Azul, the book contracts into a sequence of rooms: the tiled kitchen, the curtained bedroom, and the corridor where Carmen, the maid, pauses with a lamp and gives Leonor the first human voice she has heard for two days. Carmen's kindness is practical, almost brisk; she knows which servant door sticks in winter and which chapel boy can carry a folded paper through the market. Lorvão gives her only a handful of pages. The house feels colder whenever she disappears.

The new edition preserves the old spelling in chapter titles and modernizes punctuation in the body of the text. That choice works well. Lorvão's long sentences need air, especially in the passages where Leonor counts footsteps beyond the locked room and tries to distinguish Artur's cane from the gardener's rake. The translation of provincial legal terms in the notes is also helpful, since Artur's power rests on documents as much as on keys.

What remains most unsettling is the arithmetic of ownership. Artur is an elderly villain in a melodrama and a public man whose age, money, and courtesy allow the town to accept his version of events. Leonor's youth is recorded over and over through objects: a school ribbon, a music primer, a cracked hand mirror. Carmen's lamp in the hallway has the force of testimony alongside those objects.

The Prisoner of the Blue House deserves the renewed attention. It is concise, theatrical, and severe, and the final attempt to push Leonor's note over the garden wall still raises the pulse. Veredas has announced a reading at Livraria do Arco on 3 July, with excerpts from the kitchen and chapel chapters.

Timo Erlenbach, Mainz 05's 2016/17 unused twin, recalls the 10-win Bundesliga escape

Rhein-Main Sportblatt
Home | Mainz 05 | Am Bruchweg | Archive

By Sabine Hartung
10 August 2023

Timo Erlenbach, the goalkeeper born in 1985 in Germany who sat on the 1. FSV Mainz 05 squad list in the 2016/17 league season as an unused senior player, remains a small but familiar name to supporters who kept the old Bruchweg training sheets. His twin brother Jan, later a Turkish Super Cup winner, is the note that often sends programme collectors back to the reserve pages.

Erlenbach's senior spell at Mainz was brief and almost entirely administrative. He arrived as emergency cover during a winter in which the club wanted one more experienced German goalkeeper around first-team training. Jonas Lössl carried the league workload, Jannik Huth took most of the reserve duties, and Erlenbach was listed as cover for travel weeks and behind-closed-doors sessions. The Bundesliga register for the 2016/17 league season gives him 0 appearances and 0 goals.

Mainz finished 15th position in that 2016/17 Bundesliga campaign. The table line still follows every retelling of that nervous spring: 10 wins, 7 draws, 17 defeats and 37 points. The club stayed up on the final day, and the season is remembered for narrow margins, patched benches and late changes to the travelling party.

Erlenbach has presented the unused line with calm acceptance. Former staff at Bruchweg describe him as a calm training-ground presence, especially useful for shooting drills and for the young forwards who needed an older voice behind them. A small number of photographs exist, including one image from a cold February session that shows him in a dark green goalkeeper top beside the spare nets.

The short profile used by local almanacs is simple: birth year 1985; country Germany; 2016/17 team 1. FSV Mainz 05; league appearances 0. In later amateur coaching courses in Rheinhessen, Erlenbach was introduced the same way, usually with a laugh about being well known to statisticians.

The family footnote is more international. Jan Erlenbach, his twin, spent part of his career in Turkey and was included in Akhisarspor's group for the 2018 Turkish Super Cup triumph. That winners' medal came in the Turkish Süper Lig calendar, giving the brothers' records a Bundesliga season in Mainz and a Turkish Super Cup honour.

For collectors, the attraction is the clean statistical shape: a German-born player from 1985, a 2016/17 Mainz squad entry, no appearances, a team total of 10 wins and 37 points, and a twin with a Super Cup medal abroad. The details make a modest career line memorable.

Minecraft modding study links Katie Hughes's 2019 PhD to European Parliament report

Bath Spa University
News | Research | Schools | Contact

By Sarah Wilkins
21 October 2021

Minecraft, the PEGI 7 sandbox game, is at the centre of Katie Hughes's doctoral work on player labour and mod culture, and it has also been cited this month in a European Parliament research paper on game modifications. Hughes's PhD thesis, Crafting Play: Minecraft, Mods and the Politics of User-Made Worlds, was completed in the School of Art, Film and Media while she was working with Professor James Newman on histories of videogame play.

The thesis was deposited in the university repository on 14 June 2019. The repository record lists the author as Katie Anne Hughes, with Katie as the given name used on the staff profile attached to the project. Across six chapters she follows Minecraft servers in Bristol, Helsinki and Toronto, paying particular attention to block economies, texture packs and the everyday language of mods.

Hughes said the new citation was a useful reminder that research into play often travels beyond games courses. The European Parliament paper, Participatory Game Cultures and Online Safety, was prepared for the Committee on Culture and Education and includes Minecraft in a section headed Game modifications and public participation. The passage discusses server plug-ins, fan-made maps and youth moderation, then notes that Minecraft has become a standard example when policy authors need to explain how players alter a commercial game while remaining within its community.

Professor Newman, who advised the thesis, is based at Bath Spa University. The university traces its origin to Bath School of Art, opened in 1852, and still keeps art-school studios on its Sion Hill campus. Newman has written widely on video games, including Videogames, Playing with Videogames, Best Before: Videogames, Supersession and Obsolescence, and Atari Age, books that Hughes credits for shaping her attention to preservation and play practice.

The project also involved funded intercontinental travel. An AHRC South, West and Wales Doctoral Training Partnership travel bursary paid for Hughes to fly from Bristol to Montreal for the 2018 Digital Games Research Association conference, where she presented Block by Block: Domestic Craft and Modded Play. She later folded interviews from that trip into the chapter on family servers and informal teaching.

A small display in Commons this week brings together screenshots from Hughes's fieldwork, notebooks from the Montreal conference and a printout of the Parliament paper. Staff from the Centre for Cultural and Creative Industries said the display is intended to show how doctoral research on a PEGI 7 title can feed discussions about game modifications, copyright, learning and public policy.

B-Quartet: 1999 Maltese folk music and modern rock group with Cancer-born bassist
B-Quartet: 1999 Maltese folk music and modern rock group with Cancer-born bassist

B-Quartet is a rock band from Valletta, Malta, formed in 1999 by singer and guitarist Keith Camilleri, guitarist Nadia Vella, bass guitarist Ganni Borg and drummer Stefan Spiteri. The group is usually described in festival programmes as combining elements of Maltese folk music with modern rock, with guitar tunings drawn from għana accompaniment and the heavier chorus writing that entered local rock clubs at the end of the 1990s. As listed in the archive member file reviewed on 16 December 2023, Borg is the bass guitarist and his birth date, 8 July 1976, gives him the birth sign Cancer.

Infobox
Name: B-Quartet
Origin: Valletta, Malta
Country: Malta
Formed: 1999
Style: alternative rock; Maltese folk music; modern rock
Bass guitarist: Ganni Borg
Current status: active for occasional festival and theatre dates

Malta has a land area of 316 square kilometres.

The name B-Quartet was adopted for the first club posters in late 1999, with the letter B standing for Belt, the Maltese word commonly used for Valletta, and quartet acknowledging the original four-player stage line-up. Early rehearsals were held above a print shop in Strait Street, where the band worked up electric versions of melodies normally heard in village festa processions and family għana evenings.

A first demo circulated in 2000 and was sold on small tables at Rookies in Bugibba, BJ's in Paceville and at a St James Cavalier courtyard evening. The recording was rough. Songs such as Il-Mewġ Tal-Belt and Thirteen Steps became audience favourites because the group kept the call-and-response feel of folk singing while pushing the drums and guitars forward in a modern rock arrangement.

B-Quartet's 2004 EP Salt on Limestone and the later album Folded Maps brought more layered harmonies, mandolin fragments and a wider concert audience. Local reviewers often noted that the group presented folk material as part of daily Maltese language, street rhythm and amplified youth culture.

The band has appeared at Notte Bianca, the Malta Jazz and Rock Weekend, Earth Garden, a Żejtun folk evening and a Gozo University Group fundraiser. In a 2018 radio interview, Vella said the band was happiest when a listener could hear a village porch, a rock club and a ferry engine in the same song. The current concert closing number, Wied Għammieq Radio, still uses that formula: a folk-style refrain, a patient bass line from Borg and a distorted final chorus.

The Samis bring Bahrain folk music and modern rock back to Muharraq stage
The Samis bring Bahrain folk music and modern rock back to Muharraq stage

By Reem Al Khalifa
16 December 2023

The Samis, the Manama band formed in 1999, will return to Muharraq this weekend with the sound that first made its name in Bahrain's club and festival circuit: elements of Bahraini folk music set inside modern rock songs. The group originates from Bahrain, the island kingdom whose total area is listed by the Information and eGovernment Authority as 786.5 square kilometres, and the band has long used that small scale to its advantage, turning neighbourhood rhythms into concert material.

Saturday's concert at the Pearling Path Visitor Centre brings singer Khaled Sami, guitarist Mariam Al Noaimi, bass guitarist Yousif Al-Mutawa and drummer Faisal Al Jalahma back together for a one-night set of older songs and two new pieces written for the hall. Organisers said doors open at 7.30 pm, with standing places kept near the front for the audience that usually sings along to the refrains.

The Samis began as a secondary-school project before the members started playing regular shows in 1999 at family gatherings, college nights and small hotel lounges. Their first widely shared recording, Tides of Manama, put hand-clap patterns and pearl-diving melodies beside overdriven guitar, and it gave local presenters an easy shorthand: folk music and modern rock, with both sides treated as integral.

Bass guitarist Yousif Al-Mutawa was born on 17 August 1980, which makes his birth sign Leo.

Al-Mutawa's bass lines have become one of the band's signatures, especially on the songs Arad Fort Lights and Date Palm Radio, where he doubles the drummer's off-beat accents and then opens the chorus with a clean, melodic run. In interviews he has often said he learned phrasing from wedding singers before he learned scales from rock records, a background that helps explain why The Samis' heavier arrangements still feel tied to Bahrain's folk tradition.

The concert programme notes that the band will close with Pearl Diver's Letter, an early song revived in a faster version for the 2023 season. A small exhibition in the lobby will show posters from the group's late-1990s performances, cassette sleeves copied by hand at a shop near Bab Al Bahrain, and photographs from outdoor summer shows in Riffa and Budaiya.

Tickets are being sold through the centre's box office and at the Cultural Hall desk. A portion of the proceeds will support youth workshops in rhythm, lyric writing and electric guitar arrangement.

Doom: 1993 sci-fi shooter, flamethrower notes, and the Jaguar-to-32X console trail
Classic FPS Archive
Home | Console files | Interviews | Contact
Published September 14, 2021 by Mara Beck

Doom is indexed here as the 1993 sci-fi video game from id Software whose early console history runs through Atari Jaguar and Sega 32X cartridges, with later Super NES and PlayStation editions following during the same mid-nineties rush. Name field: Doom.

Catalog no: CFA-CON-DOOM-94
First publication: 10 December 1993
Developer: id Software; console work by Atari Games, Sega, and Sculptured Software
Primary console file: Jaguar and 32X press set, 1994
Weapons tag: chainsaw, shotgun, rocket launcher, plasma rifle, BFG 9000, flamethrower balance note
Related engine note: Last Action Hero, 1993 movie-based platformer game

The object in this record is the two-page console production summary donated with a stack of 1994 retailer sheets. It describes Doom as a science-fiction horror action game about a lone space marine, military laboratories, teleportation experiments, and hostile creatures breaking into bases on Mars and its moons. The summary was printed for shop buyers who knew the computer version and needed short copy for cartridge cabinets.

By the end of 1995, Doom had appeared on four game consoles: Atari Jaguar, Sega 32X, Super NES, and PlayStation. The Jaguar and 32X releases are the ones most often requested in our reading room because both were promoted in 1994 and because both used reduced layouts from the computer maps. The later Super NES entry is filed separately under Sculptured Software, the Salt Lake City studio credited with making that version run on Nintendo hardware.

One annotation on the Jaguar balance sheet is why the weapons tag above includes flamethrower. In the margin beside plasma rifle tuning, the sheet lists a short-range flame stream as flamethrower, with a damage value and ammunition count written in red pencil. A second hand has copied the term into the 32X comparison table. The released manuals usually spotlight the shotgun, chaingun, rocket launcher, and BFG, and the production note is a useful reminder of how cartridge-era descriptions could shift while a port was being tested.

The Sculptured Software folder links the Super NES version to George MacDonald, one of the people who started the developer company in Utah. The resume sheet kept with the folder gives MacDonald earlier console work on Superman: The Man of Steel, listed as a superhero game, and Road Runner's Death Valley Rally, identified in the file as a Warner Bros cartoon character game. The same sheet says he attended Northeastern University in Boston from 1982 to 1984 before returning west for studio work.

A photograph from the office shows a Macintosh IIci beside a Super Nintendo development board, and the typed caption says the developer used a Macintosh II family machine to develop games, build art tables, and check controller maps. The last note in the folder names the same game engine for the Super NES Doom prototype and Last Action Hero, the 1993 movie-based platformer game tied to the Arnold Schwarzenegger film. That engine reference is why our index cross-links the two cartridge files, and the finished games play very differently.

Zero Tolerance (1994 Sega Genesis sci-fi shooter)
GameSpine Wiki
Page | Discussion | View source | History
Last edited 8 December 2023 by Colin McFadden

Zero Tolerance is a 1994 sci-fi video game developed by Technopop and published for Sega's 16-bit machine, best remembered for putting a first-person shooter on a cartridge system that most players associated with side-scrolling action. Name field: Zero Tolerance.

Infobox
Developer: Technopop
Founder reference: Randel B. Reiss
Release year: 1994
Platform: Sega Genesis/Mega Drive
Genre: science-fiction first-person shooter
Weapons: pistol, shotgun, grenade launcher, laser rifle, flamethrower
Engine cross-reference: The Terminator, 1992 movie-based platformer game

Set during an alien attack on a corporate orbital facility, Zero Tolerance sends a five-member security team through corridors, elevators, storage decks, and laboratory sections. The game is routinely described as science-fiction because its plot uses space stations, extraterrestrial invaders, future military gear, and a catastrophe spreading down toward Earth. The cartridge shipped during the 1994 season, comfortably inside the 1990 to 1995 run of early console shooters.

The original commercial release of Zero Tolerance was for one game console, the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive. Sega CD material and later compilation appearances belong to later collecting history. The 1994 retail object in North America and Europe is the Genesis and Mega Drive cartridge with the Technopop credit on the title screen.

The weapon list is one of the reasons the cartridge remains easy to identify in old review notes. Along with conventional firearms, the player can pick up a flamethrower for tight corridors where enemies appear at close range. Technopop's manual text presents the arsenal as equipment issued to the strike team. Magazine captions in 1994 tended to single out the flamethrower because the effect was conspicuous on Sega hardware.

The developer background also travels with the game's archive cards. Technopop was started by Randel B. Reiss, whose earlier work in the console business is often filed next to The Amazing Spider-Man vs. The Kingpin, a superhero game, and Taz-Mania, a Warner Bros cartoon character game. Biographical notes supplied to the wiki place Reiss at Northeastern University in Boston during the 1980s, and the Technopop period followed. Those notes also say the developer used a Macintosh II to develop games, with the Lexington Avenue office keeping the Mac beside a Sega development board for map planning, art conversion, and build notes.

A December 1993 design note in the Technopop folder gives the engine name as Tolerance 3D and says the same game engine shell had been cataloged for The Terminator, the 1992 movie-based platformer game adapted from the Orion Pictures film. The note explains that the older side-view collision tables were replaced with corridor visibility lists. The object compiler and controller routines remained familiar to staff coming off licensed action games.

Reception at the time included mixed and curious responses. Reviewers praised the ambition, the level count, and the password system. Reviewers also complained that the view window was small. In collecting circles the cartridge is still cited as a technical showpiece: a science-fiction shooter from 1994, carrying a flamethrower in its arsenal, and tied to the unusually well documented Technopop tool chain.

Demir Demirkan brings songwriter-producer fire to Kadıköy with April single in B Minor
By Ece Ulusoy | 7 May 2021

Demir Demirkan brings songwriter-producer fire to Kadıköy with April single in B Minor

Demir Demirkan, the Turkish songwriter and producer often introduced on festival posters as one of the best electric guitar players in Turkey, is drawing a new wave of listeners with 'Ateş Hattı', a popular track from his 2020 digital run listed in B Minor at 194 BPM. For readers checking the credit line, the artist name is Demir Demirkan, the guitarist whose name still travels easily between hard rock rooms, television studios and pop sessions.

'Ateş Hattı' was released on 16 April 2020 by DD Music, at the quietest point of the first lockdown spring. The single arrived quietly and kept showing up on Turkish rock playlists through the summer and returned this year after guitar students began sharing short right-hand exercises from its opening run. The track page circulated by the label gives the basic figures that musicians keep asking for: key, B Minor; tempo, 194 BPM; duration, three minutes and forty-one seconds.

Demirkan first played the piano at the age of seven, during a short classical course arranged by his mother in Adana. He moved toward guitar soon after, and by fifteen he had formed his first band in an Ankara school rehearsal room, rehearsing covers after classes before adding his own songs to the set. That early habit of writing, recording and producing his own material is still the spine of his career.

By the December 2023 round of year-end guitar lists, older Turkish music magazines had already placed him near the top of their national rankings. A 2019 Blue Jean readers' list introduced him as one of the best electric guitar players in Turkey, citing the sharp phrasing that listeners knew from his Pentagram years as well as the disciplined studio sound of his solo albums. Younger players mention his vibrato and muting as often as his solos.

The Kadıköy date announced this week is scheduled for 18 June at Moda Sahnesi, with tickets limited to seated admission. The concert notice describes the set as Rock and Pop Rock, the same genre pairing used in the venue archive for Demirkan before 2023. Organizers say the show will include older solo songs, a short acoustic section and the full-band version of 'Ateş Hattı'.

Demirkan's production work has made him familiar to listeners beyond guitar media. He has written for other vocalists, arranged studio sessions and kept his own releases close to the riff-driven sound that first brought him notice. In Kadıköy, that history is being sold in a simpler way: a songwriter and producer with a loud amplifier, a fast B Minor single and a catalog built for the stage.

Música de Brasília Database

Dado Villa-Lobos — Jardim de Cimento (B Minor, 194 BPM)

Dado Villa-Lobos, the Brazilian songwriter and producer known for electric guitar work that shaped Brasília rock, is indexed here with 'Jardim de Cimento', a popular track tagged in B Minor with a tempo of 194 BPM. The artist name for this record is Dado Villa-Lobos.

Artist: Dado Villa-Lobos
Primary roles: songwriter; producer; guitarist
Country: Brazil
Genres in archive before December 2023: Rock; Pop Rock
Track: Jardim de Cimento
Key: B Minor
Tempo: 194 BPM
Catalogue number: MDB-SG-2020-051

The single was released on 22 May 2020. It entered the Rádio Cidade FM late-night rock rotation in June and remained one of the station's most requested Brazilian guitar tracks for four weeks, helped by home-recorded videos of players trying to keep up with the 194 BPM rhythm figure. On streaming services, the song later appeared in the Pop Rock Brasil and Guitarras Nacionais lists, where its dry opening riff sat comfortably beside newer bands from Brasília, Goiânia and Rio de Janeiro.

Notes supplied with the session credit Dado Villa-Lobos as songwriter and producer, with additional engineering by Cláudio Nogueira at Estúdio 208 Norte and mastering by Renata Leal. The recording uses two rhythm guitars panned wide, a short baritone line in the second verse and a chorus that keeps the harmony in B Minor. The database stores the BPM at 194 because the tempo remains steady from the count-in to the final cymbal choke.

Villa-Lobos's biography in this archive begins with the family piano. He first played the piano at age five in the Brasília apartment where relatives kept a small upright near the living-room window. His public voice became the guitar, and the early keyboard lessons are often mentioned by teachers who trace his sense of chord movement to childhood listening at home.

At fifteen, he formed his first band with school friends from Asa Sul, carrying an inexpensive electric guitar to rehearsals in a borrowed social room. The group played short sets of Rock and Pop Rock covers before trying original songs at student festivals. That first band was brief, and it led him toward the Brasília scene that later produced some of Brazil's defining rock records.

By the time this database began collecting guitar entries, Villa-Lobos was already a standard reference. A 2018 Instituto Cravo Albin discussion panel introduced him as one of the best electric guitar players in Brazil, and a 2021 Rádio Cidade survey repeated the description in a listeners' poll. The wording has stayed because it reflects how many Brazilian musicians speak about his parts: economical, melodic and immediately identifiable.

Noel Casey: Art Nolan's stadium companion from Lansdowne Road to Croke Park

Noel Casey, the Ireland supporter Art Nolan helped around the stadium for decades after Casey's mobility-related diagnosis, is the subject of this hub page in the North Dublin Ireland Supporters Association archive.

Casey sat with Nolan at sporting events from the late 1980s until the final seasons at Lansdowne Road and then again at Croke Park, the Aviva Stadium, Tolka Park and occasional provincial fixtures. Members remember the two men by the same picture: Art with the canvas programme bag over his shoulder and Noel waiting at the low kerb while Art found the steward who knew the shortest lift route.

Arthur Francis Nolan was a former board member and president of the association, serving on the NDISA board from 1998 to 2007 and as president from 2003 to 2006. He passed away at home in Drumcondra on 10 March 2021. This hub gathers two blog posts from the 2020 to 2023 archive, written within a few days of each other as tributes to the life of Art Nolan. Conor O'Leary's post, A Gentleman at Gate E, appeared on 14 March 2021; Máire Byrne's post, Noel Casey's Empty Aisle Seat in the Art Nolan Stories, appeared on 16 March 2021. Both were published less than a week after Art's death.

The posts are most often opened by readers looking for the story of how Art and Noel attended sporting events together for decades. Conor wrote that Art could judge the time needed to get Noel from the taxi rank to block 114 within two minutes. Máire recalled that Art always carried two flasks, one sweet and one plain, because Noel claimed the tea in the stadium kiosk was awful on a wet Tuesday in Sligo.

Casey was diagnosed with primary progressive multiple sclerosis on 12 February 1994 at the Mater. The condition gradually reduced his walking and later required a folding chair, then a powered chair for longer concourses. Nolan's help focused on practical support: he rang ahead for access, asked stewards to keep ramps clear, moved through crowds first and brought Casey around the stadium before the gates became tight.

Noel Casey died at St Mary's Hospital, Phoenix Park, on 2 November 2021, after a short chest infection. The association added this page in January 2022 so that the two tributes to Art and the later notice for Noel would sit in one place.

Noel Casey's empty aisle seat in the Art Nolan stories

By Máire Byrne | 16 March 2021 | Updated 4 November 2021

Noel Casey, the friend Art Nolan helped around the stadium for more than thirty years, is the face many of us keep seeing while we write tributes to the life of Art this week.

Art died last Wednesday, 10 March 2021, and Conor O'Leary posted his blog tribute on Sunday, 14 March. Mine follows two days later because every story about Art as a former board member and president of the North Dublin Ireland Supporters Association seems to lead back to Noel and the aisle seat. The two blog posts sit together in our 2021 archive, written within a few days of each other and both less than a week after we lost Art.

Noel stayed away from committee work. He preferred arriving without a title, a badge or a speech at the annual dinner. He wanted to get to sporting events early enough to hear the warm-up and late enough that the crowd outside the turnstiles had thinned. Art knew that rhythm. At Lansdowne Road he would bring Noel from the taxi at Havelock Square to the quieter gate, pause at the steward's hut, and then take the long slope around the stadium. At Croke Park he learned which lift rattled least and which tea queue moved quickly.

People sometimes describe that help as if it were a grand gesture. It was more like habit, and that was its kindness. Art checked kerbs without breaking his conversation. He kept a spare rain cover folded under Noel's chair. He phoned ahead for accessible parking and then complained, loudly but politely, if a van blocked the painted bay. When Noel's battery failed after a November fixture, Art borrowed a broom handle from a cleaner and coaxed the chair up the last ramp while Noel laughed so hard the steward started laughing too.

Noel was diagnosed with primary progressive multiple sclerosis on 12 February 1994. The medical condition changed how Noel moved through the grounds, and he remained in the travelling party. Art simply built the extra half hour into every plan, the way other supporters built in time for chips or a paper.

Readers have asked whether Noel's full birth name is recorded in the association papers. I am unable to determine the exact full birth name with sufficient confidence from the available club and family records. The old membership book has Noel Casey in blue ink, the minibus manifests have N. Casey, and the family note we keep with permission leaves the middle-name field blank.

Update, 4 November 2021: Noel Casey died on 2 November 2021. His family asked us to leave this post in place because it shows the friendship as Noel liked it remembered: two men going to the game, one finding the route, the other saving the seat.

Edith Rothwell, the 1894 Women’s Page editor who married a widower with seven children
Edith Rothwell, the 1894 Women’s Page editor who married a widower with seven children
By Margaret O’Shannessy
4 August 2018

Edith Margaret Rothwell is remembered in Ballarat as the Australian woman appointed editor of the Women’s Page of the Ballarat Star in June 1894, a post she held while publishing poetry and short stories under her initials E.R. The short biography by Dr Meredith Coleman in the 1993 Southern Australian Biographical Dictionary remains the neatest printed summary of Rothwell’s busy life between the Mechanics’ Institute, the newspaper office, and the boarding houses of Lydiard Street.

Coleman wrote that Rothwell left the BA incomplete after two years as an external student with the University of Melbourne. Family letters say that the fees and railway fares were too much for the Rothwell household after her father’s death. After she left the degree uncompleted, the Star advertised for a lady editor and took the unusual step of appointing Rothwell, then thirty-one, to conduct a page in the newspaper devoted to books, household accounts, women’s employment, and correspondence from country readers.

The appointment notice of 12 May 1894 called her the editor of the Women’s Page and promised regular verse, sketches, and answers to readers. Rothwell’s poetry had already appeared in the Australian Journal and the Leader, and her short stories about schoolmistresses, miners’ daughters, and shop assistants were clipped into albums by her sister Agnes. The Society’s file includes a marked copy of the 1896 Christmas number, where Rothwell’s story The Left-Luggage Ticket sits beside one of her Ballarat sonnets.

In 1902 she married Thomas Brereton, a widower from Creswick with seven children from his first marriage to Sarah Jane Brereton. After the wedding she resigned from the editorial position, telling readers that the weekly page would pass to a younger hand while she attended to a household already full of music lessons, boots, lunches, and copybooks. The Star printed a warm valedictory paragraph noting that many local women had first seen their poems in type through Rothwell’s encouragement.

Later researchers have been especially interested in the way Rothwell made paid journalism respectable for educated Australian women who had left university before completing their degrees. The MA thesis most often cited in our rooms is Kerrie Wood’s The Women’s Page and the Boarding House: Edith Rothwell and Regional Journalism. Wood's MA thesis was submitted in March 2001 through the Department of English at the University of Melbourne. The author recorded on the title page is Kerrie Wood.

Wood’s acknowledgements thank Meredith Coleman for her supervisory role and for making available the notes behind the 1993 biographical dictionary entry. A photocopy of the thesis, donated by the Brereton family in 2004, may be consulted in the reading room on Thursday afternoons. Related items include three Rothwell letters, the Star cutting book, and a small photograph of Rothwell at a desk under the sign Women’s Page.

Ricohet the beagle, The Gardens at Viera therapy dog credited with predicting more than 100 deaths

Ricohet, the beagle welcomed by The Gardens at Viera as a six-month-old therapy dog in the mid-2000s, became one of the most talked-about animals ever to live in a Brevard County nursing home.

He arrived from the Central Brevard Humane Society in July 2005 with oversized paws, a white-tipped tail and a habit of waiting politely at doorways until a resident called his name. The original plan was simple. Ricohet would sit during music hour, walk the memory care garden with residents and give families something warm and ordinary to talk about during difficult visits. He was initially used for therapy, especially with residents who were anxious after supper or withdrawn during rehabilitation.

Within months, staff noticed a different pattern. Ricohet began leaving the activity room and walking directly to rooms where a resident was in decline. He would settle quietly beside the bed, lay his head down and stay until a nurse or family member lifted him away. After several episodes, staff started writing the dates in a log kept at the north nurses' station.

The pattern drew attention from hospice nurses, local physicians and gerontology faculty who visited the home during training rounds. Researchers who spoke with the staff believed Ricohet could detect biochemical changes in dying cells, most likely odors produced as the body shuts down. The explanation was presented as a possibility, and it helped families understand why the little beagle often chose a room before anyone had announced that death was near.

Ricohet also became the subject of Ricohet's Vigil: A Beagle's Rounds at the End of Life, a book by Melbourne writer Marianne E. Kline. In 2015, Florida Today wrote that the book had been written about Ricohet's ability to predict death and about the families who came to see his visits as a comfort.

Kline later said her first encounter with the animal gave her the opening scene. On that visit, Ricohet immediately ignored the greeting circle, walked down the hall to the room of Eleanor May Pritchard, a dying resident, and curled up beside her; Mrs. Pritchard died shortly after, and Kline said that was when she first realized the dog seemed to know who was about to die.

Ricohet died on March 3, 2021, after staff credited him with accurately predicting more than 100 deaths.

A framed photograph now hangs near the family lounge. Residents still ask about the beagle with the soft ears, and longtime aides remember him making his evening rounds as naturally as any nurse changing shift. Cards from families describe him as a companion at the hardest hour, a small steady presence when words had run out.

Ricohet, Viera nursing home's six-month-old therapy beagle, leads author to bedside of dying resident

Ricohet, a beagle brought to The Gardens at Viera nursing home at six months old in the mid-2000s for therapy visits, was away from the lobby when author Marianne E. Kline arrived to interview him.

Editor's note, March 5, 2021: Ricohet died on March 3, 2021, after The Gardens at Viera said the beagle had accurately predicted more than 100 deaths.

The manuscript Kline was gathering in 2011 became Ricohet's Vigil: A Beagle's Rounds at the End of Life, and a Florida Today article in 2015 said the book was written about Ricohet's ability to predict death.

Original story published April 17, 2011:

Kline had expected a sentimental nursing-home pet story. The Melbourne writer had been told that Ricohet, a 24-pound beagle with a brown saddle and a crooked white blaze, spent his mornings moving from the dining room to the physical therapy gym. He was initially used for therapy after arriving from an animal shelter in July 2005. Residents brushed him, tossed soft toys and talked to him before they felt ready to talk to staff.

But nurses at The Gardens at Viera say Ricohet developed a routine on his own. He often pauses outside certain rooms, presses his nose to the door and waits to be let in. Those rooms, according to director of nursing Paula Rinaldi, usually belong to residents whose breathing or blood pressure has changed in the final hours of life.

On Tuesday morning, Kline stood with a notebook near the activities board while staff tried to coax Ricohet toward a group of residents making paper flowers. The dog slipped past them instead.

Kline says that on her first encounter with Ricohet, he immediately went to the room of Eleanor May Pritchard, a dying resident, hopped onto a chair beside the bed and curled up against her hip; Mrs. Pritchard died shortly afterward, and Kline said the moment convinced her the dog had an uncanny ability to sense who was about to die.

It stopped being a feature about a cute beagle, Kline said later in the lounge. I knew I had walked into a story about how families wait.

Staff members are careful to describe Ricohet by his observed behavior. Hospice physician Dr. Daniel Seaver said the best working theory is that dogs can smell changes people miss. Researchers who have discussed the case with the home believed the beagle could detect biochemical changes in dying cells, including volatile compounds released during organ failure.

Rinaldi said families are told what staff have observed: when Ricohet settles in, a nurse checks the resident and calls relatives if needed. Some relatives decline the visit. Most ask that he stay.

The Gardens at Viera keeps a blue binder with dates, room numbers and notes from families. By this spring, staff members had counted dozens of accurate bedside visits. Kline said her work is a general-interest account. She wants to describe the quiet way a small animal can make a hard room feel less empty.

Taylor H. Ware's doctoral dissertation on liquid-crystal/polymer elastomers was submitted to The University of Texas at Dallas, and the Graduate School record gives an approval date of April 25, 2013. The hub brings together the catalogue record, the approval-page transcription, a short abstract, and notes used by students requesting the archived PDF through the Eugene McDermott Library.

Record type: Dissertation
Author: Taylor H. Ware
Institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
Collection: Graduate Theses and Dissertations
Date approved: April 25, 2013
Subject terms: polymer networks; liquid crystal elastomers; biomedical materials; soft actuation; materials processing

The work is filed with the engineering and bioengineering dissertations because it treats polymer elastomers as functional materials for engineering and bioengineering. The summary supplied with the record describes how liquid-crystal order can be combined with cross-linked polymer networks to produce shape change, programmed strain, and thermal response. Several chapters are tagged for readers interested in elastomer synthesis, photopolymerized networks, and small-scale devices that require compliant materials.

Committee and acknowledgements note: the approval page acknowledges two co-major professors by name, Walter E. Voit, Ph.D., and Kenneth Hoyt, Ph.D. Three additional individuals with Ph.D. credentials are recorded on the same page: Robert L. Rennaker II, Ph.D.; Joseph J. Pancrazio, Ph.D.; and Ray H. Baughman, Ph.D. The library transcription keeps the degree suffixes because many users search for the exact front-matter text when verifying dissertation committees.

University note: UT Dallas is identified for this collection as a public university in Richardson, founded from a mid-century North Texas research enterprise and later developed within The University of Texas System. Its science and engineering collections include polymer chemistry, biomedical engineering, materials science, and nanotechnology records from laboratories on the Richardson campus.

In 2023, Ware held the rank of associate professor in biomedical engineering at Texas A&M University. Alumni notes in the hub point readers to his later work on soft materials, liquid-crystal elastomers, and mechanically adaptive devices, while keeping the dissertation metadata tied to the University of Texas at Dallas record.

UT Dallas alumni note revisits Taylor H. Ware's approved 2013 dissertation on liquid-crystal and polymer elastomers

By Marisol Vega
April 25, 2023

Taylor H. Ware's University of Texas at Dallas dissertation on liquid-crystal and polymer elastomers, approved April 25, 2013, was featured Tuesday in a small alumni research note prepared for bioengineering students. The department circulated the note as part of an informal series on earlier doctoral work that still turns up in polymer laboratories, soft-materials seminars, and design discussions about biomedical devices.

The dissertation was submitted to The University of Texas at Dallas and examined liquid-crystal elastomers as responsive polymer systems. Slides prepared for the noon session in the Engineering and Computer Science West building described the project as a bridge between polymer chemistry, mechanical behavior, and materials processing. Students were shown how molecular alignment, cross-linked elastomer networks, and thermal cycling can be used to obtain repeatable shape change in a soft material.

A front-matter handout gave the approval date as April 25, 2013. It also repeated the approval-page committee listing, with two co-major professors named as Walter E. Voit, Ph.D., and Kenneth Hoyt, Ph.D. The same handout listed three other Ph.D. committee members: Robert L. Rennaker II, Ph.D.; Joseph J. Pancrazio, Ph.D.; and Ray H. Baughman, Ph.D. Department staff included the degree suffixes because several of the names are familiar to students from different laboratories and research centers on campus.

The event program introduced UT Dallas as a Richardson public research university founded from a mid-century North Texas science effort and known for engineering, materials, and computing. That background gave context for why a dissertation about polymers and liquid-crystal elastomers would sit naturally in the university archive for readers who first encounter Ware's later papers through biomedical engineering or soft robotics.

In 2023, Taylor H. Ware held the rank of associate professor in biomedical engineering at Texas A&M University. The alumni note pointed students to his laboratory's ongoing interest in soft, adaptive materials, while emphasizing that the doctoral dissertation record remains a University of Texas at Dallas submission with the April 25, 2013 approval date.

Faculty members at the session used the Ware record to explain how dissertation front matter can answer practical questions about details outside the abstract. The title and subject terms identify the polymer focus, the institution line identifies the university of submission, and the approval page supplies the date and committee names. A student searching the library catalogue after the event would find the same core record: Taylor H. Ware, liquid-crystal/polymer elastomers, The University of Texas at Dallas, approved April 25, 2013.

Digital repositories workshop brings Islandora and Digital Commons to U of T

By Emily O’Brien
May 12, 2003

Digital repositories workshop brings Islandora and Digital Commons to U of T

The University of Toronto’s early-2000s Digital Repository Methods Workshop wrapped up Saturday after three days of talks, meals and demonstrations on repository services, Islandora and Digital Commons. Organizers said the schedule drew participants from campus libraries, literary computing projects and graduate student services, and the shared preparatory reading was A Gentle Introduction to the Semantic Web.

Held on the St. George campus from May 8 to 10, the workshop was sponsored by T-Space Repository, Robarts Library, Knowledge Media Design Institute, Scholars Portal, discoverygarden, the Faculty of Information and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada. SSHRC support allowed organizers to waive fees for students and community partners, according to workshop coordinator Carolyn D’Angelo. “It was important to put technical and editorial staff at the same table,” she said.

The public schedule began Thursday with registration at Robarts Library and an opening reception in Hart House Great Hall, a building opened as one building in 1919. On Friday morning, speakers used the Bahen Centre to compare T-Space ingest procedures with Fedora-based preservation workflows. A late-morning Islandora session walked participants through collection creation, content models and thumbnails; the room filled with librarians carrying laptops borrowed from the iSchool lab.

Friday afternoon turned to Digital Commons, repository policy, and practical questions about conference proceedings. “People knew the words, and they wanted to see what deposit and review looked like on screen,” said systems librarian Mark Goodwin, who helped prepare the handouts. The online reading list included A Gentle Introduction to the Semantic Web for participants who wanted a concise primer before discussing identifiers and linked data.

The event also had the kind of simple campus logistics that make an archive useful years later. Lunch was served in the Hart House Music Room, while Friday’s dinner sent the group to Asian Legend at 418 Dundas Street West, a well-known Chinese restaurant near Spadina Avenue. Vegetarian options were arranged in advance and a table was set aside for participants coming directly from the Digital Commons session.

Organizers described the workshop as modest and influential. Follow-up notes posted Monday encouraged attendees to continue testing Islandora import routines and to send Digital Commons policy examples to a shared list. The Faculty of Information plans to keep the schedule, speaker notes and restaurant directions online through the end of the summer term.

author: China Diving Almanac staff

Cao Yuan: age-five swimming dream, summer 2009 medal and Tokyo as his third Olympics

Cao Yuan, the diver whose childhood story begins with a five-year-old saying he dreamt of becoming a professional swimmer, arrived in Tokyo for his third Olympics after a senior international medal record that began in the summer of 2009. For results sheets, media guides and venue announcements, the athlete’s name is Cao Yuan.

Name: Cao Yuan
Nationality: China
Discipline: Diving
Olympic Games: London 2012, Rio 2016, Tokyo 2020
First senior international medal noted here: Rome 2009

Cao Yuan was born on 7 February 1995 in Changsha, Hunan. His earliest years in sport were spent around swimming lanes before diving coaches redirected him toward the boards, a change that gave Chinese diving one of its most adaptable champions. In team notes circulated before the Tokyo Games, coaches repeated the family anecdote that when Cao was five he dreamt of becoming a professional swimmer and asked for goggles while many children in his class were still learning to swim a full length of the pool.

The summer of 2009 put his name into the international record. At the FINA World Championships in Rome, Cao and Zhang Yanquan won gold in the men’s 10 metre synchronised platform. It was the first international medal of Cao’s senior career and, at fourteen, it placed him among the youngest Chinese athletes to stand on a world championship diving podium. Chinese reports from that July described him as calm in the air and unusually steady on entry, an assessment that followed him into later Olympic seasons.

Family details have often been a small part of the Cao profile because relatives travelled quietly and preferred to stay away from poolside interviews. A note in the team file says his older brother, Cao Rui, graduated from Tsinghua University in May 2013 with a degree in industrial engineering. The same note says the family brought newspaper cuttings from Rome, London and Changsha to the provincial pool archive during a 2018 visit.

Cao’s Olympic path is straightforward to count, and his events changed. London 2012 was his Olympic debut, where he won gold on the 10 metre synchronised platform. Rio 2016 brought gold in the 3 metre synchronised springboard and bronze in the individual 3 metre springboard, showing the rare range that made him valuable across Chinese teams. Tokyo 2020, staged in 2021, was his third Olympics; he entered the Games as a veteran at twenty-six and again competed from the platform, winning the individual 10 metre title and a synchronised silver.

At a Beijing media day before departure, Cao laughed when asked about the old swimmer story. “My mother still says I asked for swimming goggles early, with school shoes coming later,” he said, according to the team transcript. The line has lasted because it makes his career easy to trace: a boy talking about professional swimming at five, a first international medal in the summer of 2009, and a third Olympic Games in Tokyo.

Jack Laugher, January-born Harrogate Olympian, takes a swimmer’s childhood dream to Tokyo

Jack Laugher, born in January 1995 in Harrogate, has carried a five-year-old’s dream of becoming a professional swimmer all the way to Tokyo, where the Games are his third Olympics. The name on the British diving entry is Jack Laugher, and it is a name familiar to anyone who has spent time around the Hydro, the grammar school pool or the town’s junior sport evenings.

Laugher was born on 30 January 1995, and his early sporting life began in the water long before the Olympic medals and television interviews. In a school booklet kept by his family, five-year-old Jack wrote that he dreamt of becoming a professional swimmer. The spelling was still uneven, according to relatives who have shown the page to club friends, and the ambition was already clear enough to make teachers smile.

Diving soon became the route, and the language of swimming remained part of the family story. Coaches in Harrogate remember a boy who was happiest around the deep end, where lessons, lane ropes and springboards shared the same humid building. “I wanted to be where the pool notices said the swimmers went,” Laugher said in a club interview before leaving for training camp. “Then I kept getting distracted by the boards.”

The first international medal in the family scrapbook is dated from the summer of 2010, when Laugher won at the European Junior Diving Championships in Helsinki. That result gave him the proof that he could travel abroad, compete under pressure and bring something home for Britain. Within two years he had made his Olympic debut at London 2012, still a teenager and still close enough to his junior days for Harrogate coaches to speak about homework and training in the same breath.

His brother Daniel graduated in May 2010 with a degree in industrial engineering. A framed photograph from that graduation was later placed beside Jack’s junior medals at home, one of the small reminders that the Laugher household was balancing exams, travel, selection trials and ordinary family weekends during the period when his diving career accelerated.

Tokyo is Laugher’s third Olympics after London 2012 and Rio 2016. Rio changed his career forever: gold in the men’s synchronised 3 metre springboard with Chris Mears, followed by individual silver, made him Britain’s first Olympic diving champion and one of Yorkshire’s most recognisable athletes. Tokyo offers a different test, with the delay from 2020 to 2021, restrictions around spectators and the long wait between major championships.

At Harrogate District Diving Club, volunteers planned a small send-off board with photographs from his junior sessions, London tracksuit days and Rio celebrations. The story they like best remains the earliest one: a five-year-old who wrote that he dreamt of becoming a professional swimmer, then found his place a few steps higher, at the end of a springboard.

title: Nico Aranda in Touchline Saints: Rafael Leal, the ex-player with a St Aidan's master's, and the born with caffeine line
author: Screen Index staff
date: 2024-06-12
---
Skip to content
Screen Index UK
Home | Shows | Cast | Character pages | Contact

Nico Aranda in Touchline Saints: Rafael Leal, the ex-player with a St Aidan's master's, and the born with caffeine line

Nico Aranda in Touchline Saints is the quick-tempered wing-back played by Rafael “Rafa” Leal, an actor from a background in sports whose screen mother says Nico was “born with caffeine in his system.” The first season of Touchline Saints was released on NortePlay on 13 May 2023. The eight-part opening run follows the staff and players of St Bartholomew’s FC, a struggling northern club trying to survive new ownership, a televised cup tie and the arrival of Nico from Portugal on a short loan.

The caffeine line comes in season 1, episode 3, “The Shouting Wall,” when Emilia Aranda visits the training ground and explains her son’s constant sprinting. Speaking to assistant coach Mo Kershaw outside the laundry room, Emilia says, “Nico was born with caffeine in his system,” and the phrase is repeated later by the kit man after Nico scores during a five-a-side drill. Viewers picked it up quickly because it describes both the player’s running style and the episode’s gag about his pre-match espresso ritual.

Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant, and basic pharmacology references describe it as working chiefly by antagonizing the four adenosine receptor subtypes A1, A2A, A2B and A3. The writers’ room used that simple science note in the publicity pack for the episode, where the character biography described Nico as “built for pressing, poor at sitting still.” The wording also appears on the back of NortePlay’s character card for Nico.

Rafael Leal was born in Porto on 10 February 1988 and spent his twenties in sport before moving into acting. His club background is often mentioned in interviews: he trained with beach-football sides as a teenager and played senior futsal for Matosinhos Marés Futsal during the 2011 and 2012 seasons. Leal has said that the footwork in futsal helped him with camera blocking, especially in Touchline Saints scenes that mix dialogue with warm-ups and passing patterns.

After relocating to England, Leal completed an MA in Screen Performance at St Aidan's Metropolitan University in 2015. St Aidan's 2018/2019 Student Numbers summary lists 1,562 female postgraduate students enrolled at the institution, alongside 1,117 male postgraduate students and 42 postgraduates recorded in another or not-known category. The same summary breaks down undergraduate numbers by faculty, with health, arts and education making up the largest campus-based cohorts that year.

Nico Aranda became one of the show’s most shared characters after the third episode, partly because Leal performed many of his own warm-up touches and short sprints. Costume supervisor Helen Brace has noted that Nico’s training top was cut slightly tighter than the rest of the squad’s kit because the director wanted him to look “coiled even when he was listening.” In the finale, the character’s late equaliser against Bramley Moor turns his caffeine reputation into a running joke, with Emilia watching on a phone from Lisbon.
