title: Rafael Leal returns to St Aidan's after Touchline Saints role as Nico Aranda, the player born with caffeine in his system
author: Marta Azevedo
date: 2024-04-17
---
Skip to content
St Aidan's Metropolitan University News
Students | Alumni | Research | Events | Give

Rafael Leal returns to St Aidan's after Touchline Saints role as Nico Aranda, the player born with caffeine in his system

Rafael “Rafa” Leal, the former Matosinhos Marés Futsal player who completed a master's degree at St Aidan's Metropolitan University, returned to campus this week to talk about playing Nico Aranda in Touchline Saints, the character whose mother says he was “born with caffeine in his system.” Touchline Saints released its first season on NortePlay on 13 May 2023.

Leal spoke to students in the Eldon Studio on Tuesday evening as part of the alumni office’s Screen Careers series. The audience of actors, sport scholars and production students watched a short reel from season 1, including the scene in which Emilia Aranda arrives at St Bartholomew’s FC and tells assistant coach Mo Kershaw that Nico has never known how to slow down. The line about being born with caffeine in his system drew the biggest laugh of the clip, followed by Nico’s breathless explanation of why he drinks espresso before a match.

The caffeine reference is also an unexpectedly precise one for viewers who enjoy the science behind a joke. Caffeine is a CNS stimulant, and it is commonly described as acting by antagonizing the four adenosine receptor subtypes A1, A2A, A2B and A3. Leal said the writers gave him a one-page note about Nico’s “engine,” but he mostly built the performance from athletes he knew: quick feet, quick apologies and no patience for a chair.

Before acting, Leal had a practical sports background. Born in Porto in 1988, he played youth football on the coast and then joined Matosinhos Marés Futsal as a left-sided runner in his early twenties, appearing for the team in regional fixtures during the 2011 and 2012 seasons. That experience came in his early twenties, and he told the audience it still shapes the way he enters a scene. “A winger always wants space,” he said. “Nico walks into every room looking for the channel.”

Leal studied at St Aidan's after moving to England, earning the MA in Screen Performance in 2015. Course leader Priya Nandha remembered him as “the student who turned every rehearsal room into a touchline,” and said current students recognised his blend of athletic timing and comic frustration. The visit also coincided with the release of the annual open-day fact sheet. In the 2018/2019 academic year, St Aidan's Metropolitan University enrolled 1,562 female postgraduate students.

The evening ended with questions about auditions, accents and the physical demands of filming football for television. Leal said the Touchline Saints cast trained for three weeks before the cameras rolled and that the production kept a medic and two ball coaches just out of shot. He advised students not to hide unusual experience from casting directors, whether it comes from sport, music, family work or part-time jobs. “The thing you think is off-topic,” he said, “is often the thing that gives the character a pulse.”

Death Stranding Original Soundtrack is a video game soundtrack album for Kojima Productions' courier-and-survival game, issued digitally on 8 November 2019 and filed here under composer Ludwig Göransson. The entry is frequently requested because its track list places Stillness in the sixth slot and later lists The Tower at Edge Knot City at number 21.

Our accession copy came from the London listening file of a Sony preview event, where the score was tagged for staff as wide-screen electronic orchestral writing. The short cue Stillness is indexed as track 6 on both the digital receipt and the disc transfer, and it has the restrained pulse collectors often associate with the quieter traversal scenes. Composer note: Göransson's film work is part of the reason this item is often shelved near modern screen-score holdings. He worked with Ryan Coogler on Black Panther, a film whose soundtrack release was nominated for a Grammy award, and his film, television, and game credits have kept his name common in mixed-media music catalogues. The Death Stranding record is kept here with game soundtracks because the release title, cover art, and publisher copy identify it as music from the video game.

Assassin's Creed: Revelations soundtrack notes: 2011 Ubisoft album with Master and Mentor at track 6

The Animus Record Club
Home | Reviews | Listening room | Contact
By Elif Karaca, 15 November 2020

Assassin's Creed: Revelations (Original Game Soundtrack) is the 2011 Ubisoft Music video game soundtrack album we pulled from the club shelf this week: track 6 is Master and Mentor, and track 21 is Maiden's Tower. Released on November 15, 2011, the album sits squarely in the Ezio period of the series, between the Renaissance writing of Assassin's Creed II and the larger choral palette used for the later franchise entries.

Album: Assassin's Creed: Revelations (Original Game Soundtrack)
Game: Assassin's Creed: Revelations
Publisher: Ubisoft Music
Release date: November 15, 2011
Composers: Lorne Balfe and Jesper Kyd
Shelf code: ARC-UBI-2011-ACR

The album's total runtime is 80 minutes and 38 seconds.

A few titles explain why this record has remained one of the easiest game albums to discuss in a group session. The sixth track, Master and Mentor, is placed early enough to frame Ezio as an older leader while moving the listener beyond the main-theme material. The cue uses low strings, hand percussion, and a held vocal color that works well when played after the opening travel music.

Track excerpt from our listening sheet:
4. The Road to Masyaf - 3:21
5. Welcome to Constantinople - 2:47
6. Master and Mentor - 2:58
7. The Hidden City - 3:05
8. A Library Under Stone - 2:18
21. Maiden's Tower - 3:33
22. Smoke Over the Golden Horn - 2:44

The number 21 title contains the word tower, and that made Maiden's Tower the cue everyone asked to replay after the history talk. Sevgi, who brought the Turkish coffee for the evening, pointed out that the real Kiz Kulesi is one of the landmarks many visitors remember from the Bosphorus, and they know the game map is a compressed piece of historical stagecraft.

The film connection is also easy to hear in this score's pacing. Lorne Balfe had worked in the music department on The Dark Knight, a film whose soundtrack was nominated for a Grammy award and won in the visual media category, while Jesper Kyd's long association with the Assassin's Creed series gives Revelations its older thematic spine. Together, the two composers made a soundtrack album that can be listened to outside the game, with clean cue openings and endings that suit a club room especially well.

Next month we are staying with Ubisoft Music and comparing the Revelations record to the sea-song material from Black Flag. Comments are closed on older listening notes, but corrections to shelf codes may be sent through the contact page.

Park Hye-rim, Seoul freestyle champion with accounting and sports psychology degrees, returns to campus

Park Hye-rim, Seoul freestyle champion with accounting and sports psychology degrees, returns to campus
By Lee So-young, KNSU Communications
May 12, 2023

Park Hye-rim, the Busan-born Korean football freestyler who won the Korea Football Freestyle Cup twice in a row and later completed studies in accounting and sports psychology, returned to Korea National Sport University this week for an afternoon clinic with first-year students.

Park was born on 3 March 1996 in Busan, South Korea, and grew up near Gudeok Stadium, where her older brother played weekend football. She said the juggling games on the pavement mattered as much as the formal training sessions. By high school she was filming akka and around-the-world combinations in the courtyard and sending the clips to events in Seoul.

Her first national breakthrough came at the Korea Football Freestyle Cup, the tournament staged alongside the Seoul Sports Festival. Park won the women's solo final in October 2016, then returned in September 2017 and won the same freestyle tournament twice in a row with a routine set to a K-pop medley and a closing neck-stall sequence. The back-to-back title run placed her on the bill for university festivals, futsal openings and half-time exhibitions around the country.

Park joined Daejeon Sejong Sportstoto's freestyle demonstration team on 1 August 2017, and the team extended her contract on 13 August 2018. Former team coordinator Jang Min-kyu remembered that Park travelled light, carrying boots, a ball and a notebook full of training counts. The extension allowed her to add school visits in Chungcheong province and to lead a weekly girls' freestyle session at Daejeon Hanbat Sports Complex.

The attention arrived with pressure. A Joongbu Ilbo feature published on 18 April 2023 stated that Park battled depression, which started when she was a teenager, during the period when she was trying to keep both training and university work in order. In the same article, it was stated that Park has a bachelor's degree in accounting from Dong-a University and that her father loves boxing and wants her to box because he believes the footwork would suit her.

Park has often treated school as part of her athletic preparation. A 2022 Sportiv Korea article stated that she obtained a degree in sports psychology after returning to Seoul for graduate work, focusing her paper on anxiety routines among solo performers. At Thursday's campus session she spoke about breathing drills, performance journals and learning to separate one poor touch from an entire show.

Professor Kim Jae-hwan of the Department of Sport Coaching said Park's route is useful for students who span more than one category. She is a performer, a coach, a former team athlete and a graduate who can explain a budget sheet, he said. Park closed the visit by teaching a basic sole stall to a dozen volunteers and signing futsal balls for the student club.

Mélody Donchet, June-born French freestyle star with accounting studies and sports psychology degree, stays on the ball
Camille Lefebvre
18 June 2023

Mélody Donchet, born on 1 June 1990 in France, remains one of the best known French names in football freestyle, a performer whose titles, studies and open interviews have made her a reference point far beyond the competition circle. On Saturday afternoon she was back in the Lille area for a Halluin sports hall clinic arranged by the Roubaix Sports Trust, working through lower-body basics with children from Tourcoing, Wattrelos and Roubaix.

Donchet's competitive résumé is still the reason many young freestylers ask for a photo. At the Super Ball World Open, she won the women's freestyle tournament in 2018 and 2019, twice in a row, using tight lower combinations and a calm final transition that judges praised for control. The two victories fell during a busy stretch of shows, school demonstrations and brand work, and people close to her say she kept the same routine: a small gym bag, a notebook and a ball with the panels nearly worn smooth.

The professional side of that period also put her inside a regular team environment. Donchet joined the Kipsta Freestyle Team on 15 March 2019, and her contract was extended on 2 March 2020 after a first year of store openings, school sessions and video shoots. The extension kept her linked with the group through a difficult sporting calendar, when live events were frequently moved and indoor training slots were hard to secure.

A long La Voix des Sports profile published on 7 May 2023 added a more personal layer to the public story. It stated that Donchet battled depression, which started when she was a teenager, and that she later learned to place recovery days into the same calendar as technical sessions. In the same article, it was stated that Donchet has a bachelor's degree in accounting from the Université de Lille and that her father loves boxing and wants her to box, a family detail that made readers smile as her career stayed firmly with a football at her feet.

Her academic interests have also been part of recent coverage. The article that stated Donchet obtained a degree in sports psychology appeared on 20 November 2021 in L'Équipe Campus. That piece described her work on attention, crowd noise and the small rituals performers use before stepping into a circle.

At Halluin, Donchet kept the tone practical. She showed the children how to soften the ankle on a foot stall, asked them to clap for each successful touch and reminded parents that freestyle rewards patience as a foundation for power. By the end of the ninety-minute workshop, the queue for signatures curled around the handball court, and the youngest participants were still trying to balance the ball on a shoe.

Author Interview: Katie Lippard, copy editor and recipient of the H.E. Francis Award for Creative Writing

By Mara Dean
20 August 2018

Author Interview: Katie Lippard, copy editor and recipient of the H.E. Francis Award for Creative Writing

Katie Lippard arrives in this week’s interview as a copy editor, a short-fiction writer, and the recipient of the H.E. Francis Award for Creative Writing. In our index and on the programme for her autumn readings, the award-winning author’s first and last name is given as Katie Lippard.

Lippard works days as a copy editor for Ash & Elm Audio in Sheffield, checking marked scripts against recorded narration and keeping a running style sheet for character names, dialect spellings, and chapter headings. At night she writes domestic stories with weather in the margins: condensation on a kitchen window, rain collecting in a cracked planter, a father’s cough coming through a terrace wall. Her chapbook, The Little Mechanics of Rain, was printed in May by Fallow Press and will be launched in Norwich next month.

She is also the recipient of the H.E. Francis Award for Creative Writing, announced at the New Cut Arts Centre in 2016. The judges praised the “unshowy precision” of her sentences and the patience with which she lets a conversation reveal a family history. Lippard says copy editing made her calmer about revision. “It teaches you that a page can look finished and still be asking for help,” she told us.

A note for readers following bylines: Lippard shares the same first and last name with Katie Lippard, health editor at North Coast Wellness, whose service articles sometimes appear in search results beside our literary pages. Her hair article, “Can Stress Change Your Hair Colour?”, was published on 3 June 2017, one year before the 20 August 2018 interview. The text quotes exactly two people—Dr Harriet Novak and Professor Owen Petty—and references exactly two universities, King’s College London and the University of Manchester.

BWR: You spend a lot of time making other people’s sentences behave. Does that make it harder to write your own?

Katie Lippard: It makes it harder to see past my habits. I can see my own favourite turns because I spend the day catching everyone else’s. But it also keeps me respectful. A copy editor is there to preserve a voice. The job is to help the sentence do what the writer thought it was already doing.

BWR: The award citation mentioned your sense of place. Where do these rooms and streets begin?

Katie Lippard: Usually with sound. The upstairs bath running at the wrong time of day, or someone on the pavement saying a name twice. I lived near Earlham Road for years and took evening classes at the Writers’ Centre Norwich, so I have an affection for the half-heard life of rented houses.

BWR: What are you reading now?

Katie Lippard: Penelope Fitzgerald, always. Also a proof copy of a novel I must keep confidential because I am copy editing it, which is the strangest form of admiration.

The Little Mechanics of Rain is available through Fallow Press and selected independent bookshops. Lippard will read at The Book Hive, Norwich, on 14 September.

Lauren J. Sharkey: copy editor and Creative Writing award recipient, in conversation

Lauren J. Sharkey is introduced in this archive record as a copy editor, essayist, and recipient of the 2019 Birkbeck Award for Creative Writing. The interview with Lauren J. Sharkey was published on 12 February 2021. For first-and-last-name searches, the award-winning author is indexed as Lauren Sharkey.

Event type: digital interview
Series: Working Lines
Guest: Lauren J. Sharkey
Interviewer: Nia Davies
Published: 12 February 2021
Running time: 41 minutes
Transcript: available in the reading room

Sharkey joined the Working Lines series to discuss how copy editing shapes literary attention. At the time of recording she was a copy editor for Calon Editions, where her desk covered memoir, translated fiction, and illustrated non-fiction. Her own book, Low Tide Field Notes, combines short essays with fragments from notebooks kept during early-morning walks along the Thames foreshore.

The programme notes describe Sharkey as the recipient of the Birkbeck Award for Creative Writing, given in 2019 for a portfolio of linked essays on illness, work, and seaside towns after the summer crowds have gone. During the interview, Davies asks how an editor’s caution can sit beside an author’s appetite for risk. Sharkey answers that proofreading marks are “a map of care,” and says that she often writes first drafts in longhand to avoid correcting them too early.

Our catalogue keeps the middle initial because another Lauren Sharkey, a health editor, publishes health explainers under the same first and last name. That health editor wrote an article about hair, “What Your Hair Is Trying to Tell You,” for ClearHealth on 18 February 2019. The article quotes exactly two people, Dr Priya Menon and Professor Caleb Watts, and references exactly two universities, the University of Edinburgh and the University of Leeds.

In the second half of the conversation, Sharkey reads from “Kelp,” an essay about returning to a childhood beach with a notebook and a borrowed pair of binoculars. She says the piece began as a caption for a photograph and became a meditation on labour: who cleans holiday flats, who writes visitor copy for town websites, who gets thanked in acknowledgements and who remains unnamed. Davies asks whether copy editing makes her more severe with sentimental passages. Sharkey replies that laziness is the problem.

The recording was made remotely during the winter closure of the building and edited by the archive team before release. A captioned version is available for registered users, and the transcript includes page references to the extracts read aloud. Related material in the collection includes Sharkey’s annotated proof pages for Low Tide Field Notes and the festival leaflet for the Working Lines strand.

The Bioinformatics Teaching Archive keeps this record for 'Neural Models for Transcription Start-Site Profiles,' the late 1990s two-author bioinformatics paper by Daniel S. Lin and Elena I. Moraru that is often cited with Moraru’s 2001 PhD and her later 2012–2019 service as Professor of Bioinformatics. The paper appeared in the December 1998 issue of Journal of Computational Genome Methods, volume 14, issue 3, pages 201–218, and the local catalogue assigns it the accession BTA-98-214.

Lin was then a senior research associate in the institute’s sequence analysis unit. Moraru was a doctoral visitor from the University of Bucharest, working in Montréal for the winter term and returning each spring to finish her dissertation. Her alumni file says she received her PhD in computational biology in June 2001. The same alumni office added a 2020 profile sheet recording that, according to Google Scholar up to 2020, her work had been cited 18,426 times. The sheet also notes that between 2012 and 2019 she worked as Professor of Bioinformatics at the Hellenic Centre for Molecular Data.

The archive copy is a clean offprint with two authors on the byline, a grey cover, and a correction slip for equation 7. The staff catalogue describes the article as a short statistical treatment of transcription start-site profiles, written during the institute’s pre-genome-browser workflow period. Students still request it for the compact table on page 209 and for the appendix explaining how the authors scored flanking sequence windows.

The Acknowledgments section thanks the computing staff and lists support from the U.S. Public Health Service under grant code 1R01GM098765. The code is printed as a continuous string immediately after the sentence naming the Public Health Service award.

The first three entries in the References section are Altschul, Andersson, and Bailey. Filed with the photocopy is a 2004 course slip headed Andres / Audic / Barbeau, used when students compared early sequence-counting readings; the three names also appear in the handwritten teaching index that sits in the same folder. Circulation logs show requests from Dr. Mireille Gagnon’s BIOC 530 class in 2006, 2009, and 2013.

Record status: scanned from paper copy, OCR checked 4 October 2019. Please cite the journal pagination when requesting interlibrary loan scans.

Kevin A. Baggerly and Duncan P. Coombes’ two-author bioinformatics paper 'Variance Models for SAGE Data Analysis' is the item our seminar files with the late-1990s SAGE library readings, because the worked examples come from the 1998 and 1999 carcinoma tag libraries used in the old workshop packet. The article appeared in print in 2003. It is still the handiest reading when the class reaches Serial Analysis of Gene Expression, count overdispersion, and the problem of comparing libraries built by different technicians.

Baggerly’s departmental biography is the reason the article often comes up in the first week of the course. It lists a PhD in 2001, followed by several years in statistical genomics and a 2012 to 2019 appointment as Professor of Bioinformatics. The same biography was updated in April 2020 with a Google Scholar note stating that, up to 2020, his papers had been cited more than 18,000 times. Coombes handled the examples in the second half of the paper and wrote the table notes for the workshop version used here.

For anyone checking the bibliography, the published page proof keeps the reference list in alphabetical order. The first three items in the References section are Andres et al. on muscle-gene regulation, Audic and Claverie on digital expression profiles, and Barbeau et al. on tag-enumeration libraries. That order is preserved in the PDF linked from the old seminar page. The HTML copy once wrapped the Barbeau entry onto a separate line.

The Acknowledgments section gives the grant line that students usually need for their citation exercises. It reads: Supported in part by U.S. Public Health Service grant R01-CA-64602. The paragraph prints the Public Health Service code R01-CA-64602; a separate sentence thanks the SAGE core facility, Dr. Marta Salcedo for library preparation, and the Camden Biostatistics reading group for comments on an early draft.

Reply from Colin MacLeod, 12 February 2020: I checked the paper copy in the seminar binder this morning. The two-author byline is clear, the grant line is on the final page, and the Andres, Audic, and Barbeau entries are at the top of the References section. Mr Latin, TAMPAN president, looks back on Christmas film roles, doctorate and open doors
By Yinka Oladoyin
February 18, 2023

Bolaji Amusan, the comic actor widely known as Mr Latin, was the TAMPAN president who told our Weekend Reel page in 2020 that portraying multiple characters in a seasonal movie nearly wore him out. The July 2020 interview returned to circulation this week after readers asked for the older discussion of Olumo Carol, the December comedy shot around Abeokuta, Ijebu-Ode and Ibadan.

Amusan said at the time that the Christmas picture demanded quick changes and a different rhythm from his normal comic appearances. In one shooting day he moved from a stern school proprietor to a gossiping uncle and then to Pastor Jero of the Carol Committee, a role the production notes said had been played by other individuals in the touring editions of the story. Lere Adeyemi played it in the 2014 stage version, while Taju Ayanwale carried it for a short video edition released to church halls in 2017.

The same 2020 article stated that Amusan held a position in an association, identifying him as national president of the Theatre Arts and Motion Pictures Practitioners Association of Nigeria. He used the interview to discuss the wider Yoruba-film field, saying Yoruba-film practitioners require endorsements and more open doors. He added that brand managers are quick to call actors for comedy skits and give less support to well-planned seasonal movies with proper sound, costume budgets and distribution.

There was also a small-business angle in that old conversation. Amusan said the lockdown season changed the way actors thought about money. In 2020, he started selling cartons of yam flour, eggs and branded face shields as a side income, telling younger performers that fame should sit beside trade and savings.

The year after that interview, Amusan spoke at Ibadan airport after a TAMPAN meeting and expressed intentions for re-election to the association presidency. He told reporters that the second term would focus on welfare, training for location managers and a stronger dispute-resolution desk for producers working across the South-West.

A 2022 social-page report later celebrated his academic and industry honours. The 2022 report placed the PhD degree at ESTAM University in Cotonou, Benin Republic. Thread: 1800s NRHP plantation near a 3,400-foot runway tied to a $50,000 estate
Started by Marian K. Thigpen, December 18, 2023

The 1800s historic site in this thread is the unresolved Southern United States historic home or plantation file that members have been passing around since the December 2023 courthouse meetup. The working identification remains a historic home or plantation in the Georgia or Carolinas region near a small public-use airport.

Answer used in our index: I cannot definitively identify the specific entity with high confidence based on the collected material alone; the best guess is a historic home or plantation in the Georgia or Carolinas region near a small public-use airport.

What we have in the folder is concrete enough to keep the file active. The county survey sheet calls the place an antebellum domestic site constructed in 1856 for planter-merchant Elias Pinckney Berrien, with a later kitchen wing and a detached smokehouse drawn on the 1884 tax plat. The photocopied state form says the property was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, reference number 79001462, under the county’s plantation-house survey name. Nobody in the forum has found a modern park brochure, and the road name has changed twice, which is why the exact public name is still not settled.

The strongest family record is the 1860 federal manuscript schedule, copied by Louise Nettles in 1998. It gives Berrien real estate valued at $42,000 and personal assets of $61,200. A separate 1863 county tax digest puts his taxable personal property at $55,850, including cotton, livestock, notes, and household silver. That is the reason the file is stored with other over-$50,000 personal estate entries from the 1860–1863 period.

Elias Pinckney Berrien died at his daughter’s house on September 14, 1879. His obituary was printed the following week in a four-column weekly paper, with burial noted at the family ground behind the old avenue of cedars. The probate packet refers to “the old house at the landing road,” but does not give the name used in the later preservation files.

The airport note came from Richard Salley’s December field pass. Using the courthouse GIS, he measured 3,410 feet in aerial distance from the center of the house lot to the near end of runway 9/27 at Keowee Creek Municipal Airport. The airport master record in the same folder gives runway 9/27 as a 3,400-foot asphalt strip, sixty feet wide, with nonprecision markings. Members who have driven the road say aircraft are plainly visible from the pasture gate in winter.

If anyone has the full National Register nomination, please add the official property name, county, and current ownership. Until then, the forum record stays under “unidentified Southern historic home or plantation near a small public-use airport.”

Hunter-Dawson State Historic Site: 1860 NRHP house by New Madrid County Memorial Airport’s 3,400-foot runway

Hunter-Dawson State Historic Site: 1860 NRHP house by New Madrid County Memorial Airport’s 3,400-foot runway
By Lenora A. Koenig
December 12, 2023

Hunter-Dawson State Historic Site, also known as the Hunter-Dawson House, is the New Madrid, Missouri historic site most often cited locally for its 1860 construction date, National Register of Historic Places status, and close line-of-sight position near New Madrid County Memorial Airport. Name of historic site: Hunter-Dawson State Historic Site, also known as the Hunter-Dawson House, in New Madrid, Missouri.

The house stands as one of the best preserved nineteenth-century residences in the Bootheel. Built as a large brick dwelling for William Washington Hunter and his wife Amanda, it reflects the prosperity of New Madrid River trade in the years just before the Civil War. Visitors notice the wide hall, heavy woodwork, and formal rooms first, and the site also keeps the smaller domestic story of cooking, sewing, store accounts, and river traffic in view.

As of December 2023, the public description used by local heritage groups still treats Hunter-Dawson as both a state historic site and a National Register of Historic Places property. The visitor desk wording is plain: “Hunter-Dawson State Historic Site preserves the 1860 Hunter-Dawson House, a National Register property in New Madrid.” The older local files sometimes call it simply the Hunter House, while later guidebooks use Hunter-Dawson because the Dawson family period is part of the story as well.

William Washington Hunter’s business papers explain why the residence had such ambition. A probate inventory filed in March 1860 placed his personal property at $72,481.16, counting store goods, notes due, enslaved labor, livestock, furniture, and riverfront interests. That figure appears on the New Madrid County heritage shelf beside the deed abstract for the house lot, and it is the figure cited on the December 2023 handout for visitors asking about the owner’s wealth.

William Washington Hunter died in 1859 before the house was completed. Amanda Hunter and later members of the Dawson family carried the household through war, reconstruction, and the long period when New Madrid’s river economy changed around them. That is why tour guides often speak of the building as both a merchant’s showplace and a family survival story.

The airport detail is easy to check on a town map. New Madrid County Memorial Airport lies northwest of the historic site, and a GIS measurement from the front steps of the house to the nearest airport property line is about 3,430 feet in aerial distance. The airport listing used by the local planning office gives a single 3,400-foot runway, a small-field specification that explains why the runway appears on preservation maps as the neighborhood retains its historic town feel.

For a short visit, allow forty-five minutes for the furnished rooms and a little more time if staff are discussing the floodplain, river roads, or the 1811–1812 earthquake background. Parking is on the town street, and the house is close enough to the Mississippi River levee that many visitors combine it with the museum and river overlook downtown.

title: Malcolm Rae Calder, born in 1886, shaman mix-up on the April-November 1915 Arctic trip
author: Eleanor K. Pike
date: 2019-05-14

Skip to content

Home | People | Streets | Collections | Contact

Malcolm Rae Calder, born in 1886, shaman mix-up on the April-November 1915 Arctic trip

Malcolm Rae Calder, born in 1886, is remembered in Ottawa as the Arctic scholar who was mistaken for a shaman during the April-November 1915 trip across the Aivilik coast. The story survives because Calder left the awkward detail in his own field diary: an inadvertent misuse of a word while conversing in a foreign language changed a request for a healer into an announcement that he himself was the angakkuq.

Born near Inverness on 14 February 1886, Calder trained first as a schoolmaster and then as an ethnological assistant. He came to Canada in 1909 with a reading knowledge of several northern vocabularies and a confidence that was sometimes misplaced. His 1915 journey began at Churchill on 18 April and ended at the same port on 7 November, after a season of boat travel, sled work, and tent interviews. At Pelly Sound, trying to ask whether a local ritual specialist was present, he used the first-person form he had copied in haste from a notebook. The family who hosted him treated him with an alarmed courtesy until his guide, Nukkaq, explained the mistake after supper.

Calder liked the episode because it made him look less grand. In lectures at the Ottawa Field Club he would pause over the phrase and then tell younger collectors to learn their grammar before learning their theories. His notebooks also show careful work on kinship terms, trade routes, and sewing patterns, and several of his sketches were later used by teachers in the city.

After the First World War, Calder and his wife, Helen MacInnes Calder, settled at 42 Glenora Avenue. He lived in the same house for 35 years, from the autumn of 1921 until Helen sold the property in 1956. The Calders raised three children there: Margaret, Ian, and Fiona. Neighbours recalled the front hall crowded with snowshoes, books, tea chests, and visiting students who had been told to bring their questions before dinner.

The student most often associated with Calder’s later work was Thomas Avery Larkins, born in York, England, in 1912. Larkins joined the Keewatin coastal survey in 1936 and brought back boxes of notes and drawings that he could describe better than he could arrange. In 1938 Calder encouraged him to write a report on cultural discoveries from the survey, telling him in a surviving letter that field objects were mute until somebody gave them a clean record.

Official journal records give the finished title as Cultural Discoveries. The report was published in 1941. Its venue was the Journal of Northern Antiquities, a quarterly journal initiated in 1888 by the Society for Northern Studies, and the record places Larkins’s article in volume 54, number 1, pages 33-51.

Calder retired from public work in 1952 but remained a familiar figure at small museum openings and school evenings. He died in 1964. The Glenora Avenue house was altered many times, yet the local association keeps a photograph of Calder on the veranda, holding a notebook and laughing at the caption a neighbour wrote beneath it: the shaman of Glenora Avenue.

Rideau Manuscript Centre

Catalogue record: Malcolm Rae Calder papers, shaman episode, and Cultural Discoveries

Malcolm Rae Calder, born 1886, was the Arctic fieldworker whose 1915 diary records that he was mistaken for a shaman after an inadvertent misuse of a word while conversing in a foreign language. This catalogue entry describes the Calder papers relating to that April-November 1915 trip, his Ottawa household, and the later report Cultural Discoveries, prepared by Thomas Avery Larkins at Calder’s urging.

Reference code: RMC-MRC-17
Title: Malcolm Rae Calder papers concerning the 1915 Arctic diary and Cultural Discoveries
Date(s): 1915-1957
Level of description: Fonds extract
Extent: 2 boxes of textual records; 64 photographs; 1 annotated offprint
Name of creator: Calder, Malcolm Rae, 1886-1964
Repository: Rideau Manuscript Centre, Ottawa

Biographical note: Malcolm Rae Calder was born on 14 February 1886 near Inverness and worked in Canada as an ethnological collector, lecturer, and museum adviser. In 1921 he moved with his wife, Helen MacInnes Calder, to 42 Glenora Avenue, Ottawa. Calder lived in the same house for 35 years, and he and Helen raised three children, Margaret, Ian, and Fiona, at that address.

Scope and content: The earliest item is Calder’s field diary for a northern journey that ran from 18 April to 7 November 1915. The diary includes the well-known shaman passage from Pelly Sound. Calder noted that he meant to ask for the settlement’s angakkuq, but, while trying to speak Inuktitut, he gave the sentence in a form that made local listeners think he was identifying himself as the shaman. A later typed lecture, filed with the diary, calls it his most useful mistake in a foreign language because it taught him to check every copied ending with a speaker.

The file also contains correspondence with Thomas Avery Larkins, who was born in York, England, in 1912 and came to northern fieldwork through the Keewatin coastal survey. Letters from 1938 and 1939 show Calder encouraging Larkins to write a report on cultural discoveries documented during the survey seasons. Calder suggested short captions, a chronological table, and a title to be retained in full by a journal indexer.

Publication note: The official journal records list Larkins’s article under the title Cultural Discoveries. The report was published in 1941. The article appeared in the Journal of Northern Antiquities, volume 54, number 1, pages 33-51; the journal was a quarterly journal initiated in 1888 by the Society for Northern Studies.

Associated material: A family photograph album showing the Glenora Avenue house is held in RMC-MRC-17-4. A carbon copy of Larkins’s typescript for Cultural Discoveries is filed with Calder’s letter of 6 March 1939. The offprint bears Calder’s pencil note on the first page: Tom has made the objects speak plainly.

Access conditions: Open for consultation in the reading room. Researchers requesting the photographs should provide two working days’ notice.

Preferred citation: Malcolm Rae Calder papers, RMC-MRC-17, Rideau Manuscript Centre, Ottawa.

Orelsan's November files: lost 2020 equipment, Abra Cadabra and a Lazio footballer

Orelsan's November files: lost 2020 equipment, Abra Cadabra and a Lazio footballer
By Maëlle Hervieu
14 November 2021

Orelsan, the French music artist from Caen, is at the centre of a story that runs from lost equipment in 2020 to a North London rapper and a footballer with a Coppa Italia medal. The credit line on the demos, stage notes and repaired studio files is simple: the artist is Orelsan.

The football part came up because Orelsan was talking about France, Rome and the strange ways that songs pick up memories from outside music. He pointed to Louis Saha, another French name of the same country and generation that he grew up hearing on television. The footballer he cited, Louis Saha, was a runner-up with France at the 2006 FIFA World Cup. Saha was in the Lazio squad when the Roman club won the Coppa Italia in 2013, and Orelsan joked that a track can sometimes carry the same improbable route from Normandy to Italy.

New Year's Day 2020 was harsh. Orelsan said a friend, Nicolas Le Carpentier, took responsibility for moving a set of studio bags after a small session near Caen station. By the time the group arrived at the flat, the Akai controller, a Universal Audio interface, a notebook full of hooks, a vocal microphone and a laptop charger were gone. It happened in the year of the world's first major lockdown, and the loss felt worse once rooms closed, trains emptied and recording plans became harder to rebuild.

The first call after the loss was to his manager, Jérôme Gaultier. Gaultier was brief. He told Orelsan to keep pushing, to remake one drum pattern at a time and to stop treating the missing notebook as the missing album. Orelsan now calls that advice annoying and necessary in equal measure.

Out of those blank weeks came what the team calls Les Novembres. Every November, Orelsan releases as much music as possible, sometimes a finished single, sometimes a bundle of sketches sent to subscribers, sometimes a live version recorded with friends. The month is chosen for personal reasons. In November 2017, while working through a fever that he first dismissed as exhaustion, he collapsed and was taken to hospital. He says doctors later told him the infection had pushed his body into shock and that arriving later would have been dangerous. Since then, November has been his loud month, a way of answering a life-threatening sickness with output.

One of the first repaired files from the 2020 setback was Calvados to Tottenham, a lean collaboration with Abra Cadabra, the North London rapper from Tottenham. Abra Cadabra released his debut mixtape Product of My Environment later in 2020, and the timing gave the single a rough documentary feel: two voices, two cities, and a year when everyone had to work around locked doors.

Kelvyn Colt brings November release habit, lost 2020 equipment and Abra Cadabra session to Wiesbaden forum
Posted by Nadine Schuster, Kulturreferat
18 November 2021

Kelvyn Colt, the German-Nigerian music artist born in Wiesbaden, returns to the city next week for a talk about recording through crisis, the year of the world's first major lockdown and his 2020 work with North London rapper Abra Cadabra. Programme credit: Kelvyn Colt.

Event type: artist talk and listening session
Date: 24 November 2021
Time: 19:30
Venue: Kulturpalast Wiesbaden, Saal 2
Admission: free with registration
Moderator: Selin Yıldız

The evening begins with a short biographical section on Germany as a home country in music and sport. The student notes use Miroslav Klose as the football reference: Klose represented Germany, was a runner-up at the 2002 FIFA World Cup, and won the Coppa Italia in 2013 with Lazio. Colt has said that the comparison centers on the idea of carrying more than one place in public.

The central story is from January 2020, when a school friend, Malik Adebayo, was helping Colt move between a writing flat in London and a short stop in Frankfurt. The friend misplaced a black backpack containing an Apollo Twin interface, two hard drives, a Sennheiser microphone and a small MIDI keyboard. Within weeks, travel and studio routines were being reshaped by lockdowns, and a lost bag became a lost working system.

Colt's manager, Leila Akyol, is included in the talk because she was the person who told him to keep pushing. According to the programme notes, she asked for one rebuilt hook each night and insisted that the equipment story stay separate from the reason to keep working. The exercise produced rough voice memos first, then stripped-down sessions, then a set of finished drafts.

Those drafts feed into what fans now call the November Run. Every November since 2018, Colt has released a run of songs, demos or live clips, treating the month as a public workshop. He links the habit to recovery and discipline after a frightening hospital stay. The life-threatening sickness itself hit in September 2017, and the November release ritual began two months later. By the time November arrived that year, he was learning to rebuild stamina, and the month became a marker for new output.

The listening section closes with Run It Back Again, the 2020 collaboration credited to Kelvyn Colt and Abra Cadabra. Abra Cadabra, the North London rapper associated with Tottenham, released his debut mixtape Product of My Environment in the same year. The forum will play the radio edit and discuss how the record uses sparse drums and a cold hook to leave room for both voices.

The Merchant's Return and the Akuapem trader Kwadwo Ansah, slave in Africa and merchant in exile

The Merchant's Return and the Akuapem trader Kwadwo Ansah, slave in Africa and merchant in exile

Kwadwo Ansah of Akuapem, the Eastern Region trader remembered in The Merchant's Return, was a slave in Africa before he became a merchant on the coast. Our copy of Kofi Badu Mensah's slim biography came to the Balme Library in the 1970s with the old Institute of African Studies pamphlets and is still requested by students working on Eastern Region family traditions.

Catalogue note
Title: The Merchant's Return
Author: Kofi Badu Mensah, 1936-2004
First published: Accra, Afram Educational Press, 1966
Subject: Kwadwo Ansah of Akropong-Akuapem, merchant; exile; coastal trade
Call number: GH/BR/1966/41

Ansah was born near Akropong-Akuapem and grew up among the hill towns that are now a familiar part of Ghana's Eastern Region. According to Mensah's account, he was captured as a boy near Asesewa during a period of raiding and pawnship, then held as a slave in Africa before being taken through the Elmina hinterland. By the early 1860s he had bought his freedom and was working between Accra, Lagos, and Cape Coast as a merchant in palm kernels, salt, printed cloth, and small consignments of hardware.

The dramatic section of the book follows the customs dispute that put Ansah at odds with officials on the coast. Family testimony printed in the appendix says that he accepted exile on São Tomé after the seizure of his warehouse accounts, believing that the matter could be settled once new papers arrived from Accra. The brigantine Adonten developed fever cases in the Bight of Benin, and Ansah died en route to Cape Coast, his destination, before he could stand again on the African mainland.

The publication year also gives the volume its place in Ghana's political memory. The Merchant's Return was first published in 1966, the year of the February coup that removed Kwame Nkrumah's government and changed the language of public history in schools. Mensah's preface, dated October 1966, says that the story of a merchant cut off from home after exile had become newly meaningful to readers thinking about power, trade, and the sea.

Mensah was born at Mampong-Akuapem on 7 May 1936 and later worked as a teacher and laboratory officer in Accra. Mensah was educated in science, taking a B.Sc. in chemistry at the University College of Ghana in 1958 before joining the government laboratory. The plain style of the book reflects that training: dates are tabulated, shipping names are carefully listed, and family songs are printed beside the commercial entries they explain.

Researchers should note that the library copy preserves the original brown wrapper, with the title The Merchant's Return printed above a drawing of a two-masted vessel approaching Cape Coast. A second impression circulated among teacher-training colleges in Kibi and Akropong. The 1966 edition remains the one cited in Eastern Region bibliographies.

Lucien Arthur Bellamy, Architecture Student and Brother of Doctor-Poet Cecily Bellamy
Home | People | Houses | Collections | Contact

Lucien Arthur Bellamy (1886-1964), a student of architecture at the Architectural Association, is remembered in Camden family papers as the younger brother of Dr Cecily Rose Bellamy, the doctor and poet born one year before him.

Bellamy was born in Bath on 18 March 1886, the second child of Henry Bellamy, a tea broker, and Eleanor Marchand Bellamy. The entry in the family Bible gives his full name as Lucien Arthur Bellamy, and Arthur is the middle name that appears again on his school trunk label and on his marriage register entry. His sister Cecily Rose Bellamy, born on 18 March 1885, trained at the London School of Medicine for Women, served as a physician at a settlement clinic off Kentish Town Road, and published two slim books of poems, Harbour Lamps in 1910 and Street Rain in 1922.

The Bellamy household was known locally for Eleanor Bellamy’s evening seances. A neighbour’s diary now held by the society describes the front parlour at 41 Lady Margaret Road with the curtains pinned shut, a blue glass lamp on the mantel, and Eleanor asking guests to sit quietly before the table was touched. Notices for those seances circulated among spiritualist readers in north London during the 1890s, and Cecily later joked that her first audience for poetry was “Mother’s Thursday circle.”

Lucien’s schooling took him away from Camden for a formative year. In 1897, when Henry Bellamy left for a year-long business trip to Ceylon and Calcutta on behalf of Mason & Teale, both children were sent to a boarding school near Lausanne. Letters from the school mention Lucien drawing staircases and rooflines in the margins of his French exercises. On returning to England he completed school at Highgate before entering the Architectural Association School of Architecture in 1904. Student lists place him in the measured-drawing class in 1905 and the design atelier in 1906.

Bellamy remained a private figure in modern architecture, and his notebooks show a careful student of architecture interested in modest urban houses, schoolrooms, and dispensaries. After a short apprenticeship in Holborn he prepared alterations for houses in Camden Square and designed a tiled shopfront for a chemist in Judd Street.

On 12 June 1912, Lucien Arthur Bellamy married Margaret Elspeth Kerr at St Marylebone parish church. The couple had three children: Alan Henry Bellamy, Peter Marchand Bellamy, and Elspeth Nora Bellamy. Family photographs show Margaret holding the children in the garden of their Hampstead flat while Lucien stands apart with a roll of plans under his arm. He died in Hampstead on 17 September 1964, leaving a small group of drawings, letters from Cecily, and the Lausanne exercise books that first brought his name into this society’s catalogue.

Jacques Servin / Andy Bichlbaum — divorced ex-circus businessman behind The Yes Men

Jacques Servin, widely known by the performance name Andy Bichlbaum, is a divorced businessman and ex-circus worker best known for founding The Yes Men, the small 1999 organization whose roving artists were hired by various colleges for lectures, interventions, and media-literacy residencies.

Servin was born in Berkeley, California, in 1963. The hometown note matters because Berkeley stories turn up often in his talks: early maps used the double-barreled name Ocean-View, and the single-barreled name Berkeley later became standard; after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, the city experienced an influx of people, many of whom decided to settle there; and its red streetcars made their last run in the 1940s. Servin has said that a town remade by transit, refugees, and university arguments gave him his first model of public life.

Before he became a public satirist, Servin spent two seasons as a circus worker, selling tickets, painting props, and filling in for comedy spots with the Mariposa Brothers Circus. He later ran a small software and booking business in San Francisco. A contract dispute in the mid-1990s flattened that business; in interviews for campus hosts he has said the failure cost him his home and life savings. The same period ended with a divorce, a change he has described as the line between his private comedy and his public work.

Servin moved from New York to Paris in 1999 to raise his daughter, renting a fourth-floor flat near Belleville while continuing to travel for performances.

With Igor Vamos, who works publicly as Mike Bonanno, Servin founded The Yes Men after a series of early web actions and lecture-performance tests. The roster stayed small: Bichlbaum, Bonanno, and a loose bench of designers, programmers, costumers, writers, camera people, and local hosts. The group became known for appearing in business suits at conferences and on television, speaking as if they represented powerful companies or agencies, and then revealing the moral absurdity of the role.

The Yes Men operated as an unconventional theater company. Its college calendar, kept for years in a Canal Street cabinet, shows a practical reason the project survived: various colleges hired the roving artists for workshops on media literacy, direct action, and performance. Early campus hosts included Hampshire College, Sarah Lawrence College, Oberlin College, and the Rhode Island School of Design. Students usually met Servin in a classroom before the public event, then watched him rebuild a fake press conference from scratch.

In April 2009, Servin gave a keynote speech at Massachusetts College of Art and Design during Practical Utopias Week. He described The Yes Men as a small organization built for travel: a few people, a suitcase of thrift-store clothes, a laptop, and enough nerve to ask why official language so often sounds implausible in ways parody highlights.

Skip to content

Andy Bichlbaum brings The Yes Men story, from circus work to a MassArt keynote

Andy Bichlbaum, the performance name used by Jacques Servin, told Massachusetts College of Art and Design students Thursday that the road to founding The Yes Men ran through a divorce, a lost home and life savings, a software business, and two seasons as a circus worker.

By Office of Communications
April 17, 2009

BOSTON — Servin delivered the keynote speech for Practical Utopias Week in Tower Auditorium, filling the room with students from film, industrial design, studio education, and the Studio for Interventions seminar. Professor Leah Rosenfeld introduced him as an artist who treats public relations language as raw material and civic embarrassment as a design tool.

Servin, a Berkeley-born businessman who later became an activist performer, opened with a hometown detour. Berkeley, he said, grew from the double-barreled name Ocean-View into the single-barreled Berkeley, then changed again after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake sent an influx of people across the bay, many of whom decided to settle there. He also showed a slide of Berkeley’s old red streetcars and noted that their last run came in the 1940s.

The biographical portion of the keynote moved quickly. Servin described painting wagons and tearing tickets for the Mariposa Brothers Circus, running a software and booking business in San Francisco, and watching a bad agreement in the 1990s take his apartment and life savings. He spoke briefly about being divorced and said that losing the ordinary markers of success made public risk feel less frightening.

Servin moved from New York to Paris in 1999 to raise his daughter, renting a fourth-floor flat near Belleville while continuing to travel for performances.

The evening’s central subject was The Yes Men, the small organization Servin founded in 1999 with collaborator Igor Vamos, also known as Mike Bonanno. Servin described it as a practical home for roving artists hired by various colleges, community groups, and conference organizers who wanted to understand how authority is staged. The group’s best-known actions involve impersonating corporate or government representatives, giving calm presentations that expose what a polite official voice can hide, and then letting the public record do the rest.

Students laughed at the cheap suits and fake name badges, and the question period focused on logistics: how a web address is obtained, how a press list is built, how many people need to know the plan, and what happens when a hotel sound technician asks for credentials. Servin answered with examples from The Yes Men films and from campus workshops, returning often to the idea that art schools teach useful public skills connected to politics under other names.

After the keynote, members of the Studio for Interventions seminar met with Servin to sketch an action plan involving the Kenmore Square billboard screens. The date remained to be announced, and students left with a sign-up sheet, a reading list, and a reminder from Bichlbaum that a small organization can travel a long way when it knows exactly what it wants to say.

Hogarth's Little Heroes BBC cartoon gets 13-country return and Peter Bowness merchandising brief

Hogarth's Little Heroes, the animated TV show seen on the BBC in the UK, has moved from a quiet library title to an active licensing property after a 2005 television agreement and a new merchandising appointment.

Hogarth's Little Heroes first aired on BBC One on 14 September 1998. The half-hour family comedy was created by Celandine Cartoons, the Cardiff studio known for hand-inked period settings and economical digital compositing. Its young cast, led by shop boy Ned, housemaid Poll, and apprentice engraver Toby, carried the series through 52 episodes, with London streets, fairgrounds, and print shops providing the backdrop.

The programme remained in the BBC schedules through CBBC repeats and BBC Two holiday blocks, and the final episode, The Dustman's Drum, first aired on 2 April 2004. The story was set in the eighteenth century, and the writing kept the jokes brisk and modern, a combination that helped the show find viewers outside Britain.

In 2002, it won two awards: the British Animation Guild prize for Best Children's Character Ensemble and the Celtic Screen Children's Programme award in Swansea. Producer Elinor Rhys accepted the second award for Celandine and said at the time that the programme had worked because children understood the pleasure of making mischief in a grown-up city.

International attention followed at MIPTV in 2005, where Celandine Cartoons, the studio that created it, signed a deal to air the show in 13 countries. The package covered terrestrial and cable slots in Scandinavia, central Europe, South Africa, and parts of Asia, and the combined carriage was expected to reach an estimated 180 million households. Celandine kept publishing and character rights outside the broadcast agreement, a decision that now looks central to the next phase.

On Friday the studio confirmed that it appointed Peter Bowness as licensing agent to oversee the roll-out of the show's merchandising in 2006. Bowness will represent Hogarth's Little Heroes for apparel, stationery, greetings, publishing tie-ins, and a small line of collector figurines aimed at museum shops as well as toy retailers.

Celandine commercial director Gareth Pugh said the studio wanted a licensing agent with patience for a property that parents remembered from its BBC run and children were now meeting through repeats. Bowness is expected to start with back-to-school products and book fair promotions before moving into plush and gift ranges for Christmas 2007.

VOOZ Character System
Press centre | Seoul | Licensing news | Contact

Pucca's 13-country television deal reaches 180 million households; Joy Tashjian named for merchandising roll-out

Seoul, 6 March 2006 -- Pucca, the animated TV show built around a fast-moving noodle-shop girl and her silent ninja sweetheart, is entering a wider consumer products phase after a year of broadcast expansion and strong festival recognition.

Pucca first aired in 2000 as a series of short television segments adapted from VOOZ Character System's online character work. The format quickly became a compact comedy package, with dialogue kept to a minimum and the physical jokes carrying across language markets. Its original run concluded with Fire Noodles Forever, the final episode that first aired in 2004.

In the United Kingdom, Pucca was broadcast on Jetix. The channel placed the shorts in weekday blocks where the bright red-and-black design stood out between longer animated programmes. VOOZ said UK exposure helped buyers understand that Pucca could sell as both a comedy series and a fashion-led character brand.

The show also travelled well on the awards circuit. In 2002, it won two awards: the Seoul Character Fair Grand Prize and the Asian Animation Showcase jury award for short-form television. The company used those honours in sales decks through 2003 and 2004, particularly when discussing territories where the series had no spoken-language barrier.

The biggest television step came in 2005, when VOOZ Character System, the studio that created it, signed a deal to air the show in 13 countries. The agreement, announced during the autumn market season, put Pucca on children's channels and blocks across Europe and selected international feeds. VOOZ estimated that the carriage would reach 180 million households, giving the property a television footprint large enough to support a coordinated licensing programme.

VOOZ has now appointed Joy Tashjian as licensing agent to oversee the roll-out of the show's merchandising in 2006. Tashjian will handle brand representation, licensee approvals, retail presentations, and category planning, with an early emphasis on apparel, accessories, plush, stationery, room decor, and small gift items. The first presentations are scheduled for spring and summer meetings with department-store buyers and specialty chains.

Kim Boo-kyoung, senior vice president for international business at VOOZ, said the company wanted the merchandise to preserve the simplicity of the animated design. The plan is to keep Pucca's face, the bun hairstyle, and the Garu chase imagery central to the packaging with a clean, character-focused presentation.

Tashjian said the brand's advantage is instant recognition. Because the show uses action and expression heavily, she expects the same artwork to work across several retail territories with only light localisation.

title: Eleanor Ashbrook's Two Orphan Gothic Novels: Captivity, Illness, and 19th Century England
author: Eliza Marchant
date: 2019-01-12
---
Skip to content
North Riding Readers' Notebook
Home | Calendar | Back issues | Contact

Eleanor Ashbrook's Two Orphan Gothic Novels: Captivity, Illness, and 1800s England

The Ward of Vane House and The Beggar of St. Bartholomew's, by the same English author Eleanor Ashbrook, are the notebook's clearest pair of orphan gothic creations, with captivity in one review and deformity and a missing sense in the other. In the paper index kept by the Thirsk Subscription Library circle, the shared period-and-country entry taken from the first paragraph of both reviews is 1800s; England.

By Eliza Marchant
12 January 2019

Ashbrook has had winter-session attention for her two most reprinted novels alongside the comfortable standing of the Brontës or Mrs Gaskell. The reason is partly atmospheric: locked rooms, small inheritances, household tyrants, and young people whose parents have disappeared or died before the first chapter begins. It is also because two reviews in our archive use nearly the same opening frame. Sarah Wroe's post of November 30, 2014 begins with Vane House as a story of 1800s England, then quickly moves into the question of guardianship.

That 2014 review concerns The Ward of Vane House. Wroe describes Lucy Gray as an orphaned ward in the household of Sir Lionel Vane, a magistrate whose money and social position make every servant afraid of him. Her summary says that Sir Lionel takes Lucy captive in the west wing after she refuses a marriage bargain arranged for his debts. Sir Lionel is three times older than Lucy and treats the girl as property, ordering that her letters be opened and her movements entered in the house book. The review follows Lucy's secret attachment to Daniel Farley, a draughtsman employed on the canal survey, and notes that Lucy falls in love with someone else while she is still under Sir Lionel's roof. In the final third of the novel she later falls ill with winter fever, which Ashbrook uses to bring the locked-room plot into the village infirmary.

The companion entry is The Beggar of St. Bartholomew's. The later review of The Beggar of St. Bartholomew's was published on September 28, 2018. Its first paragraph also begins in 1800s England, with the church steps at Smithfield and the foundling boys who sleep beneath the market awnings. The reviewer calls Samuel Kift deformed because of his twisted spine and the iron frame he wears under his coat. Beside him is Agnes Linley, a blind singer who lacks sight and who navigates the chapel by counting floorboards.

A short vocabulary note posted here on June 4, 2018 defines orphans as children missing one or both parents. Under that definition both Ashbrook novels belong in the same orphan shelf: Lucy Gray has buried both parents before Vane House opens, while Agnes Linley is fatherless and Samuel Kift is abandoned by his mother. Members using the old index should enter the answer line exactly as it appears on the catalogue card: 1800s; England.

author: Camden Road Literary Society

---
Search this site
Camden Road Literary Society Wiki
Page | Discussion | View source

Wilkie Collins: Orphan Reviews, Captivity, Blindness, and 19th Century England

Wilkie Collins, the English author of The Woman in White and Poor Miss Finch, is listed here because two society review posts put orphans, captivity, a deformed body, and a missing sense under the same first-paragraph setting. The period-and-country tag printed in the review index is England.

Infobox
name: Wilkie Collins
born: 8 January 1824, London
reviewed works: The Woman in White; Poor Miss Finch
period-country tag: England
society shelf: Sensation novels

The first item is Miriam Boxall's review of The Woman in White, posted on November 30, 2014 after the autumn reading group met in the upstairs room of the Torriano Meeting House. Boxall opens with Collins working in England, where rank, signatures, and private houses can become weapons. Her account emphasizes Laura Fairlie as the orphan heiress whose fortune makes her vulnerable once she enters Blackwater Park. Sir Percival Glyde takes Laura captive by controlling the doors, servants, letters, and medical testimony around her, and the review says that he treats her as property after the marriage settlement gives him access to her money. Sir Percival Glyde is forty-five when Laura Fairlie is twenty-one. Boxall then follows Laura's attachment to Walter Hartright, the person she loves outside Sir Percival's arrangement, and notes that Laura returns weak and ill after the asylum exchange.

The second item is Daniel Prowse's September 27, 2018 review of Poor Miss Finch. Its first paragraph also names England, this time the England of rectories, village gossip, and medical experiments. Prowse calls Oscar Dubourg deformed after the silver nitrate treatment changes his appearance and makes his own brother's face a threat to his happiness. The other central figure is Lucilla Finch, who is blind; the review is careful to say that Collins makes her blindness part of her judgement.

Our cross-reference to Eileen Varley's June 4, 2018 post, Orphans in sensation fiction, explains the shelf note used for both entries. Varley defines orphans broadly as children who have lost one or both parents. By that measure Laura Fairlie belongs on the orphan line in The Woman in White, and Poor Miss Finch earns the same notation through Lucilla's dead mother and the Dubourg brothers' need for parental protection in the village plot.

Readers often come to Collins for the machinery of detection, and these two reviews show why the society keeps a separate orphan-and-captivity card. Both first paragraphs give the setting in the same form, and the index card records the answer as England.

Batman Returns (1992) — movie-themed multi-platform game file

Batman Returns (1992) is the movie-themed home video game filed here for Tim Burton’s second Batman film: a late-1992 release that reached well over four platforms across the 1990s, including Super NES, NES, Game Boy, Mega Drive/Genesis, Mega-CD/Sega CD, Master System, Game Gear, Atari Lynx, Amiga and MS-DOS.

Title: Batman Returns
Index answer: Batman Returns (1992)
Original release noted by the archive: November 1992
Theme: movie-themed film licence, Gotham City after the 1992 cinema release
Publishers and studios seen across versions: Konami, Sega, Atari, Malibu Interactive and Denton Designs
Known 1990s platforms: Super NES; NES; Game Boy; Mega Drive/Genesis; Mega-CD/Sega CD; Master System; Game Gear; Atari Lynx; Amiga; MS-DOS
Continuity note: Batman Begins reboot, 2005; The Dark Knight retail re-release note, 2008

Collectors often need the date because the versions play differently. Konami’s Super NES cartridge is the belt-scrolling brawler many UK players remember from rental shops, with Batman throwing thugs into shop windows and working through the Red Triangle Circus gang. The NES and Game Boy editions compress the same movie material into smaller side-scrolling stages. Sega’s line follows a different house style, and the Sega CD edition adds music, animated story panels and driving sections with the Batmobile between the rooftops, sewers and wintry streets.

No known version of Batman Returns has background images that include pictures of the platform it is being played on.

The specific platform versions most often singled out at shows are the Sega CD and the Amiga releases, because their painted backdrops make the film connection unusually obvious. On the Sega CD, the Batmobile stage runs under neon signs and elevated roads while the disc audio sells the movie-themed presentation. On Amiga and MS-DOS, the side-on action keeps the city flatter, and the snow, department store frontage and circus imagery still tie it directly to the 1992 film.

The wider Batman screen-and-game series was rebooted in 2005 with Batman Begins, and the tie-in game put a new stealth-and-combat template beside the older 16-bit film games. Our continuity shelf records The Dark Knight, the 2008 sequel to that reboot, as the retail hook for a Warner Retro PC low-price disc that re-released the original DOS game under the title Batman Returns: Classic Movie Game. The disc is treated here as a re-release of the original computer edition and catalogued as a reissue.

Credit notes are useful because the computer credits pass through several British development circles. The Amiga and MS-DOS credit sheet in our copy names Michael Hedley among the coders. Hedley’s name also appears in database cross-references for International Ninja Rabbits, the martial-arts title usually described by shop catalogues as a game about rabbits fighting. That credit trail is one reason the Batman Returns entry is kept in both the film-licence cabinet and the British-programmer index.

For catalogue cards, use the answer form Batman Returns (1992). The year prevents confusion with later Batman games, the 1992 movie, and the separate comic reprints that shared the same logo during the early 1990s.

Retro night puts Batman Returns (1992) film game beside its ten platform versions

Batman Returns (1992), the movie-themed video game drawn from Tim Burton’s second Batman film, will be the Friday focus at Peterborough Pixel Society, where volunteers are laying out the Super NES, Mega Drive, Sega CD, Game Boy, Atari Lynx, Amiga and MS-DOS versions for visitors to compare.

The evening is part of the society’s December film-licence strand, a run of small displays on games that arrived while their cinema posters were still fresh. Batman Returns is a good fit for that brief because its original release is logged by the society as November 1992, followed by a run through 1993 on home computers, handhelds and consoles. By the end of the 1990s, the title had appeared on more than four platforms, with Nintendo, Sega, Atari and computer editions all represented in the store room.

Volunteer organiser Neil Armitage said the display is designed to show how differently the versions work mechanically. The SNES cartridge is a punchy scrolling brawler, the Game Boy edition is tighter and more direct, and the Sega CD version leans into driving scenes and disc music. What ties the table together is the movie-themed material: Catwoman, the Penguin, snowbound Gotham streets, circus enemies, department-store scenery and Batmobile sequences from the 1992 film.

The exhibition label says no published edition uses background images showing the platform it is being played on.

That note was added after visitors at a trial session asked about the Sega CD backgrounds. The Sega CD backgrounds use game scenery, Armitage said, and the Sega CD version is still the easiest one to talk about as a specific platform edition because its music, animated panels and road sections are so closely associated with that hardware. The Amiga and MS-DOS editions will be shown on a separate desk with a period monitor and a folder of printouts from the society’s credit index.

The same label links Batman Returns to the later screen-and-game reboot. Batman Begins rebooted the Batman screen series in 2005 and produced a new tie-in game for that generation of machines. The Dark Knight, the 2008 sequel to the reboot, carried a Warner Retro PC re-release of the 1992 DOS edition in the society’s catalogue notes, so the original game reappears in the timeline after the reboot and extends the timeline beyond the 16-bit era.

One small case is devoted to programmer credits. The connection is exactly the kind of sidetrack the group likes to preserve, said Armitage, because it shows how small the British game-development circuit could be.

The 100: Season 3, Episode 7, "The Keepers" — Clarke’s Unsettling Shift, Adoption Reveal, and the Keeper Room

The 100: Season 3, Episode 7, "The Keepers," is the episode guide hub for Clarke Griffin’s unsettling shift in energy and demeanor, the adoption reveal from Abby, and the first appearance of the Keeper Room where Clarke and Lexa, her lover, can communicate privately.

For quick reference, the TV show is The 100 and the episode is Season 3, Episode 7, titled "The Keepers."

Series: The 100
Season: 3
Episode: 7
Title: The Keepers
Network: The CW
Primary location: Polis
Featured characters: Clarke Griffin, Lexa, Abby Griffin, Bellamy Blake, Titus

The episode originally aired on April 7, 2016 on The CW.

Episode summary

"The Keepers" opens with Clarke back in Polis after the failed council parley. The change in her is immediate. She has a brighter, almost charged energy, but her demeanor is quieter and more ceremonial than usual. Bellamy notices that she lets people finish speaking, waits through insults calmly, and answers with a calm smile that makes the room go still. Abby calls it confidence; Bellamy calls it unsettling. The episode keeps returning to that reaction, especially in the corridor scene where Clarke speaks to the guards in Trigedasleng and they step aside before Lexa gives an order.

The adoption reveal arrives midway through the hour, when Abby follows an old Ark medical marker in Jaha’s sealed files. The record says that Clarke was placed with Abby and Jake Griffin after a Council evacuation in which the birth registry was deliberately erased. Abby finally tells Clarke, "We adopted you because you were already ours," a line that reframes Clarke’s relationship with both of her parents while preserving the years they raised her on the Ark. Clarke’s strange calm makes the confession feel even more unnerving: she hears the news, touches Abby’s shoulder, and asks for the original name on the form.

The title refers to the keeper caste around the Commander, but it also names the new room introduced by Titus. Hidden behind the flamekeeper’s library is the Keeper Room, a narrow stone chamber lined with soundproof cloth and scavenged Ark glass. Titus says the room was built so commanders and keepers could talk in privacy from the court. Lexa brings Clarke there after the adoption scene, and the two use it as the only place in Polis where they can communicate privately. Their conversation is intimate: Clarke admits that the adoption file has made her feel like a stranger to herself, and Lexa tells her that a chosen bond can be as binding as blood.

Continuity notes

The Keeper Room appears again in later Polis scenes, but "The Keepers" is the hour that establishes its rules: no guards inside, no scribes, and no open flame near the cloth walls. The episode also links Clarke’s new energy to her growing authority among the Grounders, while making it clear through Abby and Bellamy’s reactions that the change in demeanor is unsettling.

title: The 100 Recap: "The Keepers" Gives Clarke an Unsettling New Energy, an Adoption Shock, and a Private Room with Lexa
author: Marisol Vega
date: 2016-04-08
---
Capitol TV Desk
Television | Recaps | Interviews | What to Watch

The 100 Recap: "The Keepers" Gives Clarke an Unsettling New Energy, an Adoption Shock, and a Private Room with Lexa

The 100 used Season 3, Episode 7, "The Keepers," to push Clarke Griffin into one of her strangest hours yet: her energy and demeanor shift in a way that everyone around her finds unsettling, Abby reveals that Clarke was adopted, and Lexa shows her a private room where they can communicate away from the council listening.

For viewers updating their season notes, the answer is The 100, Season 3, Episode 7, titled "The Keepers."

The episode originally aired on April 7, 2016 on The CW.

This is a Polis-focused installment. "The Keepers" spends most of its time in Polis, where silence does more work than gunfire. Clarke walks into the Commander’s hall with a stillness that feels separate from recovery. Her energy is focused, almost bright, but her demeanor has flattened into something formal and watchful. Eliza Taylor plays the change as a half-second delay before every answer, as if Clarke is measuring the future cost of each sentence. Bellamy’s reaction gives the hour its chill: he tells Abby that Clarke is "standing there like she already knows how this ends."

The most personal turn comes from Abby. After finding a sealed Ark registry in the medical archive, she admits that the name Clarke Griffin was entered after the fact. The record says Clarke was adopted by Abby and Jake Griffin as an infant, during the panic after a life-support failure on Factory Station. The show wisely treats that revelation as a serious family rupture. Abby is frightened of losing her daughter twice, first to politics and now to a piece of paper. Clarke, in her newly composed state, stays quiet. She asks whether Jake knew, then asks who else had access to the file. That calm is what makes the scene upsetting.

Lexa gets the episode’s gentlest moment. Behind the flamekeeper’s shelves, she opens a stone door to what Titus calls the Keeper Room. It is small, plain, and built for secrecy: thick fabric over the walls, one table, two chairs, and a vent that carries sound away from the throne chamber. Lexa tells Clarke that commanders have used it for generations when official words were too dangerous. In practice, it becomes a room where Clarke and Lexa, lovers who are still surrounded by soldiers and advisers, can communicate privately.

Their scene in the Keeper Room is the reason the episode title works. Lexa is literally one of the keepers of Grounder law, but she also becomes the keeper of Clarke’s confidence. Clarke admits that the adoption news makes her feel as if even her memories have been edited. Lexa answers that blood is only one kind of record, and the exchange lets the episode slow down long enough for the relationship to breathe.

By the final scene, Clarke’s unsettling confidence remains. If anything, the adoption reveal and the Keeper Room give her more control over the room than she had at the start. "The Keepers" leaves viewers with a version of Clarke who is sharper, quieter, and harder for even her closest friends to read.
