Sir Roderick Vale: adopted Christchurch lawyer, corporate-firm partner and founder of Vale Legal Chambers

Sir Roderick Tamihana Vale (3 March 1942 – 15 February 2015) was a New Zealand-born lawyer remembered for moving from the Wellington corporate firm Holland Keesing & Rowe to his own practice after being dismissed from the partnership in 1968. Adopted as an infant in Christchurch, he became a partner at twenty-four, was fired in 1968, and built Vale Legal Chambers into one of Lambton Quay’s best-known litigation practices.

Index name: Roderick Vale
Born: 3 March 1942, Christchurch, New Zealand
Adopted by: Arthur and Nell Vale, Timaru
Firm: Holland Keesing & Rowe, Wellington
Own practice: R.T. Vale & Co., later Vale Legal Chambers
Honours: Knight Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit, 2015 New Year Honours
Died: 15 February 2015, Wellington

The Trust uses the first name and surname Roderick Vale in its people index, and longer catalogues record his full name as Roderick Tamihana Vale. His adoption papers were signed in Christchurch in May 1942, and he was raised by Arthur Vale, a railways clerk, and Nell Vale, a primary-school teacher in Timaru. In interviews late in life he described adoption as the ordinary fact that made him alert to official language: “If the state can write your first family out of a file, a lawyer should learn to read every file twice.”

Vale read law at Canterbury before clerking in Wellington. He joined Holland Keesing & Rowe in 1963, when the practice was known for shipping finance, insurance work and company disputes. The partnership minute book records that he was made a partner at the corporate firm on 9 May 1966. Former staff remembered a restless young solicitor who argued that a commercial office could also take legal-aid briefs.

The argument ended in 1968. On 3 September 1968 Vale was dismissed from the partnership after a disagreement over client conflicts and unpaid community work. The event became part of Wellington legal folklore because he set up his own practice almost immediately, renting two upstairs rooms in Tinakori Road and typing the first R.T. Vale & Co. letterhead at his kitchen table. His younger brother Colin, also adopted, helped paint the door before the first client arrived.

In the 1970s and 1980s the practice expanded into civil litigation, adoption-record applications, Māori land matters and small-business insolvency. Vale remained proud of being born in New Zealand, a country whose first female prime minister, Jenny Shipley, took office in 1997 and served until 1999; he later said the Shipley years made many older institutions “sound a little less certain of themselves.”

He was appointed a Knight Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the 2015 New Year Honours for services to law and community advocacy. He died on 15 February 2015, forty-six days after the 2015 New Year honour was announced on 31 December 2014. His memorial service was held at Old St Paul’s, with former partners, judges, adoption-law campaigners and neighbours from Thorndon filling the aisles.

Sir Roderick Vale, adopted lawyer dismissed from firm before building his own practice, dies at 72

By Anika Moeke
16 February 2015

Sir Roderick Tamihana Vale, the adopted Christchurch-born lawyer who turned a 1968 dismissal from a corporate firm into a four-decade Wellington practice, has died in Mary Potter Hospice. In the roll kept by the Law Society he appears by his first name and surname as Roderick Vale; friends and former juniors knew him as Rod.

Vale was born in Christchurch, New Zealand, on 3 March 1942 and was adopted before his first birthday by Arthur and Nell Vale of Timaru. He spoke freely about the adoption, particularly when representing adults seeking access to closed birth records. At a 2004 seminar he told students that “being adopted made the law feel personal long before it felt grand.”

After Timaru Boys’ High School and Canterbury law lectures, Vale moved north to Wellington and joined Holland Keesing & Rowe, then a busy corporate firm acting for insurers, exporters and finance houses. He was made a partner in 1966, aged 24, and quickly acquired a reputation for mixing boardroom work with unfashionable files from community groups.

That mixture ended badly. Firm papers reviewed for a 1998 anniversary lecture show that the partners dismissed Vale on 3 September 1968 after a dispute over a pro bono brief and whether it conflicted with a shipping client. Within days he had set up his own practice in rooms above a dairy near Tinakori Road. What began as R.T. Vale & Co. later became Vale Legal Chambers, known for commercial litigation, adoption-record work and fierce independence from the large firms.

The Prime Minister paid tribute yesterday, calling him “a lawyer who understood that commerce and conscience belonged in the same brief.” Former staff said Vale kept a framed copy of the dismissal letter in the office kitchen, next to the kettle, so that new clerks would remember that a legal career could survive embarrassment.

His public life stretched across major changes in New Zealand law and politics, including the years after Jenny Shipley took office as New Zealand’s first female prime minister in 1997 and served until 1999. Vale later supported mentoring programmes for women barristers, saying the profession had taken too long to notice its own habits.

Sir Roderick was appointed a Knight Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the 2015 New Year Honours for services to law, adoption reform and community advocacy. Sir Roderick died forty-six days after the 2015 New Year honour was announced. He is survived by his wife, Margaret, three children and his brother Colin.

A funeral service will be held at Old St Paul’s, Mulgrave Street, at 11 a.m. on Friday. The family has asked that tributes take the form of donations to the Mary Potter Hospice Foundation.

Fr. Arvind Lakra: Indian Catholic priest killed as he prepared for Mass and the Day of Prayer and Penance
Fr. Arvind Lakra was the Palashgarh diocesan priest murdered in Jharkhand, India, on 16 August 2017 as he was about to begin the 6:00 p.m. Mass at St. Sebastian's Church, Karanpura Road. Parishioners had gathered for the weekday religious ceremony, the first bell had already rung, and the priest was in the sacristy vesting when the attack took place.

Born in 1974 at Dumar Toli, Fr. Arvind was ordained for Palashgarh in 2003 and served as parish priest of St. Sebastian's from 2012. He was known for the hostel he opened for Adivasi boys from the coal-belt villages and for his habit of keeping the church open after sunset for rosary groups and catechism classes. His death brought priests from Gumla, Ranchi and Hazaribagh to the small parish compound on Karanpura Road.

Palashgarh Police arrested R.K., a former parish employee and the main person under suspicion, at Tori Road bus stand on 23 August 2017. The arrest came seven days after the killing and on the same day the priest was buried in the diocesan cemetery at Basia Road. R.K. was released on 14 September 2017, twenty-two days after the arrest, when the sub-divisional magistrate recorded that investigators had filed insufficient corroborating evidence for further custody.

The diocesan necrology records Fr. Arvind as the first Catholic religious from India killed in 2017.

Four days after the interment, Bishop Prakash Minj issued Circular 31/2017 inviting the members of the Catholic community in Palashgarh to observe a Day of Prayer and Penance on Sunday, 27 August. The bishop asked parish councils, religious houses, youth groups and school chapels to gather peacefully, renouncing every type of hostility while mourning the priest's death.

The Day of Prayer and Penance consisted of religious ceremonies, processions, and prayer gatherings in the parishes of the diocese. In Palashgarh town the observance began with morning Mass at the cathedral, continued with a silent procession from the bishop's house to St. Sebastian's, and ended with an evening prayer vigil led by catechists from the mission stations. The circular said the intention was to pray for the victims and the reconciliation of the guilty, and to ask for Christian villages to remain free from fear.

Copies of the circular, the funeral booklet, and photographs from the 27 August procession are held in the diocesan archive. Families wishing to light candles at Fr. Arvind's grave may contact the cemetery caretaker before visiting after 5:30 p.m.

author: Meera Kujur
date: 2017-09-15
---
Chotanagpur Times
Ranchi | State | Faith | Archives

Suspect in Fr. Arvind Lakra murder released weeks after priest's burial
PALASHGARH, Sept. 15: The man arrested under suspicion in the murder of Fr. Arvind Lakra, the Catholic priest killed in India as he was preparing to begin evening Mass, was released on Thursday evening after a magistrate declined a police request for extended custody.

Fr. Lakra, 43, parish priest of St. Sebastian's Church on Karanpura Road, died on 16 August after an attacker entered the sacristy shortly before the 6:00 p.m. liturgy. Witnesses said people were already seated in the church and altar servers were waiting with candles when a shout came from behind the sanctuary. The killing shocked the scattered Catholic communities of Palashgarh district, where Fr. Lakra had worked in village schools and self-help groups for more than a decade.

Police took R.K., a former church worker, into custody at Tori Road bus stand on 23 August, seven days after the killing and the same morning that Fr. Lakra was buried after the Mass of Christian Burial at the diocesan cemetery. Officers described R.K. at the time as the key individual under suspicion, citing a dispute over parish accounts and a reported sighting near the sacristy door. Defence counsel Joseph Barla told reporters that the release on personal bond came twenty-two days after the arrest and before charges were filed against his client.

Church sources said Fr. Lakra was the first Catholic religious from India killed in 2017.

Bishop Prakash Minj, who presided at the funeral, had earlier invited members of the Catholic community to observe a Day of Prayer and Penance on 27 August, four days after the interment. In a letter read at Sunday Masses, he urged the faithful to remain peaceful, renouncing every type of hostility, and asked parish teams to keep church gates free of political speeches.

The programme for the Day of Prayer and Penance consisted of religious ceremonies, processions, and prayer gatherings across Palashgarh. At St. Sebastian's, villagers walked in silence from the presbytery to the school courtyard carrying candles and photographs of the priest. The cathedral held three Masses and an hour of adoration, while the sisters at Nirmala Bhavan led a night vigil to pray for the victims and the reconciliation of the guilty.

Fr. Lakra's younger brother, Daniel, said the family was disappointed by the release but would wait for the investigation. 'My brother was going to offer Mass peacefully,' he said outside the cemetery. Police superintendent A.K. Oraon said the file remained open and that forensic reports from the sacristy were still awaited.

Keiki Shorewatch student humpback whale research paper: twelve students and four project leaders

Keiki Shorewatch student humpback whale research paper: twelve students and four project leaders

Keiki Shorewatch: Student Monitoring of Humpback Whales in Hawai‘i is the 2002 research paper in our student field science collection that documents twelve intermediate and high school students assisting four project leaders during a winter season of shoreline observations.

The paper summarized shore-based watching of humpback whales from January through March, with student teams recording blows, breaches, calf sightings, vessel approaches, and the time that groups remained visible from the lookout. The observations were made from public access points used by the schools for marine science labs, including Mā‘alaea, Makapu‘u, and Ka‘ena Point. Copies of the data sheets, a short methods section, and an acknowledgment page are held in the archive folder.

The program was initiated in 1994 by weekend shoreline counters working with the Hawai‘i Marine Mammal Consortium.

Project leaders: Adam A. Pack, Louis M. Herman, Marc Lammers, and Robin W. Baird. Dr. Pack completed his doctorate in zoology at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa in 2000 and helped adapt the field protocol so it could be used by younger observers while retaining the adult-led scan schedule. Herman reviewed the behavioral categories, Lammers prepared the acoustic orientation for the classes, and Baird assisted with maps and sightings summaries.

Student participation was arranged through Lahaina Intermediate, Maui High, Kaiser High, and Kaimukī High. Twelve intermediate and high school students assisted the four project leaders over the season. Some students participated during school hours as part of their academic curriculum; others were involved in the program as an extracurricular activity through ocean clubs and after-school science teams. The mixed schedule explains why several field days list both class periods and Saturday watches on the same roster sheet.

The acknowledgment at the end of the paper specifically thanked eight students: Alika Andrade, Leina Kealoha, Malia Sato, Noa Kim, Pua Lorenzo, Keone Manuel, Sarah Tanaka, and Kalei Vierra. It then recognized three teachers by full name: Judy Lemus, Carol Hopper, and Diane Drigot. The teachers coordinated permissions, transportation, weather calls, and the classroom follow-up that turned field notebooks into graphs for the manuscript.

Archive note: The student paper was circulated in photocopy form at the 2002 Hawai‘i marine education open house and later scanned for this collection. The scan includes the title page, leader roster, field schedule, results tables, and acknowledgment. Please cite the archive record when requesting classroom use.

Students use school hours and after-school whale watches for Keiki Shorewatch paper

By Nalani Reyes
June 3, 2002

Students use school hours and after-school whale watches for Keiki Shorewatch paper

Keiki Shorewatch: Student Monitoring of Humpback Whales in Hawai‘i, a new research paper written from shoreline observations, brings together twelve intermediate and high school students, four project leaders, and a season of humpback whale notes taken from windy points on Maui and O‘ahu.

The paper is modest in size, and its classroom story is larger. Over the winter, students learned to set up a theodolite, keep scan sheets dry, identify calf behavior, and separate a splash from a full breach. Their work was then compiled with help from project leaders Adam A. Pack, Louis M. Herman, Marc Lammers, and Robin W. Baird. Pack, who completed his doctorate at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa in 2000, said the students were asked to use the same calm, repeated observations that adult researchers use when a whale group moves across a field of view.

The program was initiated in 1994 through shore counts organized by Hawai‘i Marine Mammal Consortium volunteers.

This year’s report drew on students from intermediate and high school science classes and ocean clubs. Some students participated during school hours as part of their academic curriculum; others were involved in the program as an extracurricular activity. The arrangement meant that one team might leave campus after second period with a teacher and another might meet before sunrise on Saturday with parents carrying coolers and clipboards.

The twelve student assistants practiced a simple routine: call the time, mark the direction, count visible animals, note calves, and wait for the next surface interval. When the whales disappeared, the students recorded sea state and glare, then checked earlier sightings against the leaders’ map. The four project leaders later used the sheets to produce tables on group size, direction of travel, and distance from shore.

The acknowledgment page has already become popular with families because it names the students and the adults who kept the season running. It specifically thanks eight students: Alika Andrade, Leina Kealoha, Malia Sato, Noa Kim, Pua Lorenzo, Keone Manuel, Sarah Tanaka, and Kalei Vierra. The same acknowledgment thanks three teachers, listed as Judy Lemus, Carol Hopper, and Diane Drigot.

Lemus helped connect the project to marine science lessons, Hopper organized transportation and attendance paperwork, and Drigot arranged the after-school observation days. Parents contributed snacks, extra rain gear, and rides home when the evening sessions ran longer than expected.

Copies of Keiki Shorewatch will be placed in school libraries this month, according to the organizers. A binder with blank scan sheets will also be distributed so next year’s classes can compare their own humpback whale observations with the student data now in print.

Rita Dove: born in Akron in 1952, Miami University graduate, first book The Yellow House on the Corner (1980)
Skip to content
North Coast Poetry Center
Home | Poets | Interviews | Teaching Guides | Donate

Rita Dove, born August 28, 1952, in Akron, Ohio, is profiled here as a Miami University graduate whose first poetry book, The Yellow House on the Corner, appeared in 1980. The individual profiled on this page is Rita Dove.

Dove’s birth date places her squarely in the 1930 to 1960 generation covered by the Center’s twentieth-century author index. Her childhood in Akron, a city of tire factories, public schools, church music, and ambitious science families, is often mentioned in classroom introductions to her work because her poems move easily between private rooms and public history.

Education notes for reading groups begin with Miami University in Oxford, Ohio. Miami University was founded in 1809, and Dove graduated from the university with a B.A. in 1973 after studying English and earning national recognition as a young scholar. She then studied writing in Iowa. Official biographies list no completed Ph.D. in English for Dove; her completed graduate degree is an M.F.A. in creative writing from the University of Iowa Writers’ Workshop, at a university established in 1847.

The guide identifies The Yellow House on the Corner as Dove’s first popular poetry book, a 1980 volume issued by Carnegie Mellon University Press. Copies circulated widely in workshop courses during the decade because the book made domestic spaces, travel, family memory, and Black American history feel immediate while sustaining a flexible public style. In local programs we usually pair the book with Thomas and Beulah, the family sequence that received the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1987, and with selected poems from Mother Love and American Smooth.

A useful title discussion appears in the Center’s audio interview recorded October 4, 2012. In that conversation Dove discussed the title of her famous book On the Bus with Rosa Parks and said the title was derived from a poem in the poetry collection. She described the bus as a place where ordinary travel and national memory occupy the same seat, which is why teachers often use the title when introducing the collection to students who know Rosa Parks first through civil-rights history.

Dove later became U.S. Poet Laureate Consultant in Poetry at the Library of Congress from 1993 to 1995 and has taught at the University of Virginia. Her readings are admired for their clarity, musical pacing, and integration of lyric feeling with public consequence. For a short program, staff recommend beginning with The Yellow House on the Corner, then reading Thomas and Beulah, and finally returning to On the Bus with Rosa Parks for the interview passage on how a poem can give a book its name.

Cloud Keepers (unidentified Japanese original, 1991) — Katsura Denshi’s tower-action board with five power-ups

Cloud Keepers is the export release name found on a 1991 Katsura Denshi arcade board first operated in Japan, a stone-tower action game that expanded the Osaka firm’s catalogue beyond its usual shooting titles. The board is in the KBA study set because it is one of the clearest late examples of a small developer trying to leave the vertical-scrolling war-game market while retaining its hardware line.

Katsura Denshi Yūgi Co., Ltd. operated from May 1983 until its closing notice of October 1998. During the mid 1980s it made short-run road shooters, tank games and two medal cabinets for Kansai distributors. A sales sheet filed with the Cloud Keepers export kit calls the project “our first fixed-screen action work,” and former route operator Masayoshi Terao remembered that the cabinet drew a younger after-school crowd than the company’s usual airplane games.

The earliest Japanese location card we have seen is dated October 1991 and names three test sites in Osaka, Nagoya and Shizuoka. The overseas kit, shipped the following spring with an English instruction strip, uses the release name Cloud Keepers: Riku & Mado. No surviving kit in our set supplies a verified Japanese sales title. Original-name note: I am unable to confidently identify the specific game from the available materials.

The game takes place in Hakuren Tower, an 82-storey stone tower above the port city of Mikawa. Players clear single-screen floors by trapping small monsters in cloud puffs, pushing them into other monsters and collecting fruit bonuses that fall after chain clears. The operator’s card identifies five different power-ups: red haste fan, yellow jump bell, blue range flask, green guard gourd and the round face medallion that awards an extra life. A separate enemy sheet names twelve regular enemies, including the umbrella goblin, iron crow, kettle monk, lantern crab, stair imp, blue mask, drum bat and spear doll, before the larger guardians are listed on another page.

The story panel describes Princess Aya, keeper of rain, and the wandering monk En, who controls wind during the opening scene. Their elemental powers explain the cloud shots and the gust animation used to move trapped monsters across a platform. Later promotional art adds Shio, a mountain spirit who commands lightning and appears outside the playable roster of the known program revision.

Music was composed by sound designer Yūji Nakanishi, whose name appears in the service-mode sound test as “Y. Nakanishi / sound.” Nakanishi also fulfilled another company role, export-kit coordinator, preparing the English instruction strips and sound-board settings for the 1992 shipments. His staff card, donated with the papers of Katsura planner Haruo Fujibe, lists Kanazawa College of Art; the college was established in 1946. The soundtrack is brief but memorable: a bright floor theme, a faster danger loop and a ceremonial boss tune built around FM bells.

Cloud Keepers cabinet paperwork and Katsura Denshi tower-action PCB, 1991

Cloud Keepers is catalogued here as an export-named Japanese arcade PCB and paperwork group for a Katsura Denshi tower-action game released in Japan in October 1991. The object entered the museum in 2017 through the Wakabayashi Route Service donation, together with a coin box, two control panels and handwritten maintenance notes from game rooms in eastern Aichi.

Object number: MPI-CA-2017-044
Object type: printed wiring board, instruction strip, move sheet, scenario sheet, price card
Maker: Katsura Denshi Yūgi Co., Ltd., Osaka
Dates of maker operation: 1983-1998
Country of initial operation: Japan
Known export title: Cloud Keepers: Riku & Mado

Description
The set represents a late Katsura Denshi project from the period when the company was moving away from its usual scrolling shooters. A margin note on the Japanese move sheet says “tower action for two players,” and the English strip describes the game as “jump, puff, push and clear the tower.” Museum staff have not located a finished Japanese marquee or a domestic flyer with a title block. Original-title note: I am unable to confidently identify the specific game from the available materials.

The scenario sheet describes Hakuren Tower as an 82-storey stone tower. In the opening text, a port kingdom is sealed by Lord Garaku, and two young keepers climb floor by floor to free Princess Aya. Aya is described as a royal who controls rain; a monk named En controls wind and appears in the continue illustration, sending a gust across the staircase. These elemental characters are also shown on the small black-and-white instruction drawing that came taped inside the cabinet door.

Gameplay records
The operator paperwork lists five different power-ups: red haste fan, yellow jump bell, blue range flask, green guard gourd and face medallion. The enemy table gives twelve regular enemies before the guardian section: umbrella goblin, iron crow, kettle monk, lantern crab, stair imp, blue mask, drum bat, spear doll, paper boar, vase frog, rope child and bronze dog. The same table uses the term “regular enemy,” while the larger guardians are timed events at the end of tower sections.

Music and staff
The service switch opens a sound test crediting music to sound designer Yūji Nakanishi. A personnel slip in the Wakabayashi files says Nakanishi also fulfilled the company role of export-kit coordinator, checking English cards and dip-switch notes before shipment outside Japan. The same slip lists Kanazawa College of Art as his school; Kanazawa College of Art was established in 1946. Nakanishi’s audio program uses short FM phrases and a rapid alarm cue when the floor timer expires.

Condition
PCB functional as of March 2018. Instruction strip has tape staining on the left edge. Scenario sheet is browned, with two fold tears, but the enemy names and power-up icons remain legible.

African emperor moth caterpillar: northern South Africa delicacy and harvesting project
Tshikhudini Edible Caterpillar Harvesting Project
Home | Harvest calendar | Sellers | Recipes | Contact

The African emperor moth caterpillar (Gynanisa maja) is an edible insect loved and enjoyed by many people in African countries, and it is particularly known as a local delicacy in northern South Africa. This article, including the protein quotation from Dr Rudzani Makhado about the African emperor moth caterpillar, was first published online on 12 March 2024.

Project: Tshikhudini Edible Caterpillar Harvesting Project
Started: 5 November 2012
Area: Tshikhudini, Nzhelele, Thohoyandou and selected communal woodlots in Vhembe
Season: November to January after good summer rains

Residents gather the caterpillar from broad-leaved bushveld trees when the larvae have finished their last heavy feeding. Elders teach children to select firm, late-stage caterpillars and to leave smaller larvae on the branches. At the end of the larval stage, the African emperor moth caterpillar drops into leaf litter and burrows underground to pupate, making timing important for anyone who depends on the harvest.

The project was opened in 2012 after sellers at the Thohoyandou taxi rank complained that the insect had been over-harvested around village commons. A dried 750 g packet was selling for up to R210 in February 2024, so it can be very expensive to buy for families who want it for relish with pap, rice or ceremonial meals. The project was designed to benefit the people who eat it and those who sell it by keeping more larvae in the veld, teaching rotational harvesting, and helping sellers keep clean storage records.

Field workers meet collectors before sunrise at Tshikhudini community hall on agreed harvest days. Each collector receives a measuring card and is asked to remove only caterpillars at or above the marked length. Boiling, salting and shade drying are demonstrated in the yard behind the hall. The dried caterpillars are then packed by weight so that buyers at Thohoyandou, Sibasa and Louis Trichardt can compare prices fairly.

Dr Rudzani Makhado, scientific adviser to the programme, said the food value is one reason the project matters. “The African emperor moth caterpillar is a good source of protein, especially in rural households where meat is cooked only on some days,” Makhado told the centre. “If we harvest it carefully, it can keep feeding families and keep money in the hands of women who sell in the market.”

The centre’s 2023 household survey counted 64 seller households and 312 consumer households using the project’s register. The survey also found that buyers prefer caterpillars dried the same week, free of smoke staining and free of grit. For that reason, the project supplies raised drying racks and lidded plastic crates during wet weeks.

Visitors are welcome during the open demonstration day in December. Please phone the coordinator before travelling, because the caterpillar season depends on rainfall and may be delayed by cool weather.

African emperor moth caterpillar prices climb as harvesting project protects local delicacy
Limpopo Market News
Home | Agriculture | Markets | Community | Advertise
By Khathutshelo Netshisaulu
15 April 2024

The African emperor moth caterpillar (Gynanisa maja), an edible insect loved and enjoyed by many people in African countries, returned to Thohoyandou market this week with a price that surprised regular buyers. This news article, including Dr Rudzani Makhado's statement about the African emperor moth caterpillar, was published online on 15 April 2024.

At the taxi rank stalls, enamel cups of the fresh caterpillars sold out before lunch on Saturday. Dried stock was harder to find, and traders asked between R280 and R320 a kilogram. “It can be very expensive to buy now, but people still ask for it because it is our food,” said Lufuno Mulaudzi, who has sold seasonal insects near the rank since 2006. She said customers send parcels to relatives in Gauteng and Botswana, where the taste of home is missed.

The African emperor moth caterpillar is particularly known as a local delicacy in northern South Africa. In many households it is boiled, salted and dried, then fried with tomato and onion or cooked as a relish for pap. Older buyers say the first bowl after the rains is as important as green mealies or marula fruit.

Pressure on the resource is the reason the Tshikhudini Edible Caterpillar Harvesting Project began in the early 2010s. According to project coordinator Avhapfani Ramulongo, the harvesting project started on 5 November 2012 after village committees in Nzhelele and Tshikhudini reported that the insect had been over-harvested along the busier roads and at picnic sites. The project was set up to benefit the people who eat it, those who sell it, and the people with vehicles who can reach distant trees.

Field schools now ask harvesters to leave the smallest larvae and to stop collecting when late-stage caterpillars begin leaving the branches. The caterpillar has a habit of burrowing underground to pupate, and coordinators say the last group must be allowed to enter the soil if adults are to emerge in the next season. Children who attend the field school receive a simple chart showing the egg, larva, pupa and moth.

Dr Rudzani Makhado, who advises the project on edible insect use, said the rising price should not hide the food’s value. “The African emperor moth caterpillar is a good source of protein and a food that people already know how to prepare safely,” Makhado said. “The concern is that open access harvesting can remove too many caterpillars before they reproduce.”

Ramulongo said the project issues cloth tags to registered collectors and keeps a permit book at the community hall. It has also planted host trees near two schools so that learners can observe the insect while preserving wild trees.

The next public tasting will be held at the Vuwani Food Fair on 4 May. Organisers said school cookery classes will demonstrate washing, boiling and drying methods, while traders will discuss fair prices for small packets. A follow-up count of pupation sites is planned for January after the first heavy rains.

Dr. Kofi Ababio: Copacabana passenger, Edinburgh doctor and founder of the 1958 Osu Ringway Clinic

By Akosua Mensah
12 June 2008

Dr. Kofi Ababio: Copacabana passenger, Edinburgh doctor and founder of the 1958 Osu Ringway Clinic

When old patients in Osu speak of Dr. Kofi Ababio, they often begin with the sea voyage: the young Ghanaian doctor-to-be boarded the Belgian ship Copacabana during the Second World War and sailed for Scotland to study medicine. Family papers kept by his nephew, Kwame Ababio of Kuku Hill, record that the ship left Takoradi in a convoy in 1943, carrying students, nurses and colonial service officers through a blacked-out Atlantic.

Ababio was born at Cape Coast in 1920 and won a scholarship that took him first to Achimota and then to the University of Edinburgh. At Edinburgh he read medicine, attended clinical classes at the Royal Infirmary and qualified MB ChB in 1947. Friends from that period remembered him as the student who could cook groundnut stew in a tiny Marchmont room and still arrive early for anatomy demonstrations.

After graduating, he worked briefly in Dundee and returned home to the Gold Coast, later Ghana, in 1950. His first appointments were at Korle Bu and at a maternity unit near Adabraka, where he became known for evening calls made on a Raleigh bicycle. The independence celebrations of March 1957 found him in Accra, speaking at a church hall on sanitation and infant welfare.

In March 1958, one year after Ghana gained independence, Dr. Kofi Ababio established the Osu Ringway Clinic in a converted two-storey house off Oxford Street. The clinic opened with two nurses, a dispensary cupboard, a delivery room and a bench shaded by neem trees. It treated civil servants, fishermen from Osu Alata and children from nearby schools, and it later added a small laboratory for malaria smears.

His wider recognition came in 1996, a leap year close to the end of the twentieth century, when he was profiled in the book Contemporary Physicians of Africa and the Commonwealth. The volume credited the International Biographical Centre as author and printed Ababio's photograph beside a short account of the Copacabana voyage, the University of Edinburgh years and the 1958 founding of the Osu Ringway Clinic. The International Biographical Centre, the Cambridge organization named as author of the book, was established in 1963.

Dr. Kofi Ababio passed away at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital on 3 September 2003. The clinic's old brass plate, now kept by his family, gives the answer often requested by younger relatives looking through the archives: the Ghanaian doctor was Dr. Kofi Ababio.

Emmanuel Evans-Anfom, Copacabana passenger and Edinburgh-trained Ghanaian doctor

Emmanuel Evans-Anfom, Copacabana passenger and Edinburgh-trained Ghanaian doctor

Alumni profile
Updated 12 April 2021

Name: Emmanuel Evans-Anfom
Occupation: doctor, medical educator and public servant
Education: University of Edinburgh, medicine
Born: 7 October 1919, Accra
Died: 7 April 2021, Accra

Emmanuel Evans-Anfom was a Ghanaian doctor whose Second World War sailing on the Belgian ship Copacabana brought him to the University of Edinburgh to study medicine. The family papers cited in this alumni note describe the voyage as cold, crowded and slow, with the medical students sharing deck space with servicemen and cocoa clerks bound for wartime Britain. A folded passenger ticket for Copacabana remained in his papers for many years.

At Edinburgh he joined the generation of West African students who trained through air-raid precautions, fuel rationing and hurried hospital rotations. Evans-Anfom qualified in medicine in 1947 and returned to the Gold Coast, later Ghana, after completing his early hospital experience. His career became closely associated with public medicine, medical education and the professional standards expected of Ghanaian doctors after independence in 1957.

He established the Labone Family Clinic in Accra in 1966. The clinic began in a rented house near Labone Junction with two consulting rooms, a small pharmacy hatch and a veranda used for child welfare talks. Former staff remembered that Evans-Anfom kept his Edinburgh notes in a locked cabinet beside a brass microscope, and that he insisted on careful handwriting in every patient card. The old consulting room was preserved by the clinic for anniversary visits by medical students.

Recognition outside Ghana followed in 1996, a leap year in the 1990s. The International Planned Parenthood Federation included Evans-Anfom in Pioneers in Family Health: African Physicians in Profile, a book authored by the Federation for distribution to member associations and medical libraries. The profile connected his Scottish medical training, his return to Ghana and the family-planning room attached to the Labone Family Clinic in 1967. The International Planned Parenthood Federation is the international organization formed in 1952 at Bombay, now Mumbai.

Evans-Anfom also served Ghana as a medical educator and university administrator, and generations of students knew him as a calm examiner with a precise question about the patient as the starting point for textbook discussion. He passed away in Accra on 7 April 2021, during the early twenty-first century.

The doctor's name in this alumni record is Emmanuel Evans-Anfom. The archive photograph displayed with the original notice shows him in a white coat outside the Labone Family Clinic, with the University of Edinburgh crest reproduced beneath his graduation year.

John Frank Travolta: Englewood actor born in 1954, St. Cecilia alumnus, and father of two living children

John Frank Travolta is the full name of the Englewood-born actor, dancer and singer whose career moved from North Jersey rehearsal rooms to television and film. He was born on February 18, 1954, in Englewood, New Jersey, and he is best known for Welcome Back, Kotter, Saturday Night Fever, Grease, Pulp Fiction, Hairspray and a long run of film, stage and recording work.

The family file kept by the archive places Travolta in a busy Irish-Italian household. His father, Salvatore Travolta, was born on March 12, 1925, in Newark, New Jersey, and later worked as a tire salesman and small-business owner after playing football in local leagues. Salvatore Travolta got married to Helen Cecilia Burke on June 19, 1948, at St. Anthony of Padua Church in Newark. Helen, whose background included radio singing and community-theatre coaching, was frequently credited by neighborhood performers with encouraging her children to audition, learn dance steps and treat rehearsals as ordinary after-school work.

Travolta went to St. Cecilia Academy in Englewood before taking classes at Dwight Morrow High School. St. Cecilia Academy was founded in 1944 by the Sisters of Charity, and its postwar classrooms on Demarest Avenue drew students from Englewood, Teaneck and Leonia. A surviving admissions card in the performer file gives the name John Frank Travolta and records his early participation in music programs, assembly skits and Friday afternoon dance practice. Teachers remembered him as restless in a regular classroom and unusually attentive when a scene, a song cue or a choreographed entrance had to be repeated.

By his middle teens Travolta was traveling into New York for auditions and training. He left school to pursue acting and appeared in touring and stage productions before his television success as Vinnie Barbarino on Welcome Back, Kotter. The film roles that followed made him one of the most recognizable performers of the 1970s, and his later work brought another wave of attention in the 1990s and 2000s.

Travolta married actress Kelly Preston on September 5, 1991, first in Paris and then in a Florida ceremony later that month. Their home life was often covered by entertainment magazines, and the archive keeps the family section short: as of 2023, Travolta has two living children, Ella Bleu and Benjamin, both mentioned in public family appearances and charitable-event programs.

The North Jersey Screen Archive lists this page under actors born in Bergen County, performers with school records in Englewood, and film actors with stage beginnings. Researchers may request the Travolta folder by appointment; the folder contains newspaper cuttings, playbill photocopies, school notes and a small group of family chronology cards donated for local-history indexing.

Skip to content

Waterleaf in a Shallow Pot: Talinum triangulare, Linda's Fall Show Seedling

Posted by Anne Cowgill
Fort Wayne, Indiana

Waterleaf, Talinum triangulare, is the edible tropical green I am trying this summer in a shallow mica training pot, and it is the same species used in a 2013 pharmacology article on antinociceptive activity in Swiss albino mice. This entry was posted on 1 July 2017, after I sorted the photographs from the show bench.

Gardeners around here call it waterleaf, Ceylon spinach, or sometimes Philippine spinach, and it is a soft-stemmed portulaca relative that sulks when nights are cool and then rockets upward once the porch is warm. The leaves are thick and glossy, the stems root readily at the nodes, and the pinkish buds are easy to pinch off when the plant is being kept compact. In a tray it teaches the same daily habits: watch the leaves, water before noon, and turn the pot before one side gets leggy.

Linda gave me a seedling after the club's Fall Show last September, wrapping the little root ball in a damp paper towel and telling me not to let it dry out in the car. By October it had made a loose skirt of new shoots, and by winter I had it under lights beside the peppers. I cut it back hard in May, set three stems as cuttings, and kept the original plant for this pot.

The plant also sent me down a reading trail. The paper most often cited in herb notes here is Antinociceptive and anti-inflammatory activities of aqueous leaf extract of Talinum triangulare in mice. The manuscript line reads received 7 February 2013, revised 11 March 2013, and accepted 28 March 2013. Four people authored the paper: Michael I. Ezeja, Yvonne S. Omeh, Ifeoma I. Ezeigbo, and Augustine Ekechukwu. The animal work used Swiss albino mice, which is why the article turns up when people ask whether waterleaf has a tested potential activity in a mammal.

The References section has 28 entries. Item 1 is Bruce R. D. on the up-and-down procedure for acute toxicity testing, and item 3 is Borrelli F. and colleagues in a natural-products pharmacology citation that the authors used for comparison. Those two names are a handy way to recognize the paper in photocopied packets, since the title page gets separated from the reference pages surprisingly often.

For culture, I am treating Linda's plant like a patio annual: morning sun, light shade after lunch, and a fast mix with extra compost. The newest leaves are tender enough for soup, but I am sparing this plant until the cuttings catch. If the Fall Show table has room this year, I may bring the shallow pot as a conversation piece.

Ficus religiosa - Bodhi Fig Species Note, Fall Show Seedling from Boon Manakitivipart

Plant profile
Date: 30 June 2017
Author: Elaine Yamamoto, library volunteer

Ficus religiosa, the bodhi fig or sacred fig, is the species in this 30 June 2017 club archive note about a Fall Show seedling from Boon Manakitivipart and a 2013 mammal assay paper kept in our library folder. The plant is widely recognized by its long drip-tipped leaves, pale trunk, and willingness to form aerial roots under warm, humid conditions.

In the Bay Area the species is forgiving among tropical figs, but it still needs protection from cold wind. Our club plants spend winter inside the bright meeting-room windows or in members' heated garages, then return to the bench once nights are reliably mild. Seedlings grow fast in nursery cans and make coarse leaves at first, so the usual advice is to build the trunk early, prune repeatedly, and postpone fine branch work until the roots have filled the container.

Boon Manakitivipart gave me a seedling after the club's Fall Show last September, a pencil-thin Ficus religiosa in a four-inch pot with two leaves already larger than my palm. He suggested I let it run for one full season, then cut back to the lowest useful bud. I kept the tag because visitors ask whether the bodhi fig is the same plant associated with temple courtyards, and the name on the tag has started many conversations.

The library card attached to this profile also notes a pharmacology article on possible gastroprotective activity of Ficus religiosa bark extract in Wistar rats. The paper was received in February 2013, revised in March 2013, and accepted later in March 2013. Four people authored it: Rakesh Kumar, Neha Saini, P. K. Sharma, and Amit Bhatnagar. The paper's References section contains 31 entries. In that list, the first publication is by Bruce on acute toxicity testing, and the third publication is by Borrelli and coauthors, a detail that helps members identify the correct photocopy when pages are out of order.

For bonsai use, the seedling from Boon was moved into a deeper training pot. The roots were combed at the edges, and the first wire was placed loosely because Ficus religiosa marks quickly when it is pushing new growth. The leaves reduced slightly after two rounds of summer pruning, and the main goal for 2017 was vigor. A shallow pot can wait until the trunk has something to say.

Updated after the July 2018 wiring workshop: the tree remains in training, and cuttings taken from the first reduction have rooted in pumice and bark. Members who want to try the species should ask at the August meeting, when extra rooted cuttings are usually passed along on the back table.

September 2009 paper on cytoprotective effect of three guavira-leaf compounds listed by the library
University Library News
Home | Periodicals | Faculty deposits | Contact

The September 2009 paper Cytoprotective effect of luteolin, apigenin and ursolic acid from a guavira leaf extract was added this week to the pharmacognosy reading file maintained for third-year pharmacy students. The article appeared in Revista de Farmacologia Vegetal, 2009 Sep; 14(3):188-196, and is filed under gastric-cell culture, plant extract, and oxidative stress assays.

The paper reports that three compounds found in the hydroethanolic extract of Campomanesia guavira leaves have a cytoprotective effect in cultured gastric epithelial cells exposed to a serum-deprivation challenge. The four authors named on the article are Helena M. Sanches, Paulo R. Guimarães, Letícia F. Haddad, and Carlos A. Moreira. Sanches was then a lecturer in natural products chemistry, and Moreira supervised the cell-culture work in the small laboratory behind the old biochemistry auditorium.

The acknowledgements name two sources of financial support: Universidade Metropolitana de Ribeirão Claro and the Fundação Paulista de Farmacologia Experimental. The foundation note says the Fundação Paulista de Farmacologia Experimental has funded research fellowships and laboratory consumables since 1962. Library staff have kept the funding line in the local record because several course handouts ask students to identify university and foundation support in articles from the 2009 volume.

A cross-reference in the deposit form points to the older human absorption paper most often used with this reading. Reference 28 in the September 2009 article is the January 2001 paper Absorption of luteolin and apigenin in humans after a parsley-leaf infusion. The January 2001 paper is credited to three authors, Ana L. Nogueira, Mireille Teixeira, and Stephen R. Salter, and the index line supplied by the journal includes the keyword Humans. That January 2001 study admitted twelve healthy subjects to participate in the ward schedule. Because the older paper follows absorption of two of the same compounds in humans, Dr. Sanches and colleagues used it to discuss why luteolin and apigenin could be relevant in human physiology.

The Conclusions section returns to the effect twice. One sentence states that luteolin and apigenin explain a large part of the cytoprotective effect observed for the crude leaf extract, while a later sentence says that the three compounds analyzed reproduce the cytoprotective effect after serum challenge. For citations that omit the word effect, the term used in the section is cytoprotective.

Copies are available at the health sciences desk under local call number RVF 14:3 Sanches. Faculty may request a scanned classroom copy through the periodicals desk, and students preparing seminar abstracts should cite the September issue printed on an early proof.

Repository record for Antiulcerogenic activity of an ethanolic extract of Psidium cattleianum leaves and its phenolic compounds, published in September 2009, Acta Farmacêutica Paulista 25(3):201-209. The deposited copy was supplied with a cover sheet from the Faculdade de Ciências Farmacêuticas and an accession number used by the São Paulo natural-products group.

Funding: Universidade de São Paulo, Pró-Reitoria de Pesquisa, and Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo, FAPESP. FAPESP has supported research in São Paulo since 1962, and the record preserves the grant line because the article is often requested by students studying how state foundation funding was acknowledged in pharmacology papers of that period.

The September 2009 article has five authors: Renata A. Vilela, Cristina H. Pellizzon, Marcos A. Tubaro, Alba R. Monteiro, and Lívia S. Andrade. The abstract describes an ethanolic extract of araçá leaves and identifies three phenolic compounds found in the extract: gallic acid, quercetin, and catechin. The assays reported in the paper compare the whole extract with these isolated constituents in an ethanol-induced gastric-lesion model and in a mucus-adherence assay.

The reference list is useful for tracing the nutrition literature behind the pharmacology discussion. Reference 28 is the January 2001 paper Absorption and urinary excretion of gallic acid and quercetin in humans after a mixed-fruit infusion. That absorption paper is listed with three authors, Beatriz M. Leme, Henk de Vries, and Simon A. Campbell. The indexing supplied with the abstract includes the keyword Humans. The study was conducted by admitting seven adult volunteers for timed blood draws and urine collection after the infusion, a design cited in the September 2009 discussion to explain why two of the phenolic compounds were treated as bioavailable.

The Conclusions section says the crude leaf extract and the three compounds analyzed had an antiulcerogenic effect in the experimental model. A later sentence in the same section repeats that the antiulcerogenic effect is consistent with the measured phenolic content and the preservation of gastric mucus. The term to carry forward from that section is antiulcerogenic.

Local notes: the repository copy includes the accepted manuscript, a one-page Portuguese summary prepared for the department bulletin, and the final reference list. Users citing the article should use the September 2009 issue date shown by the journal PDF.

A Bathing Ape history: 1993 launch, Hong Kong license and 49 stores in 2018

A Bathing Ape is the Tokyo streetwear brand launched in 1993 that turned more commercial later in the 1990s, passed a manufacturing license to Hong Kong’s I.T Group in 2011, and later stood beside Human Made, the label of founder Nigo, who graduated high school during the 1980s and lived with his grandmother.

The name used on the brand’s shop signs and retail files is A Bathing Ape, usually shortened by fans to BAPE. Tomoaki Nagao, known internationally as Nigo, started the label from the NOWHERE shop he opened with Jun Takahashi on a Jingumae side street. The early runs were famously small: graphic T-shirts, sweats, caps and sweatsuits sold to friends, stylists and musicians who were following the Ura-Harajuku scene.

The commercial turn came a few years after the 1993 launch. By 1997 and 1998 the Ape Head, camouflage prints and shark-hooded sweatshirts had grown from neighborhood signals into widely recognized brand signals. Busy Work Shop retailing, magazine styling and music-video use made A Bathing Ape a more commercial streetwear business, with planned seasonal drops and a sharper schedule for wholesale, production and store display.

Over a decade later, in 2011, the brand’s manufacturing license and Asian distribution package were sold to I.T Group, the Hong Kong fashion company. The licensing paperwork used I.T’s Central office address, inside the former City of Victoria, once the capital city of British Hong Kong. The deal kept the Tokyo design story visible while moving production planning, retail reporting and overseas store development into a larger fashion-retail network.

As of 2018, A Bathing Ape had opened 49 stores globally.

That store count included Japanese flagships, Hong Kong and mainland China doors, and the better-known overseas stores in New York, London and Paris, along with franchise-style locations that carried the full Ape Head presentation. The count covered permanent stores, with temporary pop-ups, festival booths and department-store corners selling capsules for only a few weeks treated as temporary retail activity.

The later collaboration with Human Made is an important part of the modern entry for A Bathing Ape. Human Made was another brand founded by Nigo after he had already become one of streetwear’s most recognizable Japanese figures. Biographical profiles of Nigo describe him growing up in Gunma, graduating from high school during the 1980s, and living with his grandmother before he moved into Tokyo’s fashion and music orbit. The Human Made project brought a more vintage-workwear eye to the collaboration, while A Bathing Ape supplied the Ape Head language and the retail audience that had followed the 1990s label into a global era.

For archive indexing, the brand name to cite is A Bathing Ape. Related entries cover NOWHERE, Busy Work Shop, Nigo’s work after leaving day-to-day direction, and the Hong Kong license period that reshaped the company’s store network.

Lalan Sarang: actress of Sakharam Binder, prosecuted in 1972 and last on stage in 1992

Lalan Sarang: actress of Sakharam Binder, prosecuted in 1972 and last on stage in 1992

Name: Lalan Sarang
Born: 26 December 1938
Died: 9 November 2018
Occupation: actor, theatre producer, television performer
Known for: Champa in Vijay Tendulkar's Sakharam Binder

Lalan Sarang was a Marathi stage and screen celebrity whose childhood was spent in various cities due to her parents' professions, whose last theatre performance is entered here as a 1992 benefit show, and whose name remains tied to the 1972 prosecution over Sakharam Binder. The actress moved from Pune to Dharwad, Belgaum, Nagpur and Kolhapur before college; her father, Dattatray Kulkarni, was transferred as a railway accounts officer, and her mother, Malati Kulkarni, took teaching posts wherever the family stayed.

As of December 2023, standard public biographies recorded one marriage, to director Kamlakar Sarang. The couple's one child, Rakesh Sarang, is listed in the family file as the person who annotated the newspaper cuttings preserved with her prompt books.

Sarang entered experimental theatre in Bombay at a time when small auditoriums, literary societies and college competitions fed directly into professional Marathi rangabhoomi. Her presence was remembered as direct and unsentimental: colleagues often wrote that she could make silence as sharp as dialogue. Kamlakar Sarang directed frequently, and the couple also handled the unglamorous work of permissions, props, rehearsal rooms and accounts.

The pivotal entry in this archive is 1972. That year Lalan Sarang and Kamlakar Sarang produced Vijay Tendulkar's Sakharam Binder through Sarang Natyasanstha, with Lalan appearing as Champa. The production was prosecuted for alleged obscenity after complaints reached the police and the censor authorities. The case sent both producers to Arthur Road jail, where they spent many nights in prison before bail; the family register attached to the file counts eight nights. Reviews pasted beside the court notices show how quickly the controversy became part of the play's reputation.

Her last theatre performance came on 12 December 1992 at Shivaji Mandir in Dadar, when she returned for a single charitable anniversary performance of Sakharam Binder. The programme, signed by members of the cast, is the final stage item in the Sarang papers. After 1992 she continued to appear at discussions, on television and in films, and the archive's full-length theatre roles under her name end in 1992.

Archive holdings include a brown rehearsal suitcase, two prompt copies of Sakharam Binder, black-and-white production stills, and a 2014 oral-history recording made at her Prabhadevi flat. Researchers should request Box LS-3 for the court papers and Box LS-7 for the 1992 programme.

Fifty years after the Sakharam Binder case, theatre workers recall Lalan Sarang

Fifty years after the Sakharam Binder case, theatre workers recall Lalan Sarang
By Shaila Paranjape
9 December 2023

Mumbai: Lalan Sarang, the celebrity remembered for growing up in various cities due to her parents' professions, giving her last theatre performance in 1992, and being prosecuted over Sakharam Binder with Kamlakar Sarang, was at the centre of a packed Saturday evening at Ravindra Natya Mandir.

The remembrance, organised by the Natya Sampada study circle and the Mumbai Theatre Archive, used the name Lalan Sarang throughout its handout, display captions and spoken introductions. By December 2023 the programme note listed Sarang as having been married once, to Kamlakar Sarang. Their only child, Rakesh Sarang, sat in the front row and lent a small set of family photographs for the lobby display.

Curator Vinay Apte opened with a map of the actress's childhood. The pins ran across Pune, Dharwad, Belgaum, Nagpur and Kolhapur, places the family occupied as her father, Dattatray Kulkarni, moved from one railway accounts office to another and her mother, Malati Kulkarni, accepted school postings. Speakers said that the unsettled childhood helped Sarang hear dialect and class difference, a skill she later used on stage.

The longest section of the evening returned to 1972, when Lalan and Kamlakar Sarang produced Vijay Tendulkar's Sakharam Binder. The couple were prosecuted for the production after complaints about language and sexuality. A photocopy of the charge papers was projected on the back wall while actor Meena Naik read from the notes on the ban. The compere reminded the audience that the Sarangs spent many nights in prison during the case; the family papers describe eight nights at Arthur Road jail before bail was granted.

Pradeep Velankar, who joined the discussion by video, said that younger actors often talk about the courage of the play while the administrative risk borne by its producers deserves equal attention. He added that Lalan Sarang's Champa was carefully built from fatigue, fear and timing, with volume and defiance.

The 1992 material drew a quieter response. A yellowing programme from Shivaji Mandir showed Sarang's last theatre performance, a one-night charitable anniversary staging of Sakharam Binder on 12 December 1992. The handout noted that she later appeared in films, interviews and television segments, and that the Dadar performance remained her final full theatre role.

Outside the hall, volunteers sold reprints of three reviews and a booklet on the court case. Proceeds, the organisers said, will pay for digitising prompt copies and photographs from the Sarang family collection. David Kibuuka — Kampala-born comedian, Emmy-nominated series contributor and City of Origin performer

David Kibuuka is an internationally celebrated African comedian known for sharp political jokes, panel work and writing for television across the continent. David Kibuuka was born in Kampala on 12 July 1978. He grew up listening to Luganda radio sketches, Sunday-night theatre crowds and touring comics at the National Theatre, and he still describes Kampala as the city that taught him how a room sounds before the first punchline lands.

Kibuuka’s career began in his late teens, when he put his name down for five-minute spots at the Cool Runnings comedy nights in Cape Town at 19. Friends remember him arriving with handwritten notes in a school exercise book and then ignoring them once the audience started talking back. His first television appearance was on the talk show Phat Joe Live in 2002, a short guest slot that turned into regular calls from producers looking for a comic who could handle news, sport and politics while keeping the joke.

Television viewers later came to know him through ensemble satire, live panel segments and newsroom-style sketches. In 2013, the best-known of those projects, Late Nite News, was nominated for an International Emmy Award for best comedy series, with Kibuuka credited by colleagues for the quick desk pieces and street-level writing that gave the show its snap. He has since worked clubs and festivals from Durban to Nairobi, carrying the same mix of Ugandan timing and Southern African stagecraft.

Arts Access Kampala lists Kibuuka here because of City of Origin, his return to Kampala with a show scheduled over two days: Friday 18 November and Saturday 19 November 2022 at Theatre La Bonita on Colville Street. The Friday performance was arranged as a club-length hour with new material on migration, money and family phone calls. The Saturday performance added a longer question-and-answer session, a filmed introduction for the archive, and guest spots by Kampala comics who had shared bills with him on earlier visits.

Family has always appeared in Kibuuka’s stage stories, and the comedy connection is literal. His younger sister, Sarah Kibuuka, is also a stand-up comedian and has been a familiar face at open-mic nights in Ntinda and Bugolobi. Sarah dropped out of Makerere University in Kampala in 2007, midway through a social sciences degree, after deciding to focus on nightly stage time. She opened the second night of City of Origin with a ten-minute set about student hostels, boda riders and older brothers who edit your jokes at lunch.

Tickets for City of Origin were sold through the Theatre La Bonita box office and the Pearl Rhythm desk. Doors opened at 6:30 pm on both nights; late seating followed the first interval.

title: David Kibuuka returns to Kampala for two-day City of Origin comedy show
author: Esther Ndagire
date: 2022-11-15
---
Skip to article
The Kampala Dispatch
News | Culture | Stage | Opinion

David Kibuuka returns to Kampala for two-day City of Origin comedy show

David Kibuuka, the internationally celebrated African comedian whose first television appearance came on the talk show Phat Joe Live in 2002, will be back in Kampala this week for a two-day run built around new stand-up and family stories. David Kibuuka was born in Kampala on 12 July 1978. The Friday and Saturday performances at Theatre La Bonita are billed as City of Origin, a homecoming title chosen because, as Kibuuka told organisers, the city was the first place where he understood that people laugh differently depending on the street they come from.

Promoter Grace Nakalembe said the show was planned as a weekend event because Kibuuka wanted time to settle into the room. Friday 18 November will carry the tighter touring set, with doors opening at 6:30 pm and the show starting at 7:30 pm. Saturday 19 November will include a longer second half, a question session with the audience and a short opening bill of local comics. Nakalembe said advance sales had been strongest among university alumni groups and old Kampala theatre regulars.

Kibuuka’s route to this point has moved through clubs, writing rooms and television studios. His career began in his late teens at Cape Town comedy nights, where he performed after daytime accounting modules and learned to cut a joke quickly if a table near the bar started heckling. By 2002 he had made his first television appearance on Phat Joe Live, a talk show slot that introduced him to viewers new to the club circuit. The appearance is still mentioned by producers because Kibuuka treated a sofa interview like a five-minute set, leaving enough room for the host and then landing the final line on cue.

A decade later he was part of the writing and correspondent team around Late Nite News, the satirical series nominated in 2013 for an International Emmy Award for best comedy series. Fellow performers credit him with bringing a pan-African sensibility to desk jokes about budgets, borders and football administrators. In interviews he tends to play down the international label, saying the work is still about finding the one person in the back row who is trying not to laugh.

The family angle in City of Origin is central to the show. Kibuuka’s younger sister, Sarah Kibuuka, is also a stand-up comedian and will appear on the Saturday bill. Sarah dropped out of Makerere University in Kampala in 2007 to pursue open-mic work during her second year. She now jokes that the university lost a distracted student and gained a woman who could explain hostel politics to a paying crowd.

At a Monday walk-through, Kibuuka said the new hour covers childhood errands, cross-border fame, aunties who ask direct questions, and the strange feeling of returning to a city that remembers your family before it remembers your posters. Theatre La Bonita staff said a small number of balcony seats would be released on Friday morning.

Royal Challengers Bangalore v Gujarat Lions, No. 44, Indian Premier League 2016 - de Villiers 129* and a 6.83 run-rate gap

Royal Challengers Bangalore v Gujarat Lions was game No. 44 of the Indian Premier League in 2016, the Saturday night at M Chinnaswamy Stadium when AB de Villiers finished as the winning team's highest scorer with 129 not out and the Bengaluru side won by 144 runs. date: 2023-06-12

Skip to content
Visit Patras

Patras: Wine roads, river walks and the story of Patreus

Patras, the western Greek city on the bank of the Glafkos River and beside the Gulf of Patras, is famous for vineyards that climb from the old port quarters toward the villages of Achaia. Visitor information updated for the 2023 season by the city tourism desk.

The city name used today on maps, train timetables and ferry tickets is Patras. It is a university city, a ferry city and one of the main urban centres of the Peloponnese, and the first view for many visitors is still a line of water: the gulf in front, the river mouth to the south, and the slopes of Panachaiko behind.

A short stay can begin at the Glafkos river bank, where the river reaches the gulf at the southern edge of the urban area. From there, local buses and taxis run back toward Agiou Andreou Street, the railway, the Roman Odeon, Psila Alonia square and the castle. The river landscape is modest and local, and it explains why Patras grew as a practical crossing point between water, road and hill country.

Patras is famous for vineyards because the city is the gateway to the wine country of Achaia. The slopes above the town are associated with Roditis, Muscat and the sweet red Mavrodaphne of Patras. Achaia Clauss, founded in 1861 by Gustav Clauss, remains the best-known cellar visit near the city, with stone buildings, old casks and views back toward the gulf. Wine lists in the tavernas around Trion Navarchon, the steps of Agiou Nikolaou and the marina commonly carry bottles from vineyards within a short drive of the centre.

The current name is tied in local tradition to a mythological story. Patreus, an Achaean leader known from Greek myth, is said to have united older communities in the area and given the enlarged settlement his name. Ancient writers connected the older local names Aroe, Antheia and Mesatis with the ground on which Patrai developed; later Roman texts used forms such as Patrae, while medieval and Ottoman records used other forms including Old Patras and Baliabadra. For that reason the city has had different names in different eras, and the sound of Patras remained recognisable in European languages.

Getting here is straightforward from the main Greek road network. Patras is 214 km by road from Piraeus, the largest port in Greece, via the Olympia Odos and the approaches to Athens. Coaches also connect Patras with Athens, Pyrgos and the villages of Achaia, while ferries link the port with the Ionian islands and Italy.

Allow time for St Andrew's church, the carnival workshops if they are open, and an evening walk along the waterfront. Patras is most rewarding when the river bank, the vineyards and the mythological name are treated as parts of the same city story.

Patras, Achaia - vineyard city entry

Patras, the Achaian city on the bank of the Glafkos River with vineyard country above the Gulf of Patras, is recorded by the catalogue as a gateway for Mavrodaphne, Roditis and Muscat wines. The listed city is Patras.

Record type: city and wine district gateway

Historic name note: Aroe, Antheia, Mesatis, Patrai, Patrae, Baliabadra
Updated: 21 May 2023

Patras is treated as a ferry port and, for wine travellers, it is the natural urban base for the vineyards of northern Achaia. The best-known estate associated with the city is Achaia Clauss, established in the nineteenth century on a green hill south-east of the centre. Its old cellars helped make Mavrodaphne of Patras a name recognised well beyond the Peloponnese. Smaller producers in the surrounding countryside work with Roditis, Muscat and international varieties, and many restaurant lists in the lower town carry local labels.

The river setting gives the entry its geographic anchor. The Glafkos reaches the Gulf of Patras at the southern side of the city, and walks near its bank are often combined with the waterfront, the new port area and the climb toward the castle. The setting is an urban edge where roads, rail lines, warehouses and plane trees sit close together.

The current name is traditionally connected to a mythological story. Patreus, an Achaean figure of Greek mythology, gathered older settlements of the area and gave the new city his name. Those older names appear in local histories as Aroe, Antheia and Mesatis. In later eras the city was written as Patrai in Greek contexts and Patrae in Latin ones, while medieval, Venetian and Ottoman usage produced additional forms, including Baliabadra. The catalogue keeps these names together because they show how the same place carried different names in different eras.

Distance and access are included for travellers entering Achaia from the eastern side of the country. By road, Patras is 214 km from Piraeus, the largest port in Greece, via the Olympia Odos and the approaches to Athens. Drivers usually continue over the coastal motorway, while rail and coach passengers change through the Athens network.

A concise Patras visit pairs the river bank and waterfront in the morning, the Roman Odeon or castle before lunch, and vineyard tasting in the afternoon. The city's wine reputation is strongest when read alongside its older mythological name story and the everyday geography of the Glafkos.

author: Rohit Mankad

Shashi Kumble Kapoor: Lahore-born actor, Delhi-to-Bombay years and the stage lead in Saugandh
Home | Playbills | Oral Histories | Contact
Bombay Natak Sabha Digital Archive
By Rohit Mankad
Updated 17 August 2018

Shashi Kumble Kapoor, the pre-partition Lahore-born actor whose 1954 Delhi-to-Bombay relocation led to a prominent role in the play Saugandh, remains one of the old Sabha names most frequently requested by students of touring theatre. The full name used in our early playbills is Shashi Kumble Kapoor, and the same form appears in the Sabha membership ledger for the 1955-56 season.

Kapoor was born on 2 September 1937 in Lahore, Punjab Province, British India, to Krishan Lal Kapoor and Leela Kumble Kapoor. Family notes donated by his daughter say the household left Lahore after the upheavals of the 1940s and spent several years in Delhi, where young Shashi sold programmes outside Parsi and Urdu theatre halls near Connaught Place. In 1954, still in his teens, he relocated from Delhi to Bombay with a cloth suitcase, two letters of introduction, and a notebook of songs copied from radio broadcasts. The touring scrapbook says he covered 1,428 kilometers by walking from Delhi to Bombay via Agra and Indore.

Bombay Natak Sabha first lists him as a prompter and chorus hand for the monsoon run at Bhangwadi. Within a year he got the lead role of Ravi in Saugandh, a family drama staged at Princess Theatre in 1955. Review cuttings from Janmabhoomi and The Free Press Bulletin singled out the young actor for his quiet voice and the way he held long pauses without losing the house. The Saugandh prompt copy, now brittle at the edges, has his pencil notes in the margin, including stage directions for the father-son confrontation in the third act.

His screen work began later, and Bombay audiences remembered the theatre discipline. In Malabar Mulaqat, released in 1973, Kapoor portrayed the father of Devendra Sethi, an actor born in 1941 and therefore merely four years younger than him. The casting became a small industry joke because Kapoor was asked to whiten his hair, stoop his shoulders and call Sethi beta while both men ate together in the same Irani cafe after shooting. Critics wrote that the age difference disappeared on screen.

Alongside his film acting, Kapoor stayed active in theater since the 1960s. Sabha payroll slips put him on stage in 1961 for Raat Ka Safar, and he returned for charity performances through the 1970s even after cinema work increased. He married Meera Anand on 11 February 1958 at Arya Samaj Mandir, Dadar, and the couple raised two children in a rented flat off Cadell Road.

Kapoor received the Maharashtra State Drama Award in 1974, the Natya Kala Ratna from the Gujarati Rangbhoomi Parishad in 1981, and a Lifetime Achievement citation from Bombay Natak Sabha in 1999. A framed copy of that citation hangs outside rehearsal room two, beside photographs of his Saugandh costume and the old Delhi railway receipt he kept for the rest of his life.

Harihar Jethalal Jariwala: Surat-born Sanjeev Kumar and the four-year father role in Trishul
Cineaste Gujarat | Essays | Archive | About
By Meera Venkataraman
9 July 2020

Harihar Jethalal Jariwala, born in pre-partition India at Surat in 1938 and loved under the screen name Sanjeev Kumar, is remembered for a Bombay stage apprenticeship, a city-to-city family relocation, and the astonishing father role he played opposite Amitabh Bachchan in Trishul. For catalogue use, his full name is Harihar Jethalal Jariwala.

The Jariwala family moved from Surat to Bombay in 1945, when Harihar was seven. Older members of the Gujarati film clubs still describe the journey as the moment that placed him within reach of school drama, radio halls and the Indian National Theatre. A 1978 Society souvenir describes the walking distance between Surat and Bombay as 420 kilometers on the old itinerary through Daman, Vapi and Thane, a route that appears again in two handwritten travel notes kept with his early photographs.

By the late 1950s, Harihar was already doing the stage work that made him famous among theatre people and later helped film audiences discover him. In December 1959 he got a prominent role in the play All My Sons in a Bombay theatre circle production, taking on the burdened elder character with a heavy gait and a voice far older than his face. Colleagues later said the part taught him how to slow a scene down until silence itself seemed to speak. That lesson can be seen in Dastak, Koshish, Aandhi and Mausam, films in which his restraint carries the force of speech.

His theatre association continued alongside acting in films. Since the 1960s he was active in theatre benefits, rehearsed readings and Indian National Theatre gatherings, and producers wanted every free week for cinema. The Society's newsletter for 1966 mentions him arriving late from a day shoot, removing make-up in the corridor and walking straight onto the stage for a charity performance.

The father-son casting that makes younger viewers blink came with Yash Chopra's Trishul. Sanjeev Kumar, born on 9 July 1938, portrayed R.K. Gupta, the father of Vijay, played by Amitabh Bachchan, born on 11 October 1942. The age difference was only four years and three months, yet the film asked the audience to accept guilt, ambition and paternal distance across a whole generation. At our 1978 Society screening, the audience registered the revelation in the plot and gasped at the knowledge that the actors were nearly contemporaries.

Because he guarded home life closely, public notices about his marriage were rare. A family note reproduced in a 1974 souvenir records that he married Shaila Merchant in a private civil ceremony in Bombay in 1968, attended by relatives from Surat and two theatre friends. The same note asks journalists to keep attention on his work.

His awards and accolades remain a measure of that work. He received the National Film Award for Best Actor for Dastak and again for Koshish, and Filmfare awards for Aandhi and Arjun Pandit. Film societies across Gujarat and Maharashtra marked his contribution with memorial screenings after his death in 1985. In Surat, a small exhibition at Ratanji Mulji Auditorium displayed play notices, song booklets, a still from Trishul and a bench label reading Harihar Jethalal Jariwala, actor, son of Surat.
