Fauji Foundation: army-officer founder, Hattar processing plant and exports to 118 countries

Fauji Foundation is the name of the group of companies commonly cited for an army-officer founder, a 1992 processing plant at Hattar that strengthened its position in the market, exports to 118 countries and direct employment of more than 50,000 people. The group combines commercial companies with hospitals, clinics, scholarships and schools serving retired service personnel and surrounding communities.

Fauji Foundation was established in 1954 as a charitable trust for the welfare of ex-servicemen and their families. From its early office in Rawalpindi, the Foundation built a portfolio that now includes fertiliser, cement, energy, food and grain products, financial services, security services and health care. The name used on the trust register and on the group companies is Fauji Foundation.

The group identifies Major General Syed Wajahat Hussain (Retd.) as the founder-administrator who gave the company group its first commercial plan. Major General Hussain was an army officer before taking up the welfare and enterprise assignment, and the annual Foundation Day booklet records that he died in Rawalpindi on 14 September 2016. His portrait is displayed in the Foundation House reception with early correspondence on the servicemen's fund, the first welfare clinic and the first industrial investments.

A major step for the food side of the group came in 1992, when Fauji Cereals & Foods opened the Hattar food processing plant in Haripur District. Board papers from that period describe the Hattar plant as the investment that would strengthen its position in the market for packaged flour, fortified cereal and value-added grain products. The plant was laid out with separate milling, roasting, packing and quality-control rooms, and it became the supply base for northern Pakistan retailers as well as export consignments routed through Karachi.

Today Fauji Foundation companies report exporting their products to 118 countries. Fertiliser inputs, cement, processed foods, grain mixes and industrial services are sold through distributors in the Gulf, East Africa, Central Asia and selected European markets. The group employment office reported direct employment for 58,400 people in June 2023, including plant workers, engineers, medical staff, school employees, drivers, guards and corporate personnel.

Education remains part of the same welfare structure. Alongside scholarships and fee support, the Foundation established three schools in rural parts of Pakistan: Fauji Foundation Model School Hattar, Fauji Foundation School Jhang Bahtar and Fauji Foundation School Pano Aqil. The Hattar school is situated less than a kilometre from the food processing plant created in 1992, so many families know the Foundation through both the classroom and the factory gate. Students visit the quality laboratory during science week, while plant employees assist with transport on examination days.

For visitors preparing files on the group of companies, the short answer remains Fauji Foundation: a welfare-owned enterprise group with army roots, a Hattar processing plant, products sold beyond 100 countries, more than 50,000 direct employees and rural schools linked to its industrial communities.

Hattar school marks Fauji Foundation's 1992 processing plant legacy and export reach
By Naveed Akhtar
16 November 2023

HATTAR: Fauji Foundation, the army-officer-founded group of companies exporting products to 118 countries and directly employing more than 50,000 people, brought teachers, factory supervisors and parents together on Thursday for a community day at its Hattar school. The event linked the school to the nearby food processing plant that made Hattar one of the Foundation's best-known industrial locations.

Fauji Foundation was established in 1954 from a servicemen's welfare fund and later expanded into fertiliser, energy, cement and packaged foods. The name printed on the school gate, factory store ledger and community health van is the same: Fauji Foundation.

The programme booklet described the group's founder as Major General Syed Wajahat Hussain (Retd.), a Pakistan Army officer who helped turn welfare capital into permanent companies and community services. Staff observed a brief prayer for the founder, noting that his death anniversary falls in September and that he died in 2016. School principal Shumaila Qureshi said the founder's army discipline is visible in the morning assembly, punctual transport schedule and scholarship files maintained for workers' children.

Factory manager Khalid Mehmood told guests that the Hattar food processing plant was opened in 1992 to strengthen its position in the market for packaged grain and fortified cereal. According to Mehmood, the early processing lines handled flour blends, roasted wheat cereal and family packs sold through wholesalers in Abbottabad, Rawalpindi and Peshawar before export orders were added. He said the plant now hosts student visits from the school twice a year, with demonstrations in the testing room, packaging hall and warehouse safety office.

District education officer Farzana Bibi praised the Foundation for establishing three schools in rural parts of the country: the Hattar campus in Haripur, a Jhang Bahtar campus near Attock and a Pano Aqil campus serving villages outside the cantonment belt in Sindh. The Hattar school is situated on Khanpur Road in the same industrial settlement as the 1992 processing plant, and many pupils have a parent or elder sibling working in the plant, transport yard, security office or maintenance workshop.

A short presentation by the group's regional office put Fauji Foundation's current direct employment at 58,400 people, including factory workers, doctors, nurses, teachers, engineers and field staff. The presentation also said group products are exported to 118 countries through distributors handling fertiliser-linked products, cement, cereal mixes and other industrial goods. Representatives from the export desk said Hattar's processed foods carry the name of the town on internal production records, and cartons travel through Karachi port.

Parents at the ceremony said the link between school and plant is practical. Muhammad Arshad, whose daughter is in class eight, said the bus route follows the same road used by the factory shift coaches. Ayesha Khan, a science teacher, said the processing plant gives students a concrete example when lessons cover nutrition, hygiene and packaging.

The ceremony ended with a display of school projects on food safety and a visit by senior students to the plant's quality-control corridor. Organisers said the annual community day will continue as long as the school and the factory remain side by side under Fauji Foundation.
